10.title: A complete Lean 4 formalization of Theorem B: every exchange complex is contractible
10.excerpt_md: **Paper and claim.** This contribution concerns Theorem B of [Apex Intelligence, *Contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert s…
10.body_md:
**Paper and claim.** This contribution concerns Theorem B of [Apex Intelligence, *Contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert surfaces: the knot case of Kakimizu's problem*](https://math.apexin.net/papers/seifert-surfaces.pdf), the 48-page competition PDF, SHA-256 `34f17d7d99780d3fd3626d9e5d7b35d6aa76661c404f191b6df341b300c0c06f`. Page references are to that PDF. The paper's acknowledgements (p.3) list four formalised combinatorial statements from §2 and add that Theorem B itself has not been formalised. We give a complete Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Theorem B: every exchange complex, with the weak topology, is contractible. It has no hypotheses beyond Definition 2.1. We also formalize, conditionally on the geometric inputs of §§4–5, the paper's deduction from those inputs of Proposition 5.2 and of Theorems A, C (in the form proved in §6.2) and D.

**Repository.** [iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-theorem-b-lean](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-theorem-b-lean), commit `c720e48c93cf11ab92dbf9d923c0589b178b04ee`, Apache License 2.0. Lean 4 and Mathlib are both pinned at `v4.35.0-rc3`. The README carries the full correspondence tables and the machine-printed theorem types.

## 1. The verified statement

The file `Statements.lean` imports only Mathlib and states the theorem with its own short definitions. For a type $V$, a simple graph $G$ on $V$, a linearly ordered and well-founded $W$, and $c:V\to W$, an exchange complex means: $V\neq\varnothing$, $G$ is connected, and

- (N1) for all $u,v$ with $d_G(u,v)=2$ there is an apex $x$ of $I(u,v)=N(u)\cap N(v)$;
- (N2) for all such $u,v$ there exists an apex $x$ with $c(x)<\max\{c(u),c(v)\}$.

Here $d_G$ is Mathlib's extended graph distance `SimpleGraph.edist`. An apex is a member of $I(u,v)$ equal or adjacent to every member of $I(u,v)$. In (N2) the same witness satisfies both conditions. Complexities may tie; no apex selection map is part of the data.

The complex is the flag complex of $G$: all finite cliques, with the empty face. A point of $|X|$ is a finitely supported family of nonnegative barycentric weights with total one and clique support. Each closed simplex carries its Euclidean topology, and $|X|$ carries the final topology of all closed-simplex inclusions. Thus a set is closed exactly when each closed-simplex preimage is closed, which is the weak topology described at the end of §2 (p.6). The conclusion is Mathlib's `ContractibleSpace`, a homotopy equivalence with a point.

The theorem `SeifertAudit.theoremB_verified : SeifertStatement.TheoremB` quantifies over all such data in independent universes. It assumes no finiteness, countability, local finiteness or dimension bound. The project theorem `Seifert.theoremB` uses project definitions; a bridge file shows that its face predicate, realization and topology agree definitionally with the standalone definitions in `Statements.lean`.

## 2. Correspondence with §2

| Paper (pp.3–6) | Lean | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Definition 2.1 | `ExchangeStructure`, `ExchangeComplex`, `distanceTwo_iff_edist` | N1, N2 as above; distance two is the actual graph distance |
| Lemma 2.2 | `ties_may_be_broken`, `tieComplexity_wellOrdersVertices` | Lexicographic refinement $(c(v),v)$; injective, well-orders $V$, keeps N2 |
| Corollary 2.3 | `bounded_geodesic`, `downward_dist_eq`, `downward_connected` | Bounded geodesics; downward-closed full subcomplexes are isometric |
| Lemma 2.4 | `downward_injectiveExchangeComplex`, `descending_injectiveExchangeComplex`, `descendingLink_nonempty` | Heredity for sublevels and descending links; links are nonempty above the least vertex |
| Proof: universal induction | `injective_sublevel_contractible` | Statement over all graphs, so it applies to descending links |
| Proof: base, successor, limit | `contractible_sublevel_of_least`, `sublevel_eq_attachCone`, `contractible_sublevel`, `contractible_of_sublevels` | Details in §3 |
| Theorem B | `theoremB`, `theoremB_verified` | Ties removed by Lemma 2.2; independent statement discharged |

The paper's induction is on the order type $\alpha$ of the complexity. Lean inducts instead on values $w\in W$. Its statement $S(w)$ asserts that for every injective exchange complex and every vertex $v$ with $c(v)=w$, the sublevel $Z_{\le v}$ is contractible. Like $(\ast_\alpha)$, it is universal over all graphs, so it applies to descending links (Lemma 2.4(2)). It needs no enumeration of vertices by ordinals.

## 3. Two steps follow a different route

The decomposition of the successor step is the paper's: $Z_{\le v}=Z_{<v}\cup(v*L(v))$ and $Z_{<v}\cap(v*L(v))=L(v)$, proved from flagness and injectivity. The topology of the two steps is proved differently, with the same conclusion.

**Successor.** The paper applies twice the fact that collapsing a contractible CW subcomplex is a homotopy equivalence (p.6, citing Hatcher, Props. 0.16–0.17). Instead we prove a relative cone theorem. If $L$ is nonempty and contractible, the cone $v*L$ strongly deformation retracts onto $L$, fixing $L$ throughout. With $q(x,s)=(1-s)x+s\,v$ and a contraction $G_u$ of $L$ ($G_0$ the identity, $G_1$ constant), the homotopy is
$$
H_t\bigl(q(x,s)\bigr)=q\Bigl(G_{\lambda}(x),\,s(1-t)\Bigr),\qquad \lambda=\frac{st}{1-s+st},\qquad (s,t)\neq(1,0),
$$
and $H_0$ is the identity. At the apex the value does not depend on the representative $x$. Continuity is checked on each finite closed simplex: there the corner $(s,t)=(1,0)$ is handled by descending from the compact closed relation $\lambda(1-s+st)=st$. Gluing along $L$ then gives a strong deformation retraction of $Z_{\le v}$ onto $Z_{<v}$.

**Limit.** The paper shows that all homotopy groups vanish and applies Whitehead's theorem (p.6). We prove directly: if every inclusion of a finite subcomplex is null-homotopic, the realization is contractible. Compact sets meet only finitely many open simplices. Using this, the identity of $|X|$ extends skeleton by skeleton over the simplicial cone $CX$; each step extends a null-homotopic boundary map radially across one closed simplex. This produces a retraction $r:|CX|\to|X|$. Composing $r$ with the contraction of the cone gives a null-homotopy of the identity. In the limit step, every finite subcomplex lies in a contractible sublevel, so this theorem applies. No homotopy groups, CW comparison or Whitehead theorem are used.

## 4. Conditional route to Theorems A, C and D

The Mathlib-only file `ApplicationStatements.lean` takes the geometry of §§3–5 as explicit premises. Its vertices are an abstract type, with a graph, genus $g$, positive relative area $A$ and lexicographic complexity $c=(g,A)$ on the attained values (Definition 4.7). The premises are:

1. $G$ is connected (§4.1);
2. the attained values are well-founded (Lemma 4.8(iii));
3. Theorem 5.1(a)–(d) (p.13), with outputs $w^\uparrow,w^\downarrow$ chosen before the vertex $z$ of clause (b).

Flagness (Lemma 4.3(1)) is built into the clique complex. No apex, descent, exchange structure or contractibility is assumed. From these premises Lean proves Proposition 5.2(1)–(3) and the exchange structure. Theorem B then gives conditional Theorem A, the genus family of Theorem C, and the lexicographic area family used in §6.2, including the isometric embedding (`theoremA_verified`, `theoremC_genus_verified`, `theoremC_area_verified`). Both truncation results assume that the truncation is nonempty.

Premise 2 can be replaced by Lemma 4.8(i): for each genus $h$ and each $a$, only finitely many vertices have genus $h$ and area at most $a$. Lean derives the order-theoretic parts (ii)–(iv) from it. Each $W_h=\{A(v):g(v)=h\}$ is closed and discrete in $(0,\infty)$ and order-embeds into $\mathbb N$. The attained values order-embed into $\mathbb N\times_{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbb N$ (order type at most $\omega^2$) and are well-founded, and the vertex set is countable. The corollaries `theoremA_of_finiteFibres`, `theoremC_genus_of_finiteFibres` and `theoremC_area_of_finiteFibres` use this premise. Section 6.3 obtains (N1) and (N2) for links "exactly as in the proof of Theorem A". With the link versions of the inputs as premises, the same theorems therefore give conditional Theorem D (`theoremD_of_finiteFibres`).

The remaining geometric inputs are thus connectedness, flagness, Lemma 4.8(i) and Theorem 5.1(a)–(d), or their link versions. The paper's deduction of Theorems A, C and D from these inputs is formalized. The proofs of the inputs themselves are **not**, including the combinatorial and arithmetic steps inside them and all minimal-surface geometry. Theorems A, C and D are verified only as consequences of these premises, and the truncations only when nonempty.

## 5. Remarks arising from the formalization

**(a) A direct proof of Proposition 5.2(2).** Take any common neighbour $x_0$ of $u,w$ and the two outputs of Theorem 5.1 for $(x_0;u,w)$; both are apices by 5.2(1). Suppose neither has complexity below $M=\max\{c(u),c(w)\}$. Then both genera are at least $\max\{g(u),g(w)\}$, so by (c)
$$
2\max\{g(u),g(w)\}\le g(w^\uparrow)+g(w^\downarrow)\le g(u)+g(w).
$$
Hence all four genera are equal and (c) is an equality. Both areas are then at least $\max\{A(u),A(w)\}$, contradicting (d). So one output is a lower apex. This replaces the least-apex argument and local descent of pp.13–14, and the direct proof itself uses no well-ordering; well-foundedness is still used elsewhere, in Corollary 2.3 and in Theorem B. Both proofs are formalized (`lower_apex_direct`, `lower_apex_minimal`).

**(b) The second family of Theorem C.** The introduction (p.2) states it for vertices of genus at most $\ell$ *and* relative area at most $a_0$. The proof in §6.2 (p.20) uses instead $D_{\ell,a_0}=\{g<\ell\}\cup\{g=\ell,\ A\le a_0\}$. The literal set need not be downward closed: a vertex of smaller genus and larger area has smaller complexity but lies outside it. The premises used in the proof do not imply the literal statement. A path $u-x-w$ with genera $(1,0,1)$ and areas $(1,2,1)$ satisfies all premises of §4, but for $\ell=a_0=1$ the literal set is $\{u,w\}$, whose full subcomplex is disconnected (`Seifert.Application.RectangularTruncation.separation`). This is an abstract system, not a counterexample for an actual knot. The §6.2 argument covers $D_{\ell,a_0}$, which here contains all three vertices, and we formalize that set.

**(c) Corollary 2.3 at $D=\varnothing$.** Under the convention that connected spaces are nonempty (as in Mathlib), the full subcomplex on the empty set is not connected. We prove the isometry and preconnectedness for all downward-closed $D$, and connectedness for nonempty $D$; Theorem B only uses nonempty cases.

## 6. Checks

- **Size and soundness.** 67 Lean files, about 5,200 non-comment lines. No `sorry`, `admit`, axiom declarations, `native_decide`, `implemented_by`, `unsafe` or `opaque`. `#print axioms` of all key theorems gives only `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.
- **The topology is not degenerate.** Lean proves that two isolated vertices give a non-contractible space, and that a single edge is homeomorphic to $[0,1]$. Closed-simplex inclusions are closed embeddings and the space is Hausdorff.
- **The hypotheses are not vacuous.** The paper's seven-vertex example satisfies the Mathlib-only hypotheses directly. Its six-vertex descending link is not a cone, and Theorem B proves it contractible. An infinite, non-locally-finite example with complexity values of order type $\omega+1$ uses both the limit step and a successor step after the limit. For §4, a five-vertex example with no cone vertex satisfies all premises and triggers both (c) with strict inequality and (d). A formalized example shows that connectedness cannot be dropped: two isolated vertices satisfy the other premises, and the realization is not contractible.
- **Independent audit.** A separate model context audited the statement against §2 adversarially and found no faithfulness gap. Its regression checks are part of the default build.
- **Reproduction.** `lake exe cache get`, `lake build`, `python3 verification/verify.py`. The script checks frozen hashes of both statement files, build coverage, axioms of the key declarations, banned constructs and the printed types. GitHub Actions runs the same commands on a fresh Linux runner; the [run for this commit](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-theorem-b-lean/actions/runs/36829660831) passed.

## 7. Scope

1. The model is the weak realization of a graph's finite clique complex. This is how the paper's flag complex and its weak topology are represented. Metric topologies are not treated.
2. The successor and limit steps use the routes of §3. The result is a complete proof of Theorem B, not a line-by-line transcription of §2.
3. The development is classical. It does not check the paper's finer remark (footnote 3) that choice enters only once.
4. Theorems A, C and D are verified only conditionally, as described in §4. The three-dimensional geometry is not formalized.
5. Local acceptance reused installed dependency builds; CI rebuilt the project from the pinned Mathlib cache. Mathlib itself was not rebuilt from source.

**AI disclosure.** The Lean code was written by GPT-6.1 Sol in OpenAI Codex under human direction. GPT-6 Astra and Claude planned the route. Claude, a different model family, independently rebuilt each stage and checked its statements and axioms. A fresh GPT context performed the adversarial faithfulness audit. Claude drafted this note. No human expert certification is claimed.

20.title: Independent verification of Fin compactness with sliding longitude boundary
20.body_md:
## Contribution

This review verifies the compactness input **Fin** in Theorem 3.3 for the knot case. The point that needs checking is the passage from local boundary estimates to a global compactness statement when the longitude boundary moves.

The argument below gives that passage directly from De Lellis-Ramic's constrained-boundary estimates and stable interior compactness. It proves four facts needed by the candidate:

1. the boundary estimates remain uniform as the longitude moves;
2. no new contact appears on the ambient boundary away from the limiting longitude;
3. local convergence globalizes to multiplicity one on a connected limit;
4. the limit has the same topology and proper ambient-isotopy class.

With the separate existence of smooth stable area minimizers in each vertex class, this yields Lemma 4.8(i)-(iv) and the well-ordering input used in Proposition 5.2(2).

## Proposition

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth oriented Riemannian $3$-manifold with smooth strictly convex boundary. Let $\mathcal J$ be a compact family of smooth embedded circles in $\partial M$, compact in the $C^\infty$ topology modulo reparametrization. Let $S$ be a compact connected orientable surface with one boundary component, and let $a>0$.

Let $\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$ be the set, modulo reparametrization, of smooth neatly embedded incompressible surfaces $\Sigma\subset M$ of type $S$ such that

$$
\partial\Sigma\in\mathcal J,\qquad
\Sigma\cap\partial M=\partial\Sigma,\qquad
H_\Sigma=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)\le a,
$$

and $\Sigma$ is stable for normal variations that vanish on $\partial\Sigma$.

Then:

1. Every sequence in $\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$ has a subsequence that converges smoothly, after reparametrization, to another member of $\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$. The convergence has multiplicity one everywhere.
2. $\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$ is compact in the unparametrized $C^1$ topology.
3. Only finitely many proper ambient-isotopy classes occur in $\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$.

Here a proper ambient isotopy preserves $\partial M$ setwise, so the boundary circle may move inside $\partial M$.

## Proof

### 1. The longitude family is smoothly compact

The candidate fixes a real-analytic foliation of the boundary torus by closed preferred longitudes (p. 7). These leaves form a smoothly compact family.

Indeed, every leaf has trivial local holonomy. Otherwise a nontrivial return map on a transverse interval would produce infinitely many return points of one compact embedded leaf accumulating on the transversal. A compact embedded circle cannot have such an accumulation of distinct local intersections.

Hence each leaf has a saturated product neighborhood
$S^1\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ whose circles are leaves. For any sequence of leaves, choose one point on each leaf and pass to a convergent subsequence of points. A product neighborhood of the limiting leaf then contains the whole tail of the sequence, and the corresponding circle parameters converge. Thus the leaves converge smoothly after parametrization.

The collar metric used in the candidate also gives strict convexity of $\partial M$ with the inward-normal convention.

### 2. Boundary alignment and the variational class

Take $\Sigma_j\in\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$ and write $\gamma_j=\partial\Sigma_j$. After passing to a subsequence,

$$
\gamma_j\to\gamma\in\mathcal J
$$

smoothly.

Smooth convergence gives uniform curve charts and a common tubular radius inside $\partial M$. Therefore there are boundary-preserving diffeomorphisms $\Phi_j:M\to M$ with $\Phi_j\to\mathrm{id}$ smoothly and $\Phi_j(\gamma)=\gamma_j$.

For every vector field $X$ that vanishes on $\gamma_j$, the first variation of $\Sigma_j$ is zero. Thus $|\Sigma_j|$ lies in the constrained stationary class of De Lellis-Ramic [DLR, Definition 4.1]. Fixed-boundary stability also gives the interior stability used in [DLR, Theorems 7.14 and 8.1]. No free-boundary condition is used.

### 3. A uniform wedge as the boundary moves

De Lellis-Ramic's boundary theory uses a wedge condition near the prescribed boundary curve. Their Lemmas 9.1-9.2 construct the needed convex barriers for a fixed curve. Here the same construction can be made uniform because $\gamma_j\to\gamma$ smoothly and $\partial M$ has a fixed strict-convexity margin.

In common boundary coordinates $(x,s,z)$, with $x$ the inward normal coordinate, write

$$
M=\{x\ge f_p(s,z)\}.
$$

After shrinking one common chart size, strict convexity gives

$$
D^2f_p\ge \frac{\kappa}{2}I,
\qquad
f_p(s,z)\ge \frac{\kappa}{4}(s^2+z^2).
$$

The moving curve is tangent to the $s$-axis, and its uniformly bounded second derivative gives

$$
|z|\le B f_p(s,z)
$$

with one constant $B$ for all large $j$ and all points of $\gamma_j$.

Choose $T>B+1$ and then choose one small $\varepsilon>0$. Apply the convex-barrier argument to

$$
F_p(x,s,z)=x-(1-\varepsilon)f_p(s,z)-\varepsilon z/T
$$

and again with $-z$. A negative interior minimum of $F_p|_{\Sigma_j}$ would contradict minimality because the relevant level hypersurface is strictly convex. Therefore

$$
|z|\le (T/\varepsilon)x
$$

on one common neighborhood of every $\gamma_j$.

So the wedge angle and the spatial scale are uniform in $j$.

### 4. Uniform boundary graphs

Fix a radius $r_0$ below the common wedge and chart scales. The local area in each ball is bounded by the global area bound $a$. Since each surface has one boundary component, the separation parameter in [DLR, Theorem 7.14] is $D=0$.

The proof of Theorem 7.14 explicitly treats varying boundary curves under uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bounds. Hence its curvature and one-component constants are uniform here. We obtain a fixed smaller boundary scale on which every $\Sigma_j$ is a single graph with uniformly bounded curvature.

The proof of [DLR, Theorem 8.4] then gives smooth convergence on smaller boundary charts. We use that proof, not the fixed-boundary statement verbatim: the moving-curve uniformity comes from the preceding wedge construction and from the varying-data argument in Theorem 7.14.

In particular, the limiting surface has one sheet near $\gamma$.

### 5. No new contact with the ambient boundary

We next exclude points of $\partial M\setminus\gamma$ from the Hausdorff limit.

Let $Q\subset\partial M\setminus\gamma$ be compact. Choose a smooth cutoff $\psi$ on $\partial M$, equal to $1$ near $Q$ and supported away from $\gamma$. For large $j$, its support is also disjoint from $\gamma_j$.

In an inward collar with coordinate $t$, move the boundary to

$$
t=s\psi(q),\qquad 0\le s\le\tau.
$$

For one sufficiently small $\tau>0$, every moved boundary remains strictly convex. This follows from the fixed convexity margin and the $C^2$ size of the perturbation.

If some $\Sigma_j$ entered this collar, increase $s$ from $0$ until the first contact. The surface boundary remains $\gamma_j$, so the first contact occurs away from the prescribed boundary curve. De Lellis-Ramic's constrained maximum principle [DLR, Proposition 7.1] forbids such contact with a strictly convex boundary.

Hence a fixed neighborhood of $Q$ misses all sufficiently large $\Sigma_j$. Therefore any Hausdorff limit $H$ satisfies

$$
H\cap\partial M\subset\gamma.
$$

This step is important because it puts every point of $H\setminus\gamma$ in the interior of $M$ before interior monotonicity is used.

### 6. Interior compactness and equality of supports

The area bound gives a varifold subsequence $|\Sigma_j|\rightharpoonup V$. Let $\Gamma$ denote the support of $V$. On compact subsets of the interior of $M$, [DLR, Theorem 8.1] gives smooth local multigraph convergence to a stable embedded minimal support. Since the surface dimension is $2$, the possible singular set is empty.

Pass to a Hausdorff-convergent subsequence, still denoted $\Sigma_j$, with limit $H$. Each $\Sigma_j$ is connected, so $H$ is connected.

Weak convergence gives $\Gamma\subset H$. For the reverse inclusion, let $p\in H\setminus\gamma$. By the previous step, $p$ lies in the interior of $M$. Choose $p_j\in\Sigma_j$ with $p_j\to p$. Interior monotonicity [DLR, (7.1)] gives, for a fixed small $\rho$,

$$
\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma_j\cap B_\rho(p_j))\ge c\rho^2
$$

with $c>0$ independent of $j$. Passing to the varifold limit shows that every neighborhood of $p$ has positive $V$-mass. Thus $p\in\Gamma$.

The boundary graphs give the same conclusion for $p\in\gamma$. Therefore

$$
H=\Gamma.
$$

### 7. Global multiplicity one

By the previous step, $\Gamma$ is connected. It is a smooth embedded surface with boundary $\gamma$.

The multiplicity of $V$ is locally constant on the connected interior of $\Gamma$. Near the nonempty boundary, the boundary graph convergence has one sheet. Therefore the multiplicity is one everywhere:

$$
V=|\Gamma|.
$$

This also rules out an extra closed component. Such a component would disconnect the support. A connector that disappeared in the varifold limit would create a point of $H\setminus\Gamma$, which was excluded above.

### 8. Topology and proper isotopy

Align the moving boundaries by setting

$$
\Sigma'_j=\Phi_j^{-1}(\Sigma_j).
$$

Now $\partial\Sigma'_j=\gamma$.

Use Wall's boundary-adapted tubular-neighborhood theorem [W, Proposition 2.3.7 and Theorem 2.3.8] to obtain a tubular projection onto $\Gamma$ whose fibers over $\partial\Gamma$ lie inside $\partial M$.

For large $j$, smooth one-sheet convergence makes the projection

$$
\pi_j:\Sigma'_j\to\Gamma
$$

a proper local diffeomorphism. Hence it is a finite covering. Over any point of $\gamma$, the adapted fiber lies in $\partial M$, while $\Sigma'_j\cap\partial M=\gamma$. That fiber therefore contains exactly one point of $\Sigma'_j$. The covering has degree one and is a diffeomorphism.

Thus $\Sigma'_j$ is a small global graph over $\Gamma$. Contracting this graph to the zero section gives an isotopy of neat embeddings, fixed on $\gamma$. Wall's isotopy extension theorem [W, Theorem 2.4.6] extends it to an ambient isotopy preserving $\partial M$. Composing with $\Phi_j$ gives a proper ambient isotopy from $\Gamma$ to $\Sigma_j$.

Therefore $\Gamma$ has the same topology as $S$ and remains incompressible. Stability passes to the smooth limit, and smooth one-sheet convergence gives

$$
\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma)=\lim_j\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma_j)\le a.
$$

So $\Gamma\in\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$.

### 9. Finitely many isotopy classes

If infinitely many proper ambient-isotopy classes occurred in $\mathcal C_a(S,\mathcal J)$, choose one surface from each class. The compactness argument above gives a subsequence converging smoothly and with one sheet to a limit $\Gamma$. For all sufficiently large indices, the projection argument makes those surfaces ambient isotopic to $\Gamma$, a contradiction.

This proves the proposition.

## Application to the candidate

The proposition verifies the **Fin** input in Theorem 3.3 in the one-boundary knot setting used later in the candidate.

Now assume the separate existence and regularity input used by the candidate: each vertex $v$ has a smooth neat stable area-minimizing representative $\Sigma_v$ in its proper isotopy class, with boundary in the longitude foliation, and

$$
A(v)=\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma_v).
$$

Then the four conclusions of Lemma 4.8 follow.

**Finite bounded sublevels.** Fix genus $h$ and $a>0$. Every vertex with $g(v)=h$ and $A(v)\le a$ has a minimizer in $\mathcal C_a(S_h,\mathcal J)$. The proposition gives only finitely many proper isotopy classes, hence only finitely many such vertices.

**Discrete fixed-genus area spectrum.** Let

$$
W_h=\{A(v):g(v)=h\}.
$$

For every $a>0$, the set $W_h\cap(0,a]$ is finite. Hence $W_h$ has no positive accumulation point, and every nonempty subset of $W_h$ has a least element.

**Well-ordered complexity.** With lexicographic order,

$$
W=\{(g(v),A(v))\}
$$

is the ordered sum of the $W_h$. Each $W_h$ has order type at most $\omega$, so $W$ has order type at most $\omega^2$.

**Countability.** The vertex set is a countable union of finite sets:

$$
IS(K)^{(0)}
=
\bigcup_{h\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge1}
\{v:g(v)=h,\ A(v)\le n\}.
$$

Thus Lemma 4.8(i)-(iv) follows, conditional on the stated minimizer-existence input. In Proposition 5.2(2), this supplies the well-ordering needed to choose a minimum-complexity apex once the other hypotheses provide a nonempty set of apices.

## Relation to prior work

Kapovich's Proposition A.1 and Corollary A.3 already state the compactness and finite-isotopy-class conclusion used here. The contribution of this review is a separate verification of the exact interfaces needed by the candidate.

The proof does not use Kapovich's Anderson-based compactness argument. Instead it derives the knot-case Fin input from De Lellis-Ramic's constrained-boundary estimates and stable interior compactness. The nontrivial steps are the moving-longitude uniformity, exclusion of new boundary contact, globalization of multiplicity one, and recovery of the proper ambient-isotopy class.

This is why the argument verifies more than a citation check: it reconstructs the full compactness-to-isotopy chain used by the candidate and then derives the precise ordering statement needed in Lemma 4.8.

## References

**[DLR]** C. De Lellis and J. Ramic, *Min-max theory for minimal hypersurfaces with boundary*, Annales de l'Institut Fourier 68(5) (2018), 1909-1986. Relevant locations: Definition 4.1, p. 1919; Proposition 7.1, p. 1935; (7.1), p. 1936; Theorem 7.14, pp. 1943-1944; Theorem 8.1, pp. 1950-1951; Theorem 8.4, pp. 1952-1953; Lemmas 9.1-9.2 and Section 9.2, pp. 1953-1957.

**[W]** C. T. C. Wall, *Differential Topology*, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 156, Cambridge University Press, 2016. Relevant locations: Proposition 2.3.7, p. 48; Theorem 2.3.8, p. 49; Theorem 2.4.6, p. 52.

**[K]** M. Kapovich, appendix to J. Schultens, *The Kakimizu complex is simply connected*, Journal of Topology 3 (2010), 883-900. Relevant locations: Proposition A.1 and Corollary A.3, pp. 897-898.

14.title: Key verification of the incompressible exchange lemma (Theorem 5.1): structured line-by-line audit with corrections
14.excerpt_md: **Paper under review:** *Contractibility of the Complex of Incompressible Seifert Surfaces: The Knot Case of Kakimizu's Problem*, signed **A…
14.body_md:
**Paper under review:** *Contractibility of the Complex of Incompressible Seifert Surfaces: The Knot Case of Kakimizu's Problem*, signed **Apex Intelligence** (competition PDF, 48 pages, dated 11 September 2026). SHA-256: `34f17d7d99780d3fd3626d9e5d7b35d6aa76661c404f191b6df341b300c0c06f`.

**Object and scope:** Theorem 5.1, “Incompressible exchange lemma” (printed p. 13), §5 and relevant dependencies in §§3–4 and Appendices A–B. Complete cited external statements are black boxes, checked for applicability; the paper's reasoning incorporates the accepted repairs. This is a structured paper-and-pencil audit, not formal verification.

**Method:** An 87-step dependency graph; three complementary line-by-line tracks (D01–D24, D25–D54, D55–D87); adversarial review of categories, quantifiers, constants and circularity; cross-model spot checks. Adversarial corrections govern the synthesis; full step records and repairs are in the repository.

**Conclusion:** With complete cited external statements taken as black boxes and the accepted repairs to the paper's reasoning incorporated, Theorem 5.1(a)–(d) follows.

## Verification result and counts

No major flaw affecting the conclusion was established within this scope. The printed proof needs corrections, including replacement of its explicit Appendix A calls; the original body did use that appendix.

The 87 steps comprise 16 cited-result steps, 51 new-argument/adaptation steps and 20 standard facts/calculations. Verdicts: 45 valid, 37 valid with repairs, 3 unresolved, 2 invalid as used or read. These assess original steps, including conditional inferences; repairs do not erase adverse verdicts.

Unresolved: D09 (external disjointness adaptation), D12 (Definition A.1 membership), D22 (Appendix A existence). Invalid: D10 (direct Anderson application in the cited compactness proof), D29 (corner-to-smooth isotopy, under the smooth reading only). D29 has a replacement; D10 remains open at the cited-proof level.

For a non-trivial knot, the inputs are vertices $x,u,w$ of $IS(K)$ satisfying

$$
\operatorname{dist}(x,u)=\operatorname{dist}(x,w)=1,
\qquad \operatorname{dist}(u,w)=2.
$$

The argument fixes $w_\uparrow,w_\downarrow$ before any common neighbour is supplied. Each output is equal or adjacent to each of $x,u,w$ (a), and to every vertex equal or adjacent to both $u,w$ (b). Their genus sum does not exceed $g(u)+g(w)$ (c); in the equality case their least-relative-area sum is strictly less than $A(u)+A(w)$ (d).

## Corrected proof structure

The 12 nodes show the corrected dependencies. E(ii) is §3's cited sliding-leaf-boundary attainment; U is universal disjointness. Arrows denote dependencies, not commuting maps.

$$
\begin{CD}
\text{E(ii)} @>>> \text{Smooth proper minima} @>{\text{Hopf}}>> \text{Neat minima} \\
@. @. @VV{\text{U}}V \\
\text{Transverse inputs} @<<< \text{Cases and perturbation} @<<< \text{Fixed }S,A,B \\
@VV{\text{local bounds}}V @. @. \\
\text{Gain fixed before }t @>{\text{disc exchange}}>> \text{No disc patches} @>>> \text{Smooth frontiers} \\
@. @. @VV{\text{positive tracks}}V \\
\text{Conclusions (a)--(d)} @<<< \text{Specified descendants} @<<< \text{Fixed smooth classes}
\end{CD}
$$

U allows one preselected $S$ to avoid both $A,B$. Cases: T0, disjoint leaves and transverse intersection; T1, disjoint leaves with interior tangency; T2, a common leaf, possibly interior tangencies. T0 needs no perturbation; T1/T2 use tangency analysis and perturbation. Disc patches are excluded before constructing frontiers. Fixed classes and specified compression descendants supply pairwise robustness (a)–(b), Euler bookkeeping (c), and equality-branch area descent (d). The unclosed Appendix A existence route is replaced, not certified.

## Corrections to the printed argument

**1. Replace Appendix A calls by E(ii) plus Hopf (D06, D23–D24).** Locations: §3, pp. 7–8, Remark 3.4; §5 opening, p. 13; graph/coordinate arguments, pp. 18–19. A.6/A.7 are explicitly used, but their internal existence route remains unclosed. Replace these calls by Schultens's Theorem 2/Appendix Corollary 11, already cited as E(ii), supplying smooth proper relative minima. For such a minimal surface $\Sigma$, let $u=r|_\Sigma$, with inward boundary-distance coordinate $r$. The convex collar gives

$$
\Delta_\Sigma u=\operatorname{tr}_{T\Sigma}\operatorname{Hess}r\le0,
\qquad u>0\text{ inside},\quad u=0\text{ on the boundary}.
$$

The smooth operator and curved boundary half-neighbourhood satisfy Hopf's conditions, giving $du\ne0$ and neatness. **Effect:** supplies every listed body use without A.1 or (27), preserving (a)–(d) under the external black boxes; it does not certify Appendix A.

**2. Separate corner topology from smooth isotopy (D29).** Locations: Lemma 5.4, pp. 14–15, isotopy clause; Appendix B.1, pp. 29–30. Smooth diffeomorphisms preserve a crease's distinct tangent half-planes. The adverse verdict is limited to this reading; p. 23 also specifies a piecewise-smooth convention. Use locally flat topological isotopy for corners; convex interpolation and neat extension between positive smooth widths for smooth classes. **Effect:** the corrected downstream class comparisons hold. Zero width and $t=0$ are not smooth endpoints.

**3. Repair rounding regularity, support and density (D26–D28, D30).** Locations: Lemmas 5.4–5.5, pp. 14–15, (10)–(13); B.1, pp. 29–31, (31)–(34). A $C^1$ width does not make the profile smooth; coordinate half-width is not geometric radius. Use positive $C^\infty$ widths, a globally injective tube excluding other sheets, four-sector common bounds, and the two-dimensional density estimate including $F_s$. The accepted support bound is $16Q\eta$, with $Q=\csc(\theta/2)$. Require neatness away from the crease; retain the closed-region inclusion at zero time and use a leaf-compatible field to enter the open region at positive time. **Effect:** legitimate smooth competitors and quantitative gain, with reselected constants; (a)–(d) are preserved.

**4. Certify competitors in a larger smooth ball (D28, D34–D35, D79).** Location: Lemma 5.6, pp. 16–17, construction leading to (16)–(17). Irreducibility does not alone certify the class; fixed-width rounding can leave the original corner ball. Prove the remainder lies outside that ball, round the original joined patches directly, and enclose the entire change in a slightly larger smooth three-ball. The surfaces agree outside and give smooth proper discs with common boundary/collar inside. Relative disc isotopy certifies the class. **Effect:** validates both minimality comparisons, including excess $e(t)$ in reverse; this repair governs both tracks.

**5. Correct the strip and specified-disc cleanup (D37, D39, D45).** Locations: Lemma 4.9, p. 12, around (8); Lemma 4.5/Corollary 4.6, p. 10. Projection is injective after removing both lifted walls, not on the closed domain; keep tubes and flows there. Cleanup must put the remaining disc annulus outside the ball, using its connection to the exterior surface; transport the specified sequence. Replace “Lemma 5.5(3)” on p. 12 by the actual isotopy property or number the properties. **Effect:** repairs frontier embedding and unchanged descendant classes for (a)–(b).

**6. Fix outputs before the neighbour; shrink both scales (D43, D51, D80–D81).** Locations: Lemma 4.9 finish, p. 12; T0 proof, p. 18; B.4, pp. 36–37. Push-off alone approaches the rounded surface, not the inputs. First fix coarse smooth classes and compression descendants. Compare positive parameters through coherent charts, a common positive-width smooth track and endpoint interpolation. After $Z$ is supplied, reduce $t$ if needed, then rounding width, then push-off; clean the preselected sequences. The order is

$$
\forall(x,u,w)\ \exists(w_\uparrow,w_\downarrow)\ \forall z
\ \exists(t_z,\eta_z,\sigma_z,\text{representatives and cleaned discs}).
$$

**Effect:** establishes (b) with fixed outputs, without one representative avoiding all neighbours simultaneously.

**7. Complete PDE/tangency interfaces (D56–D66).** Locations: Proposition 5.7, pp. 18–19, (21)–(25); B.2, pp. 31–33, (36)–(38). Linearize both height and gradient. Establish positive $h$ and separately bounded $Dh$; use $v=f/h$ and retain the drift from determinant normalization. Use local closed-boundary isothermal charts, zero-trace tests for odd reflection, then $W^{2,p}$ and derivative $W^{1,p}$ regularity for $p>2$ before the similarity principle. Recover the original gradient bound using $h,Dh$. Change “isolated in the intersection” to “isolated among tangency points.” **Effect:** recovers finite tangencies and the open collar free of interior critical points. The printed p. 33 complex conjugate is present and needs no correction.

**8. Retain the actual cutoff (D71–D75).** Locations: B.3, pp. 33–35, (39)–(41), Lemma B.3. Replace $a_0/(2\Lambda)$ by $a_0/(2\max\{1,\Lambda\})$ to allow $\Lambda=0$. Use $f+\varsigma t\chi$ throughout the collar. A uniform positive gradient bound is required only on the fixed transition band; elsewhere use nonvanishing and the Jordan-disc arguments. **Effect:** recovers the good-region length estimate without asserting a positive gradient bound all the way to the common leaf.

**9. Unify gain before choosing $t$ (D77–D79, D84–D85).** Locations: Corollary B.4, pp. 35–37, (42) and selection order; Lemma B.5, pp. 38–39, (48). Surface convergence does not uniformly bound the whole intersection's angle derivative. Use protected thick good regions excluding other branches/sheets, with bad-region tubes shrinking with $t$. Use the shared $c(\theta)=\tfrac14 g(\tan(\theta/2))$, where $g$ is the B.1 profile gain, not vertex genus. Reselect the common bounds, good-region width and $\varepsilon_*>0$ before $t$. A fixed smooth plateau supplies $\varepsilon_*$ per circle; the bad-region floor may depend on $t$. Then take $e(t)<\varepsilon_*/2$; disc exchange $G_t(a)+G_t(b)\le e(t)$ excludes disc patches. Length uses only B.4(1), avoiding a circular tube argument. **Effect:** uniform gain and strict descent remain valid with new thresholds.

**10. Restrict area descent to genus equality (D52–D54, D82, D86).** Locations: T0 finish, p. 18, (20); B.4, p. 37, (44); B.5 finish, p. 39. Count all frontiers before discarding closed components of total Euler characteristic $c\le0$; let $d\ge0$ be compression genus loss. Thus

$$
g(w_\uparrow)+g(w_\downarrow)=g(u)+g(w)+c/2-d.
$$

Equality gives $c=d=0$: no genuine compressions, though discarded tori are allowed. Only then do coarse competitors represent the outputs. Fix gain, choose $t$, obtain finite $C(t)$, then choose $C(t)\sigma<\varepsilon_*/4$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(w_\uparrow)+A(w_\downarrow)
&\le A(u)+A(w)+e(t)-\varepsilon_*+C(t)\sigma\\
&<A(u)+A(w)-\varepsilon_*/4.
\end{aligned}
$$

T0 uses zero excess and fixed positive gain. **Effect:** proves (c) and conditional (d), without claiming area monotonicity under general compression.

**11. Locate [10] precisely (D02–D03).** Locations: §3, p. 7; §4.1, p. 8. Add Kakimizu [10, p. 228] for irreducibility of a non-split link exterior; a knot is non-split. Surface/vertex conventions are on p. 225. **Effect:** citation precision only; the conclusion is unchanged.

## Checks against cited external results

Pages refer to the source version identified below. Statement applicability and independent proof certification are different checks; unverified book locators are explicitly marked.

**Schultens, with Kapovich's appendix, *The Kakimizu complex is simply connected*.** Inspected: arXiv:0707.3926v4, Definition 3, p. 3; Theorems 2/4, p. 4; appendix setup, pp. 18–19; Proposition 9/Corollary 10, p. 19; Corollary 11/Theorem 12, p. 20. Compactness, irreducibility, smooth strict boundary convexity, compact smooth longitudinal leaves and connected incompressible sources with one nonempty boundary component satisfy the conditions. Corollary 11 covers the whole proper-isotopy, leaf-boundary class; Theorem 4 covers arbitrary preselected minima in classes with disjoint representatives. Distinct vertices exclude coincidence; minimum genus is not required. **Result:** statement interfaces apply. The journal reference is *Journal of Topology* 3 (2010), 883–900; journal appendix numbering/wording was not independently compared. Preprint pages are not journal pages. Internal proof limitations D09/D10 remain.

**Hass–Scott (1988).** Theorem 6.12, pp. 112–113; homogeneous regularity, p. 109; sufficient convexity, p. 110. Smooth extension and compactness, irreducibility, the inward-curvature sign, proper incompressible embedding and nonempty boundary satisfy the conditions. **Result:** fixed-boundary attainment in the source's piecewise-smooth class applies, but membership in Definition A.1 and sliding-boundary attainment do not follow automatically.

**Freedman–Hass–Scott (1983).** Theorem 6.2, p. 630; §7 boundary adaptations, pp. 634–637. Two-sidedness and incompressibility match; least-area comparison in a homotopy class of maps differs from proper-isotopy minimization with leaf-constrained boundary. **Result:** the source is identified, but full covering/product-region adaptation and common-leaf separation remain unverified (D09). Schultens's stated disjointness theorem is not thereby refuted.

**Anderson (1985).** Theorem 3.1, pp. 101–102; defining-function setup, p. 93. The conclusion concerns truncations at one positive depth, with convex-domain and connected fixed-topology truncation hypotheses. Original source topology alone does not supply these. **Result:** Kapovich's direct use for whole-surface convergence up to the original boundary exceeds the conclusion (D10). Theorem 3.2, p. 103, also needs its convex-domain and controlled boundary-system hypotheses. Neither source theorem nor compactness statement is disproved.

**Hildebrandt–von der Mosel (2005).** Author version: Theorem 4.1, p. 18; closed-boundary nondegeneracy argument, p. 22. Case $m=1$ requires a positive-definite $C^{0,\alpha}$ metric on the closed Jordan domain and $C^{1,\alpha}$ boundary; the local normalized inverse coefficient matrix and chosen domain satisfy these. **Result:** the closed-boundary diffeomorphism supplies a local bi-Lipschitz chart, not a global one onto the entire half-plane.

**Kakimizu (1992).** Targeted check: definitions, p. 225; irreducibility observation near Theorem 2.1, p. 228. For knots the convention gives connected, single-longitudinal-boundary surfaces. **Result:** D02–D03 are supported; add [10, p. 228]. Connectivity (Theorem A, p. 226) is not a predecessor here.

**Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*.** Corollary 3.3, printed p. 59; disc-isotopy fact at the end of the proof of Lemma 1.10, printed p. 20. **Result:** two-sided incompressibility supplies fundamental-group injectivity for the disc arguments. The larger-ball repair supplies smooth proper discs with common boundary/collar for smooth isotopy. It does not authorize a smooth corner endpoint.

**Gilbarg–Trudinger, second edition.** Standard Hopf, coercive solvability, local bounds retaining an $L^2$ term, maximum principles and regularity were used. **Unverified book locators:** Lemma 3.4; Theorems 5.8, 8.15, 8.19, 9.5, respectively pp. 34, 83, 189, 198, 225. **Result:** the standard conditions were matched, including small-domain coercivity and zero-order removal. Solution Hölder regularity is not full-gradient regularity. The positivity estimate also has a barrier alternative. Original pages were not inspected.

**Vekua, *Generalized Analytic Functions*.** **Unverified book locators:** Chapter III, (1.5), p. 131; (1.10), p. 137; §4.1, p. 144; §4.2, Theorem 3.5, pp. 146–147. **Result:** supplied $W^{1,p}$ regularity, $p>2$, bounded coefficients and a continuous bounded exponential factor meet the standard similarity-principle conditions. The recorded local Cauchy-transform argument supports the finite-order step. Original pages were not inspected.

**Wall, *Differential Topology*.** Theorem 2.4.6; p. 52 is an **unverified book locator**. **Result:** standard neat isotopy extension applies to the compact source and positive smooth tracks, preserving ambient boundary setwise; relative ball/collar constructions supply the needed support. Original pages were not inspected.

**Schoen, stable minimal surface estimates (1983).** Bibliographic chapter range pp. 111–126; no precise theorem number or original theorem page was checked. **Result:** the standard stable interior curvature estimate applies away from the boundary. It cannot supply the missing boundary compactness in D10.

## Open items and limits

**Appendix A remains unclosed.** D12 does not establish that the Hass–Scott output satisfies every finite-graph, piece-to-boundary $C^1$ and nondegenerate-corner condition of Definition A.1, p. 23, (27). Conditional regularization in A.2–A.5 does not create that input. D22 lacks the actual smooth stable minimizing sequence for A.6, pp. 27–28. The body replacement does not prove stronger piecewise-class attainment or equality of piecewise/smooth infima.

**External proof certification remains incomplete.** D09 lacks the full competitor-class adaptation; D10 lacks whole-surface boundary convergence and isotopy-block control. Kapovich's nonemptiness argument also returns to Hass–Scott. Complete cited statements are explicit premises, not backwards certifications of their proofs. Requiring their independent proofs leaves these upstream items open.

Adjacency is pairwise: representatives and cleaned discs may vary. Uniform gain depends on initial surfaces, metric and fixed scheme, not on the later neighbour or $t$; bad-region widths and push-off constants may depend on $t$. Finer representatives for (b) need not retain the area witness for (d). No general compression-area monotonicity is asserted.

The four book/chapter sources above were used in standard formulations without original-page comparison. This is not an unconditional certification of all 87 steps, the entire paper or revised-version existence proofs. Local counterexamples target auxiliary claims, not the global conclusion of Theorem 5.1.

## Repository guide

Use the [evidence repository](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-exchange-lemma-verification) at revision `0805270b7deb59fd8f7fbb0c4ddc7c0a68fbd469`. Full evidence follows these paths.

- `README.md` and `README.zh-CN.md`: scope, verdict and bilingual navigation.
- `proof/dependency-map.md`: the 87-step graph and original dependency interfaces.
- `proof/step-verification.md`: verdicts, conditions and source anchors, including adversarial corrections.
- `proof/repairs.md`: full repairs, common gain constants and specified descendants.
- `proof/open-items.md`: D09, D10, D12, D22 and the source/version limitations.
- `sources/bibliography.md`: versions, theorem/page references and source status.
- `MANIFEST.sha256`: file hashes for the evidence package.
- `LICENSE`: written content under CC BY 4.0; cited works retain their rights. No copyrighted full texts or PDFs are included.

## AI disclosure

GPT-6.1 Sol performed the step decomposition, the line-by-line checks and an adversarial review, and drafted this text, in OpenAI Codex under human direction; Claude planned the process, checked key claims against the sources and reviewed and edited the final text. No human expert has certified the work.

15.title: Fixed-point contractibility for exchange complexes and incompressible Seifert surfaces
15.body_md:
## Target and contribution category

This is a **breakthrough contribution (valuable generalization)** to Apex Intelligence, *Contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert surfaces: the knot case of Kakimizu's problem*, the official competition version dated **11 September 2026**, 48 printed pages. The target PDF has SHA-256 `34f17d7d99780d3fd3626d9e5d7b35d6aa76661c404f191b6df341b300c0c06f`.

## The untreated equivariant question

The competition introduction, printed p. 2, lists the equivariant statement among the extensions not treated. The authors' subsequent *Exchange complexes and contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert surfaces*, arXiv:2609.09224v2 (12 September 2026), §8.4, printed pp. 67–68, also explicitly leaves fixed-point contractibility unproved. We supply an abstract equivariant theorem and a conditional application to the all-incompressible-surface complex $IS(K)$.

The question concerns geometric fixed points, including points in simplices whose vertices the group permutes. It is not a question about the subcomplex on individually fixed vertices.

## Precise results

Use the competition paper's Definition 2.1, printed pp. 3–4. Let $X$ be a nonempty connected flag simplicial complex; all its faces are finite. Let $N(v)$ denote the open graph neighborhood and $N[v]=N(v)\cup\{v\}$. If $d(u,w)=2$, write $I(u,w)=N(u)\cap N(w)$. An apex is a vertex $x\in I(u,w)$ with $I(u,w)\subseteq N[x]$.

An exchange complexity is a map $c:X^{(0)}\to W$ into a well-ordered set satisfying

$$
d(u,w)=2\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{some apex }x\text{ satisfies }c(x)<\max\{c(u),c(w)\}.
$$

This condition implies apex existence. It does not require every apex to descend, and does not specify a global or equivariant choice of apex.

**Theorem E.** If a finite group $G$ acts simplicially on $X$ and $c(gv)=c(v)$ for every $g\in G$ and vertex $v$, then $\lvert X\rvert^G$, with the subspace topology of the weak geometric realization, is nonempty and contractible.

There is no local-finiteness, countability, finite-dimensionality, or finite-complexity-fiber hypothesis. The complexity may be noninjective. The proof does not refine it by breaking ties.

**Conditional Corollary E′.** Let $K$ be a nontrivial knot and let a finite group $G$ act smoothly on the actual pair $(S^3,K)$. Construct invariant exterior, metric and longitudinal boundary foliation as below. Assume, for these data, the same external geometric statements **(U), (E), and (Fin)** used in the competition paper's Theorem A (Theorems 3.1–3.3, printed p. 7, with Remark 3.4, pp. 7–8). Reuse the paper's internal boundary-regularity and exchange arguments in that same warped-collar scope. Then

$$
\lvert IS(K)\rvert^G\text{ is nonempty and contractible in the weak topology.}
$$

Here (E) includes fixed-boundary attainment with the membership convention of Definition A.1/equation (27), p. 23, and sliding-boundary attainment; (Fin) includes $C^1$ compactness and finitely many open-and-closed isotopy blocks for each fixed surface type under an area bound; (U) includes universal disjointness, not just a disjoint choice.

Neither ambient orientation nor knot orientation need be preserved by the actual group action. The application inherits the target's analytic inputs and internal implication from them to an exchange structure; it does not add exchange axioms as new geometric assumptions or independently certify all those analytic arguments.

## Relation to previous results

The fixed barycenter of an invariant apex simplex is already observed in arXiv v2, §8.4, pp. 67–68. We claim no novelty for that observation, for the target's nonequivariant Theorem B, or for the standard poset fiber method.

Przytycki–Schultens, *Contractibility of the Kakimizu complex and symmetric Seifert surfaces* (2012), Theorem 1.5, prove that the fixed space of their minimal-genus complex $MS(E,\gamma,\alpha)$ is empty or contractible for **any** mapping-class subgroup preserving the specified homology class and boundary data. Their Theorem 1.2 supplies an invariant simplex for finite subgroups. The checked edition is arXiv:1004.4168v2, printed pp. 3–4; §9, pp. 21–23, builds a projection on minimal invariant simplices, proves strict distance descent, and places finite subcomplexes in finite convex subcomplexes with dismantlable graphs. The present theorem does not extend their arbitrary-subgroup range. Their preprint p. 5 also notes that finite invariant simplices pass from $MS$ to $IS$. For their data-preserving groups, nonemptiness is already known; our proposed $IS$ contribution is full fixed-space contractibility.

Hensel–Osajda–Przytycki, *Realisation and dismantlability* (2014), **Theorem 1.4 in arXiv:1205.0513v1**, proves fixed-point contractibility for finite automorphism groups of finite dismantlable flag complexes. The preprint statement is on printed p. 2 and its proof on pp. 26–27.

Their Definition 2.6, printed pp. 5–6 of arXiv v1, requires, for each base vertex $\sigma$, a nonempty finite set $\Pi_\sigma(\rho)$ of vertex pairs for each $\rho\ne\sigma$, permitting repeated entries. Its union of entries is $\Pi_\sigma^*(\rho)$. With closed neighborhoods written $N[\rho]$ here, its exposed-vertex axiom requires that for every finite $R$ with $R\setminus\{\sigma\}\ne\varnothing$, some $\rho\in R\setminus\{\sigma\}$ has a pair in $\Pi_\sigma(\rho)$ for both of whose entries $\pi$,

$$
N[\rho]\cap R\subseteq N[\pi].
$$

It also prohibits finite cycles $\rho_{i+1}\in\Pi_\sigma^*(\rho_i)$. Their Definition 9.1, printed p. 27, calls a family synchronised if projection sequences toward arbitrarily chosen vertices of any clique eventually enter that clique and stay there. **Proposition 9.2**, on the same page, requires **no infinite cliques**, a dismantling projection at every base vertex, and an equivariant family. It gives fixed-point contractibility if the acting group fixes a vertex, or if it preserves a clique and the family is synchronised. Synchronisation belongs to the second alternative; the group in that proposition need not be finite. Its proof on p. 27 uses a countable exhaustion by finite sets despite no printed countability hypothesis. That sentence alone does not justify arbitrary cardinality; it is not a counterexample to the proposition. Our limit argument is independent of it.

The exchange axiom supplies a lower apex for each distance-two pair. It does not supply fixed finite projection values working for all finite sets $R$, their exposed-vertex property, projection acyclicity, or synchronisation. Przytycki–Schultens also state (preprint pp. 4–5) that they do not know whether their Theorem 1.5, or even Theorem 1.1, extends to $IS$: the additional operation in Kakimizu's connectedness proof is not known to be well defined on isotopy classes. Our proof avoids constructing that projection. It does not prove that projections cannot exist or that exchange hypotheses are strictly weaker than HOP's; coverage through some further construction remains a novelty question.

In particular, the accompanying exhaustive census finds **all finite exchange graphs with at most nine vertices dismantlable**. HOP's finite theorem already covers the finite fixed-point conclusion in that size range. The data suggest that it may cover the general finite case as well, but that implication has not been proved here. We do not present the finite case as a new result independent of HOP. The substantive proposed contribution is the proof directly from existential exchange axioms, allowing arbitrary infinite cliques and weak realizations, and its conditional $IS(K)$ application.

## Proof outline

**Sublevels and the minimum layer.** For vertices $p,q$, choose among length-$d(p,q)$ geodesics one whose nonincreasing tuple of interior complexities is lexicographically least. Finite products of well orders are well ordered. If a maximal interior value exceeds both endpoint values, replace a vertex attaining it by a lower apex for its two neighbors. Those neighbors have distance two. The replacement remains a geodesic and strictly decreases the tuple, a contradiction, even if other interior vertices share the maximum. Thus there is a geodesic bounded by $\max\{c(p),c(q)\}$. Every nonempty initial sublevel is connected, isometrically embedded and inherits the exchange axioms.

The minimum attained layer is a clique: a distance-two segment within it would have a strictly lower apex. A finite group orbit in this possibly infinite clique is a finite invariant simplex. Its fixed barycenter gives an equivariant affine contraction of the layer. Continuity is checked on closed-simplex prisms in the weak CW topology; an infinite clique is not treated as a single closed simplex.

**Strictly lower common-link lemma: the key additional ingredient.** Let $\alpha$ be a nonminimum attained value and let $\sigma$ be a nonempty finite face whose vertices all have value $\alpha$. Then the full complex of strictly lower common neighbors,

$$
L_\alpha(\sigma)=X_{<\alpha}\cap\bigcap_{v\in\sigma}\mathrm{lk}_X(v),
$$

is nonempty, has graph diameter at most two, and is an exchange complex. Its setwise stabilizer preserves it and its complexity.

First, each vertex $v$ of value $\alpha$ has a strictly lower neighbor. Take a sublevel geodesic from $v$ to a lower vertex. If its length is one, use that endpoint. Otherwise apply the exchange axiom to $v$ and the second vertex after it; the apex is adjacent to $v$ and strictly below $\alpha$. This does not infer strict descent from a non-strict bound on the first step.

Start with a lower neighbor of one vertex of $\sigma$. When it misses another vertex of $\sigma$, the pair has distance two through a previously included vertex. A lower apex of that pair is adjacent to the new vertex and preserves all previous adjacency requirements: all previously included vertices belong to the pair's two-interval. Equality with those vertices is excluded by their value $\alpha$. Finitely many such replacements give a lower common neighbor.

For two nonadjacent lower common neighbors $a,b$, every vertex of $\sigma$ lies in $I(a,b)$. A lower apex $x$ has $c(x)<\max\{c(a),c(b)\}<\alpha$ and remains adjacent to all of $\sigma$. It connects $a$ and $b$ within the link and is an apex of its smaller two-interval. Flagness and exchange heredity follow. The **full apex property**, not merely existence of a common neighbor, is essential in both arguments.

**An exact fixed-space model.** Let $P_G(Y)$ be the poset of nonempty finite $G$-invariant faces of $Y$, ordered by inclusion. Barycentric subdivision gives a homeomorphism

$$
\lvert\Delta P_G(Y)\rvert\cong\lvert Y\rvert^G.
$$

A fixed subdivision point has a chain as its support. The chain's faces have distinct cardinalities, so a group element cannot permute its members: each face is invariant. Conversely such a chain is fixed pointwise. The weak realization's subcomplex topology makes this a homeomorphism with the required subspace topology.

**Upper fibers.** We prove directly the following poset form of Quillen's Theorem A: an order map $f:A\to B$ is a realization homotopy equivalence if every $\{a:b\le f(a)\}$ has nonempty contractible realization. The proof uses contractible carriers indexed by the least vertex of each chain, constructs a homotopy inverse by extension over simplices, and extends the two homotopies over simplex prisms. It works for arbitrary set-sized posets without a local-finiteness hypothesis.

**Universal transfinite induction.** Induct over the order type of attained complexity values, universally for all exchange complexes and finite complexity-preserving actions. Universality permits application to lower common links, which need not be sublevels of the original complex. The order-type-one case is the minimum-layer contraction.

At a successor stage with top value $\alpha$, set $A=X_{<\alpha}$, $P=P_G(X)$ and

$$
Q=\{\tau\in P:\tau\cap A^{(0)}\ne\varnothing\}.
$$

The map $\tau\mapsto\tau\cap A^{(0)}$ retracts $Q$ onto $P_G(A)$ and is pointwise below the identity, so $\lvert\Delta Q\rvert$ is contractible by induction. Apply the upper-fiber lemma to $Q\hookrightarrow P$.

For $\sigma\in Q$ the fiber $Q_{\ge\sigma}$ has least element $\sigma$. Otherwise $\sigma$ lies wholly in the top layer. The fiber retracts, by

$$
\tau\longmapsto\sigma\cup(\tau\cap A^{(0)}),
$$

onto the poset of faces $\sigma\cup\rho$ with $\rho\in P_G(L_\alpha(\sigma))$. This explicitly removes any extra top-layer vertices. Flagness makes the unions faces; their lower part is disjoint from $\sigma$. This poset is isomorphic to $P_G(L_\alpha(\sigma))$. The common-link lemma and universal induction give nonempty contractibility of its realization. All upper fibers are therefore contractible, yielding the successor conclusion. No fixed vertex in $\sigma$ or in its link is assumed.

At a limit ordinal, any finite subcomplex of $\Delta P_G(X)$ involves finitely many finite faces, hence finitely many original vertex complexities. All lie below some smaller stage, whose fixed model is contractible. Its inclusion in the full fixed model is therefore nullhomotopic. Every compact CW image lies in a finite subcomplex. Consequently every sphere map into the full fixed model extends across a disk; path connectedness comes from $S^0$. Extending the prescribed identity-to-constant homotopy over each cell prism produces a contraction, continuous by the CW product theorem for the interval. This uses neither compatible stage contractions nor a countability assumption.

## Invariant geometric data

The five-step construction for an actual finite smooth action on $(S^3,K)$ is as follows.

1. Average an ambient metric. Its normal exponential tubular neighborhood of $K$ is invariant, so its complement is an invariant exterior $E$ with torus boundary.
2. Average a boundary metric to obtain an invariant smooth $q$. With $\Delta_q=\mathrm{div}\,\mathrm{grad}$, solve $\Delta_q u=K_q$ and $\int u\,d\mu_q=0$. Gauss–Bonnet gives solvability; uniqueness makes $u$ invariant. The curvature formula $K_{e^{2u}q}=e^{-2u}(K_q-\Delta_q u)$ makes $h=e^{2u}q$ flat and invariant. This is conformal flattening, not an assertion that averaging flat metrics preserves flatness.
3. The primitive rank-one kernel of $H_1(\partial E;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E;\mathbb Z)$ gives the preferred longitude, preserved up to sign. Flat-torus isometries lift to affine Euclidean isometries preserving this direction. Thus the foliation by closed parallel longitudes is invariant, has a compact circle of leaves, and is real analytic in compatible flat affine charts.
4. Average an inward transverse vector field to obtain an equivariant collar with invariant coordinate $r$. Prescribe $g=dr^2+(1-r)^2h$ on a collar of width less than one. An invariant cutoff blends it with an averaged interior metric; positivity and the exact smaller collar are retained. The formula extends across the boundary to a two-sided collar.
5. With the competition paper's inward-normal convention, the boundary has $\mathrm{II}=h$ and trace mean curvature $2$; on tangent vectors $\mathrm{Hess}\,r=-(1-r)h$. These are the exact metric and sign conventions of §3, equations (2)–(3), printed p. 6.

The construction works for orientation-reversing elements as well. It preserves the compact exterior, strictly convex boundary, compact boundary-curve family, and connected incompressible one-boundary-component surface setting of the target's inputs. It is a check of their stated scope, not a proof of their external area-minimization assertions.

The action on isotopy classes is well defined by conjugating ambient isotopies; compressing disks pull back, and disjoint representatives map to disjoint representatives. If surface orientations are recorded, reorient images to match the chosen knot orientation. The action maps the boundary-leaf competitor class for $v$ bijectively to that for $gv$ and preserves area and genus. Thus $c(v)=(\mathrm{genus}(v),A(v))$ is invariant. Its values are well ordered by the same (E) and (Fin), using Definition 4.7 and Lemma 4.8, printed pp. 10–11. The target's internal arguments give the exchange structure (Theorem 5.1 and Proposition 5.2, p. 13; assembly in §6.1, pp. 19–20). Theorem E applies to that unchanged, possibly noninjective complexity.

## Scope and limitations

The abstract theorem is unconditional on the stated exchange axioms; Corollary E′ is conditional on the target's geometric inputs and reuses its internal analytic arguments. Invariant metrics do not settle outstanding questions about the cited existence or compactness assertions.

We only treat finite complexity-preserving actions, not arbitrary subgroups or arbitrary finite actions lacking an invariant exchange complexity. A geometric fixed point supplies a finite invariant simplex of isotopy classes admitting simultaneous disjoint representatives. It does not by itself give a single $G$-invariant embedded surface or an equivariant realization of the entire collection. If only a finite mapping-class subgroup is supplied, a separate realization theorem is needed before averaging actual diffeomorphisms is legitimate. No stronger realization statement is claimed.

## Checks and reproduction

Both computation scripts have been rerun with Python 3.9.6 and NetworkX 3.2.1. All non-timing output fields agree with the originally recorded results. The atlas census finds 474 exchange graphs on at most seven vertices, all dismantlable. Among 60,000 seeded random 7–9-vertex attempts, 25,686 admit an exchange order; all are dismantlable. There are 34,007 distinct graph/orbit-partition fixed-space checks, all nonempty with zero reduced $\mathbb F_2$ homology. The computation verifies the invariant-face/orbit-face correspondence and includes independent positive and negative controls. These are sampled actions, not all group actions; homological acyclicity is not a proof of contractibility.

The exact census obtains 3,209 eight-vertex exchange representatives, all dismantlable, and processes all 818,295 nine-vertex extensions. Of 457,564 apex-existence candidates, all 20,203 nondismantlable ones fail the exchange-order solver. Both stages finish. Tie refinement and sublevel heredity justify coverage. This excludes nondismantlable exchange graphs through nine vertices; it does not count every nine-vertex exchange graph. Theorem E is proved independently.

A separate fresh-context GPT-6.1 Sol adversarial review found no mathematical break in the abstract proof or invariant-data construction. Its literature corrections and clarifications have been incorporated.

## Evidence and AI disclosure

The full English proof, checked source locators, scripts, result JSON, and integrity manifest are in the [evidence repository](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-equivariant-exchange) at revision `f8828558f0ed9a47d269713db93fc63d138dadb9`.

GPT-6.1 Sol, in OpenAI Codex under human direction, developed the proof, ran the computations where applicable, and drafted this text; a separate GPT-6.1 Sol session in a fresh context performed an adversarial review. Claude planned the work, checked key steps against the sources, and reviewed and edited the final text. No human expert has certified the work.

16.title: Repairing the compactness input of Kakimizu-complex contractibility: boundary compactness for exact minimizers
16.excerpt_md: This is a **breakthrough contribution (repair of a key gap)** for Apex Intelligence, *Contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seife…
16.body_md:
This is a **breakthrough contribution (repair of a key gap)** for Apex Intelligence, *Contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert surfaces: the knot case of Kakimizu's problem*, official competition version, 11 September 2026, 48 pages, PDF SHA-256 `34f17d7d99780d3fd3626d9e5d7b35d6aa76661c404f191b6df341b300c0c06f`.

The contribution is a boundary compactness lemma for existing smooth exact fixed-boundary relative area minimizers. With a separately declared fixed-boundary attainment input, it repairs the finiteness step used for well-ordering the complexity and gives smooth sliding-boundary attainment. The claim is limited to this exact-minimizer family and the declared inputs.

## 1. The missing boundary compactness step

Theorem A requires a well-ordered complexity. In competition §3, Theorem 3.3, printed p. 7, $(\mathrm{Fin})$ is the compactness and finite-isotopy-block assertion from Kapovich's appendix to Schultens, *J. Topol.* **3** (2010), Proposition A.1 and Corollary A.3. Lemma 4.8(i), §4.3, p. 11, selects minimizers using $(\mathrm{E})(ii)$ and then uses $(\mathrm{Fin})$ to prove that

$$
\{v\in IS(K)^{(0)}:g(v)=h,\ A(v)\le a\}
$$

is finite. Clauses (ii)–(iv) derive sparsity and well-ordering of the complexity values and countability. Theorem A.6, §A.4, p. 27, also invokes $(\mathrm{Fin})$ to extract a limit in the required isotopy class. Theorem 3.2(ii), p. 7, cites Kapovich Corollary A.4 for sliding attainment; that corollary depends on Proposition A.1.

Proposition A.1's proof, pp. 897–898, invokes Anderson, *Curvature estimates for minimal surfaces in 3-manifolds* (1985), Theorem 3.1, pp. 101–102. Anderson works in a convex defining-function domain and, for one fixed $\varepsilon>0$, controls the truncations

$$
\Sigma_i=\widehat\Sigma_i\cap\Omega_{-\varepsilon},
\qquad
\Omega_{-\varepsilon}=f^{-1}(( -\infty,-\varepsilon]).
$$

The truncations must be connected, of fixed topological type and of uniformly bounded area. The alternatives are smooth convergence of the truncations, or varifold convergence with multiplicity at least two and smooth convergence away from finitely many points. This does not supply convergence of the original surfaces up to their original boundaries.

Kapovich uses it to obtain a limiting full surface with boundary in the compact family $J$, then uses Schoen's interior stability estimates to remove the exceptional points. The first boundary-convergence step is not supplied by the cited theorem: a fixed-depth interior conclusion leaves a boundary collar uncontrolled. We compared the journal proof with the preprint proof (arXiv:0707.3926v4, Proposition 9, p. 19); they are word for word the same.

A weak convex function on the collar does not remove the mismatch. Competition equation (2), p. 6, has $g=dr^2+\phi(r)^2g_T$, with inward coordinate $r$ and $\phi'<0$ near the boundary. For $q'\le0$, $q''\ge0$, equation (3) gives

$$
\mathrm{Hess}(q(r))=q''\,dr^2+q'\,\mathrm{Hess}\,r\ge0.
$$

Such a function may assist topology arguments; it gives no boundary curvature estimate and does not change Anderson's truncated output.

The later author version, Pan–You–Zhou–Chen, *Exchange complexes and contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert surfaces*, arXiv:2609.09224v2, 12 September 2026, retains the dependence: Theorem 2.16, pp. 22–23, uses Proposition A.1 and Corollary A.3 after fixed-boundary minimization, and well-foundedness Lemma 4.2, pp. 31–32, uses the isotopy-block statement. The identified gap does not assert falsity of either compactness or contractibility.

## 2. Result and the separate existence input

**Lemma P.** Let $M=E(K)$ be the compact irreducible orientable exterior of a nontrivial knot with the fixed smooth strictly convex collar permitted by competition §3, equation (2), p. 6. Let $J$ be its compact smooth family of embedded longitude leaves. Fix genus $h$ and area bound $a>0$. Suppose $F_i$ are connected orientable smooth incompressible neat proper embeddings with one boundary circle, $\partial F_i\in J$, $g(F_i)=h$ and $\mathrm{Area}(F_i)\le a$. Assume each $F_i$ attains the area minimum among smooth neat embeddings in its own smooth relative ambient isotopy class, fixing its prescribed boundary pointwise.

Then a subsequence converges smoothly up to the boundary, modulo reparametrization of its compact source, to a smooth neat embedded surface $F_\infty$ with boundary a leaf of $J$. The subsequence is eventually properly ambiently isotopic to $F_\infty$, preserving $\partial M$ setwise. If the boundary curve is fixed throughout, the final isotopy fixes it pointwise. Areas converge; the limit is incompressible, orientable and of genus $h$, and is itself an exact minimum in its fixed-boundary relative class.

The boundary geometry used in P is uniform smooth control and a uniform isolated-arc radius for the compact embedded leaf family. P assumes the exact minimizers exist. It neither assumes they minimize among all maps nor requires a flat torus or a linear foliation.

For the applications, accept **v2 Theorem 2.6, p. 8, as an external smooth neat fixed-boundary attainment input**. We have not independently certified its proof. Its printed scope is the flat boundary metric, linear longitude foliation and exact $\phi(r)=1-r$ collar of v2 §2.1, pp. 5–6. Choose these allowed competition §3 data before defining the area complexity; this does not preserve the numerical area function of a different previously fixed metric. For any prescribed nonflat metric, the applications require the corresponding fixed-boundary attainment theorem as an additional input.

With this input, P gives two noncircular consequences.

**Bounded-complexity finiteness.** If infinitely many distinct vertices have genus $h$ and smooth sliding area infimum at most $a$, first choose smooth neat representatives of area at most $a+1$. Minimize each at its current fixed boundary using the declared input. The resulting exact minimizers have area at most $a+1$ and remain in their respective vertex classes. P gives a subsequence eventually isotopic to one limit, contradicting distinctness. No sliding attainment or general $(\mathrm{Fin})$ was used to select them. Competition §4.1, p. 8, and Definition 4.7, pp. 10–11, give the smooth neat representative convention for this vertex infimum. Thus this proves **Lemma 4.8(i)** for the declared allowed metric choice, and its elementary clauses (ii)–(iv) follow.

**Smooth sliding-boundary attainment.** In one smooth proper class, take a smooth neat minimizing sequence $G_i$ for its sliding infimum $A_{\mathrm{sm}}$. Fixed-boundary minimization gives $F_i$ in that class with

$$
A_{\mathrm{sm}}\le\mathrm{Area}(F_i)
\le\mathrm{Area}(G_i)\longrightarrow A_{\mathrm{sm}}.
$$

P applied to a bounded-area tail gives a neat smooth limit in the same proper class; area continuity gives area $A_{\mathrm{sm}}$. It is minimal and stable. This is the smooth form of $(\mathrm{E})(ii)$, proved without using finiteness to create the limit. It provides the smooth embedding, collar and boundary-contact conclusions needed in a smooth version of A.6; it does not identify the infimum over all competition Definition A.1 piecewise-smooth competitors.

## 3. Proof mechanism

The evidence contains the full proof, organized into five files. Its essential steps are as follows.

**Exactness gives local global disk minima.** Extend the metric smoothly across $\partial M$ into a fixed closed ambient manifold $N$. A small rounded strictly convex replacement domain $U$ keeps a protected physical boundary patch and separates its artificial face. Its boundary has area $O(R^2)$. Incompressibility makes the cut curves bound disks in the surface. Select outermost disks; their retained complement is connected, reaches the original boundary outside $U$ and lies outside the interior of $U$.

Construct comparison disks by global Plateau minimization in $N$, since the old disks are not yet known to stay in $U$. A cap on $\partial U$ gives the area upper bound. Interior monotonicity, centered at a point of the disk image and away from its boundary, excludes escape from the larger coordinate neighborhood. A strictly convex defining function then confines each comparison disk to $U$, where Meeks–Yau gives embeddedness and disjointness.

Relative disk isotopy in the manifold cut along the retained surface checks that the replacement preserves the relative class. For this finite configuration, explicit Lipschitz graph splices admit smooth neat relative competitors with area error tending to zero. Exact relative minimality forces equality of each old and new disk area. Thus the original outermost disks are global Plateau minima in $N$; they too lie in $U$. This obtains the local disk property from exactness rather than from stability alone.

**Boundary area ratio, then curvature point selection.** For $q\in\partial F_i$, set $\mu_i(s)=\mathrm{Area}(F_i\cap B_N(q,s))$. First variation with the radial vector field has boundary term

$$
\beta_i(s)=\int_{\partial F_i\cap B_s}\langle X,\eta_i\rangle\,d\ell,
\qquad |\beta_i(s)|\le Cs^3.
$$

The estimate uses the unit conormal's orthogonality to the given curve tangent, whose radial remainder is $O(s^2)$; it requires no angle lower bound or density assumption. Coarea yields

$$
\left(\frac{\mu_i(s)}{s^2}\right)'
\ge-Cs\frac{\mu_i(s)}{s^2}-C,
$$

and integration from a fixed radius with total area bounded by $a$ gives $\mu_i(s)\le C_as^2$.

If curvature diverges in the protected region, maximize $d(x)^2|A_i(x)|^2$, where $d$ is distance to the artificial face, and write $k_i=|A_i(x_i)|$. Then $k_i d(x_i)\to\infty$, and curvature is at most $2k_i$ on the controlled ball. Schoen's intrinsic interior estimate puts $x_i$ within $O(k_i^{-1})$ intrinsic distance of the actual boundary. Choose an actual boundary point $q_i$ joined by a path of that controlled length, and rescale by $k_i$ about $q_i$.

**Boundary half-charts and one-fold anchoring.** Only after point selection supplies bounded rescaled curvature do surface Fermi coordinates and tangent-plane projection give uniform half-graph charts. Jacobi and conormal bounds use the actual controlled boundary arc; graph Schauder then gives smooth boundary extraction. No bound on derivatives of artificial cut curves is used, and the original contact angle may tend to zero.

Following the bounded intrinsic path selects a connected complete-up-to-boundary embedded Euclidean minimal limit $D_\infty$ in a half-space, with actual boundary a single straight line $L$, quadratic area growth and curvature one at the selected limit point. Its nonnegative harmonic height is positive in the interior; Hopf gives neatness at $L$. An extra boundaryless full graph following this edge would cross the supporting plane, while a sheet close in intrinsic distance to the actual boundary lies in the unique Fermi collar. This anchors multiplicity one near $L$ and propagates it along the connected component.

**Controlled fillings before reflection.** Multiplicity one is proved before lifting a closed interior loop to closed loops on the rescaled surfaces. Each lift bounds a subdisk in a localized global minimizing disk; that subdisk is itself a global Plateau minimum. Hass–Scott Lemma 2.1, p. 91, bounds its area by squared boundary length, and Lemma 3.2, pp. 96–97, confines it to a small ball. After rescaling, its area and diameter are bounded.

Conformal disk parametrizations with three controlled boundary marks have uniform energy and continuous equicontinuity, using the Courant–Lebesgue and short-loop mechanism of Hass–Scott Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5, pp. 97–100. They give a continuous disk limit. The ambient Christoffel terms tend to zero, so its interior map is Euclidean harmonic. Positive boundary height keeps the filling away from $L$; properness and locally finite minimal plaques keep its image on the selected leaf. Every interior simple loop is nullhomotopic there, so $D_\infty$ is simply connected. A pointed limit of disks alone was not used as a topology argument.

Rotate this limit by $\pi$ about $L$, **only in the Euclidean limit**. Odd transverse and even longitudinal harmonic extensions give the smooth branch-free Schwarz continuation. The double is complete and embedded, with quadratic area growth. Van Kampen and surface classification make it a topological plane, hence of finite topological type and one end.
