Anderson Corollary 1.5, p. 96, then makes it a Euclidean plane, contradicting the normalized nonzero curvature. No stability of the double or independent half-space classification is assumed.

**Full extraction and final isotopy.** The contradiction gives a boundary curvature bound; Schoen controls the complement. Full and half-graph extraction gives a compact embedded minimal support. In the original collar,

$$
\Delta_\Sigma r=\frac{\phi'}{\phi}
\bigl(2-|\nabla_\Sigma r|^2\bigr)<0.
$$

The barrier and Hopf lemma exclude interior boundary contact and give neatness. The unique actual boundary graph and connectedness exclude extraneous components. A transverse tubular line bundle is chosen to lie in $T\partial M$ along the boundary. Projection of late surfaces to the limit is a proper local diffeomorphism and therefore a covering; every boundary fiber has one preimage, so its degree is one. Scaling the resulting single graph sections gives the proper isotopy, relative to the boundary when that boundary is fixed. Smooth area convergence proves the two consequences.

## 4. Scope and verification limits

Universal disjointness $(\mathrm{U})$ remains an external input. This repair does not prove compactness for all stable surfaces in Kapovich's $M_a$, the full piecewise-smooth assertion of competition Appendix A, or a multiboundary version. Hass–Scott Theorem 6.12, pp. 112–113, attains a minimum in its own comparison class; membership in competition Definition A.1 and equality with its infimum are not certified by the specific disk-splice smoothing above. Arbitrary prescribed nonflat metrics require their own fixed-boundary attainment input.

Schoen's original chapter, Lawson's source, Gilbarg–Trudinger's book, Richards's article and the original Morrey/Meeks–Yau papers were not separately checked. The exact standard forms used are stated in the evidence and distinguished from the directly checked Anderson and Hass–Scott statements. The boundary area calculation, half-chart construction, continuous fillings and Euclidean reflection are proved explicitly. No exhaustive novelty search was performed; a directly applicable earlier compactness theorem could reduce this contribution to completing a citation.

## 5. Review and evidence

An independent adversarial review in a fresh context checked the proof of Lemma P and the two applications against the cited sources. It found **no fatal issue and no missing mathematical step**, and flagged one wording issue: an interior monotonicity lower bound must specify that its center lies on the disk image. That condition is now explicit in the evidence and in the outline above. The review does not certify the excluded stronger conclusions, the external existence proof or novelty.

The complete proof, edition-specific bibliography, scope statements and SHA-256 manifest are in the [evidence repository](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-boundary-compactness) at revision `6179e85e49f30e9b02e4e7956d02eb94e2931f7e`. This is an original proof exposition under CC BY 4.0; cited third-party full texts are not redistributed.

## AI disclosure

GPT-6.1 Sol, in OpenAI Codex under human direction, developed the proof and drafted this text; a separate GPT-6.1 Sol session in a fresh context performed an adversarial review. Claude planned the work, checked key steps against the sources, and reviewed and edited the final text. No human expert has certified the work.

17.title: Open question (F) of the Seifert-surface paper answered: a prime counterexample, and finiteness for atoroidal knots
17.excerpt_md: **Target and category.** This is a **breakthrough contribution** (an answer to the paper's stated open question) to Apex Intelligence, *Cont…
17.body_md:
**Target and category.** This is a **breakthrough contribution** (an answer to the paper's stated open question) to Apex Intelligence, *Contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert surfaces: the knot case of Kakimizu's problem*, official competition edition, dated 11 September 2026, 48 printed pages. Target PDF SHA-256: `34f17d7d99780d3fd3626d9e5d7b35d6aa76661c404f191b6df341b300c0c06f`.

The answer to the paper's open question (F) is **negative in general and even for prime knots**, and **positive when the exterior contains no essential torus**. A composite knot has a genus-three vertex with infinitely many distinct genus-two neighbours; a prime satellite has a genus-six vertex with infinitely many distinct genus-four neighbours. The positive result gives finitely many incompressible Seifert-surface classes at every genus bound.

## 1. The question being answered

The competition edition, Remark 1.1 and the final paragraph of the Introduction, printed p.2, leaves one question open: does $IS(K)$ satisfy (F), or can a vertex have infinitely many neighbours of strictly smaller genus?

We use the paper's §4.1 and Definition 4.1, p.8. A vertex is the ambient isotopy class of a connected, orientable, incompressible Seifert surface in the knot exterior $E(K)$, with one preferred-longitude boundary component. Boundary curves may move on the boundary torus. Distinct vertices are adjacent when they admit disjoint representatives.

For the lexicographic complexity $c(v)=(g(v),A(v))$ of Definition 4.7, pp.10–11, condition (F) requires

$$
\{u\in N(v):c(u)<c(v)\}
$$

to be finite for every vertex $v$. This set splits into neighbours of smaller genus and neighbours of the same genus but smaller relative area. Lemma 4.8(i), p.11, makes the latter part finite: for fixed $h$ and $a>0$, only finitely many vertices have $g(u)=h$ and $A(u)\le a$. Hence, using that stated lemma, the remaining assertion is precisely finiteness of

$$
\{u\in N(v):g(u)<g(v)\}.
$$

The later author edition, G. Pan, C. You, J. Zhou and Y. Chen, *Exchange complexes and contractibility of the complex of incompressible Seifert surfaces*, arXiv:2609.09224v2 (12 September 2026), still asks this question in §1.5, p.5, and Remark 7.13, p.62.

Remark 1.1 says that under (F), competition Theorem B reduces to the cited Morse lemma, reference [21], Lemma 2.3, together with the paper's heredity lemma. Thus the answer determines whether that finite-descending-link reduction is available for $IS(K)$, or whether the competition argument must accommodate infinite descending links.

## 2. Results

**Theorem A′ (bounded-genus finiteness).** If $E(K)$ contains no incompressible, non-boundary-parallel torus, then for each integer $h$, only finitely many vertices of $IS(K)$ have genus at most $h$. In particular, (F) holds.

**Corollary.** If (F) fails, the knot exterior contains an essential torus.

**Theorem B′ (an explicit counterexample).** Let $B$ be the twisted Whitehead double $K_\alpha$ of the trefoil shown in Figure 1 of Jessica E. Banks, *On links with locally infinite Kakimizu complexes*, arXiv:1010.3831v2, printed p.3. Let

$$
J=W_0^+(3_1),\qquad K=B\#J,
$$

where $3_1$ is the right-handed trefoil and $W_0^+$ denotes its positive-clasp, zero-framing Whitehead double. There are incompressible Seifert surfaces $R,R_n$ of genus 1 for $B$ and disjoint incompressible Seifert surfaces $Q,H$ of genera 1 and 2 for $J$, such that

$$
v=[R\mathbin{\natural}H],\qquad
u_n=[R_n\mathbin{\natural}Q]\quad(n\in\mathbb Z)
$$

are vertices of $IS(K)$ with

$$
g(v)=3,\qquad g(u_n)=2.
$$

The $u_n$ are pairwise distinct, and every $u_n$ is adjacent to the same fixed vertex $v$. Thus (F) fails for this knot. Here $\natural$ joins the surfaces along a spanning arc of the connected-sum decomposing meridional annulus.

**Theorem C′ (a prime counterexample).** With $B,J,R,R_n,Q,H$ as above, put

$$
K'=W_0^+(B\#W_0^+(3_1)),\qquad
v'=[D(R\mathbin{\natural}H)],\qquad
u'_n=[D(R_n\mathbin{\natural}Q)].
$$

The knot $K'$ is prime; $v'$ and all $u'_n$ are vertices of $IS(K')$, with $g(v')=6$ and $g(u'_n)=4$. The $u'_n$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, are pairwise distinct and all adjacent to $v'$. Here $D(F)=P\cup F_+\cup F_-$ attaches two oppositely oriented parallel copies of $F$ to the outer longitudes of the standard Whitehead pair of pants $P$. Thus (F) fails even for prime knots.

Together the results answer (F) negatively in general and for prime knots, and positively when there is no essential torus. In the full proof, A′, B′ and C′ are Theorems 2.1, 6.1 and 7.1.

## 3. Proof outline

### Bounded-genus counting from Wilson's theorem

Robin T. Wilson's Main Theorem (arXiv:math/0604001v2, pp.1–2) gives finitely many incompressible Seifert bases $S_i$ and closed incompressible, non-boundary-parallel surfaces $Q_j$ such that every incompressible Seifert surface of a nontrivial knot is isotopic to a normal Haken sum

$$
S_i+\sum_j a_jQ_j,\qquad a_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.
$$

In Wilson's fixed triangulation the closed fundamental summands are connected by indecomposability; boundary-parallel tori are removed (§4, p.14). Closed summands are orientable in $S^3$; irreducibility and Wilson's convention exclude spheres, and atoroidality excludes tori. Thus $d_j=-\chi(Q_j)\ge2$. Additivity of Euler characteristic (§2, p.6) and $g(S)\le h$ give

$$
\sum_j a_jd_j=\chi(S_i)-\chi(S)\le\chi(S_i)-1+2h.
$$

So the coefficients are bounded for each of the finitely many bases, and normal-vector uniqueness (§2, pp.4–5) leaves finitely many classes, which proves (F).

Banks's orientability caveat (p.6) is harmless: the count uses only fixed base Euler characteristics. Wilson's decomposition is an external input.

### Connected-sum incompressibility and disjointness

By the Loop Theorem (Hatcher's notes, Corollary 3.3, p.59), $H_i=\pi_1(F_i)$ injects into $G_i=\pi_1(E(K_i))$ for incompressible two-sided $F_i$. Linking number vanishes on $H_i$ and is injective on $\langle\mu\rangle$, so $H_i\cap\langle\mu\rangle=\{1\}$. Normal form injects $H_1*H_2$ into $G_1*_{\langle\mu\rangle}G_2$, excluding compression. The connected orientable sum has one longitude and

$$
\chi(F_1\mathbin{\natural}F_2)=\chi(F_1)+\chi(F_2)-1,
$$

so genera add. Competition Lemma 4.2, pp.8–9, gives boundary-incompressibility. For disjointness, give the surfaces distinct parallel longitudes and match disjoint spanning arcs in boundary order; the bands can be fixed once where a family agrees near the boundary (Lemmas 3.1–3.2).

### The Whitehead unequal-genus pair

$Q=P\cup A_0$ is the standard genus-one surface, with zero-framed annulus $A_0$ on $T_J=\partial V$, $V=N(3_1)$. The pair of pants $P$ has two opposite companion longitudes and one knot longitude. Replacing $A_0$ by opposite parallel once-punctured-torus trefoil fibres gives

$$
H=P\cup F_+\cup F_-,\qquad \chi(H)=-3,\qquad g(H)=2.
$$

Two same-sign clasp crossings give consecutive closed lifts in $D^2\times\mathbb R$ linking number $\pm1$. This excludes ball containment, a disjoint meridian disc, outer-torus compression, and a disc bounded by the pattern in $V$ (Lemma 4.1).

Essential curves on $P$ are boundary-parallel. Compression would kill a nonzero outer-longitude class in $\pi_1(V)$ or make the pattern bound a disc. Thus $P$ is incompressible. A sphere in the pattern exterior bounds a ball in $V$ that cannot contain the pattern, so the exterior is irreducible. Hatcher's Lemma 1.11, p.20, gives boundary-incompressibility, since $P$ is not an annulus.

Trefoil fibres are incompressible and boundary-incompressible. Innermost-circle and outermost-arc exchanges across incompressible $T_J$ exclude compression of $H$. Torus-group injection makes $J$ nontrivial, hence genus-one $Q$ is minimum-genus and incompressible.

The annulus $A_0$ lies on the same normal side of $P$ at both seams. Push a parallel $P$ to the opposite side with outer boundaries outside $A_0$, and attach fibres on the companion side, away from $Q$. Disjoint seam collars and knot longitudes give disjoint $Q,H$.

### Persistence of the product-region obstruction

Banks's Theorem 2.3, pp.3–5, supplies genus-one $R_n=\Psi^n(R_0)$ disjoint from $R$. Push $R$ off the torus-twist collar so $\Psi(R)=R$. The family agrees near the knot boundary.

Lemma 5.1 proves pairwise nonisotopy of $R_n\mathbin{\natural}F$ for any fixed incompressible Seifert surface $F$ of $J$. Reduce indices to $0,k\ne0$ by $\Psi^{-n}$. Move Banks's parallel $R'_0$ to a distinct longitude away from the twist; use adjacent parallel $F'$ and match joining arcs in boundary order:

$$
S=R_0\mathbin{\natural}F,\qquad S'=\Psi^k(R'_0)\mathbin{\natural}F'.
$$

They intersect in the twist collar; opening the boundary preserves regions and horizontal face components. Banks's Figure 4 and p.5 exhaust the types: $M_{0,a},M_{0,b},M_{1,b},M_T$ have disconnected horizontal $R_0$-face; $M_{1,a},M'_{1,a}$ are the nonproduct sutured solid tori of Figure 3, p.4. Their annular sutures wind 2 or 3 times, versus 1 for an annulus product. All $k\ne0$ retain the obstruction; negative $k$ reverses the collar picture.

- **Regions cannot merge.** Two spanning arcs cut the decomposing annulus into two rectangles. The product between adjacent parallel $F,F'$ and the connected outside region each meet one rectangle and attach to one old region. Distinct old regions cannot merge; one may receive both attachments. Both new regions meet rectangles, leaving no isolated component.
- **Face pieces cannot connect.** The joining interval avoids intersection curves; $F$ enlarges only its one old face piece, as does $F'$ on its face. If both rectangles meet one region, their edges flank the same arc in that piece. The companion-side sutured pieces are untouched: joining is at the pattern-side knot boundary away from $T_B$.

By Banks's Definition 2.1, pp.2–3, remaining vertical boundary lies on the ambient boundary. A connected product region's interior has no frontier inside the complement, hence occupies a whole complementary component with connected horizontal interior. The disconnected-face and sutured components exclude it; a small parallel patch would have forbidden interior vertical boundary.

In the irreducible, boundary-irreducible Haken exterior, $S,S'$ are proper, incompressible, boundary-incompressible and intersect in general position. Banks's Proposition 2.2, p.3, without a minimum-genus hypothesis, forces a product region if they can be isotoped disjoint. Isotopy allows a parallel copy, contradicting its exclusion.

### Assembly

Lemma 3.2 fixes disjoint joining bands for $(R,R_0)$ and $(H,Q)$. The twist fixes the centre and bands; Lemmas 3.1 and 5.1 give its infinitely many distinct genus-two neighbours. The centre has genus 3, proving B′ independently of area.

### The prime satellite

Put $M=E(B\#J)$ and write $E(K')=M\cup_T X$, with $X$ the outer Whitehead pattern exterior. Lemma 4.1 and the nontrivial companion make $T$ incompressible on both sides; normal form injects its group $\mathbb Z^2$ into the satellite group, proving $K'$ nontrivial. Its standard Whitehead surface has genus 1, hence $g(K')=1$. Schubert's standard genus-additivity theorem excludes a sum of two nontrivial knots. Thus $K'$ is prime. The full proof also gives an independent decomposing-annulus proof.

For incompressible $F\subset M$ of positive genus, the three pieces of $D(F)$ give a graph of groups with two cyclic seam groups and three noncyclic free vertex groups. Its tree maps to the Bass–Serre tree of

$$
\Gamma=\pi_1(M)*_{C_T}\pi_1(X),\qquad C_T=\pi_1(T).
$$

Let $\mu,\lambda$ be the companion meridian and preferred longitude. Boundary words are not proper powers. At a companion vertex, $\pi_1(F)\cap C_T=\langle\lambda\rangle$: any element of the intersection commutes with the boundary word, whose free-group centralizer is its cyclic subgroup. The same argument handles two edges from one boundary of $P$. Edges from its two different outer boundaries cannot fold together either: their stabilizers would lie in one abelian torus group and commute, forcing the two boundary cyclic groups to be conjugate in $\pi_1(P)$, contrary to their distinct abelianizations. The tree map is locally injective, hence injective; together with the vertex-group injections this makes $\pi_1(D(F))\to\Gamma$ injective. The surface is connected, orientable, has one longitude boundary, and

$$
\chi(D(F))=-1+2\chi(F)=1-4g(F),\qquad g(D(F))=2g(F).
$$

Hatcher's Lemma 1.11 gives boundary-incompressibility. Thus $D(R\mathbin{\natural}H)$ and $D(R_n\mathbin{\natural}Q)$ are vertices of genera 6 and 4.

For disjoint $F,G$, take their sheets from disjoint regular neighbourhoods with disjoint boundary annuli $A_F,A_G$. Push a parallel pattern pair of pants to the side opposite $A_F$ at both seams, then move its outer circles in the connected complementary annulus to $\partial A_G$ in boundary order. Extend this motion through a thin collar avoiding the first pair of pants and round disjoint seam collars. Choose the pair once for $R\mathbin{\natural}H$ and $U_0=R_0\mathbin{\natural}Q$, and put $U_n=\Psi^n(U_0)=R_n\mathbin{\natural}Q$. Extending $\Psi$ by the identity on $X$ fixes the chosen $D(R\mathbin{\natural}H)$, the pattern pieces and seams. All $D(U_n)=\Psi^n(D(U_0))$ therefore use the same pattern piece and miss that fixed centre.

Finally suppose $D(U_n)$ and $D(U_m)$ are isotopic. Their image subgroups in $\Gamma$ are conjugate, so their unique minimal invariant subtrees correspond. Minimality holds because each seam group is proper in both endpoint groups; alternating elements outside it have axes through its edge, and translates cover both edge orbits. Tree injectivity identifies each companion-vertex stabilizer exactly with its surface-piece group. There are two companion vertex orbits and a single incident seam-edge orbit at each. Adjusting the conjugating element within the target surface group, identifying the chosen parallel copy, and aligning the ambient vertex $v_M$ and edge $e$ gives $av_M=v_M$, $ae=e$ and

$$
a\pi_1(U_n)a^{-1}=\pi_1(U_m),\qquad
a\in\mathrm{Stab}_{\Gamma}(e)=C_T=\langle\mu,\lambda\rangle.
$$

Thus $a$ preserves the oriented longitude. Farb–Margalit, Theorem 8.8, printed p.234, realizes the induced boundary-word-preserving isomorphism by a homeomorphism. Truncate the puncture end and adjust in the resulting boundary collar; a boundary Dehn twist corrects the based isomorphism. Realize $a=\mu^r\lambda^s$ by a loop of boundary-torus translations extended into a collar. The final boundary translation is the identity, and the two embeddings now agree on their boundary parameters and based group maps. Hatcher's Corollary 3.9, printed p.63, gives $\pi_2(M)=0$, so handle-edge homotopies extend over the two-cell relative to the boundary. Straighten the boundary collar and push remaining interior points inward to obtain proper homotopy. Waldhausen's relative-boundary homotopy-to-isotopy theorem then applies: $M$ is compact, orientable, irreducible and boundary-irreducible, and the surfaces are two-sided, incompressible and boundary-incompressible. It gives $U_n\simeq U_m$, contradicting Lemma 5.1 for $n\ne m$. This proves C′.

## 4. Significance and limits

The contribution is a topological answer to the paper's stated question. It neither changes nor depends on the paper's area-attainment, compactness or exchange analysis. Lemma 4.8(i) is used only to explain the paper's equivalence of formulations; none of the three results needs its analytic proof.

For the knots of Theorems B′ and C′, the reduction recorded in competition Remark 1.1 is unavailable: $v$ and $v'$ have infinite descending links, so Theorem B cannot be obtained for these complexes as a restatement of the cited Morse lemma. The paper's general argument along the well-order, which does not assume (F), is needed in that generality. This does not single out one proof: the v2 edition's countable Morse formulation, Corollary 7.12 and Remark 7.13, p.62, also works without (F). What our answer settles is the finiteness question itself, which v2 still lists as open.

A prime counterexample is also given. It remains a satellite, with an essential companion torus, consistently with Theorem A′. Atoroidality is sufficient for (F) but not necessary. Let $K$ be a composite of two non-fibred knots, each with a unique incompressible Seifert surface; Kakimizu notes that many two-bridge knots qualify. By Kakimizu 1992, Theorem B, p.226, and Proposition 3.5, p.232, $IS(K)=MS(K)$ is a line, so every vertex has two neighbours of the same genus and (F) holds, although a composite exterior contains an essential swallow-follow torus. A complete classification of (F) is not treated. Nor can Banks's Theorem 1.8 simply be substituted: its pp.7–8 proof uses minimum genus to infer $\chi(S'')\ge0$ after surgery. A neighbour of strictly smaller genus than the fixed vertex need not be minimum-genus among all Seifert surfaces. We therefore infer only the necessary existence of an essential torus from Theorem A′, not Banks's full companion or winding-number restriction.

No exhaustive novelty search has been performed. In the sources examined, and in a limited web search, we found no answer to this precise question. The bounded-genus theorem is a consequence of Wilson's existing decomposition; the counterexample combines Banks's existing family with the unequal-genus pair and the proved obstruction transport. No claim is made that every ingredient is new.

Banks and Wilson were checked in their arXiv v2 editions. Sakuma's original product-region proposition, Schubert's genus additivity and Waldhausen's homotopy-to-isotopy theorem are used as stated standard inputs; their originals were not inspected, and the precise Waldhausen form is recorded in the full proof. Kakimizu 1992, p.231, cites Kakimizu's 1991 note on doubled knots (Bull. London Math. Soc. 23, 300–302) for the fact that $IS(L)$ need not be locally finite, and Banks's Remark 2.4, p.5, describes its construction. Neither presents a vertex with infinitely many neighbours of smaller genus. The 1991 note itself was not accessible to us, and nothing in our argument depends on it.

## 5. Verification and evidence

Two separate GPT-6.1 Sol sessions, each in a fresh context, adversarially reviewed the proofs against the sources: one the composite counterexample and the atoroidal theorem, the other the prime counterexample. Both concluded that the results hold, with **0 fatal issues and 0 issues requiring mathematical repair**. Their presentation clarifications and confirmed simplifications are incorporated. These reviews are not expert certifications or novelty determinations.

The [evidence repository](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-open-question-f) at revision `6115abe18e852454426a1a1be5ee9c47c3ba73c9` contains the complete English proof in eight files, English and Chinese overviews, a version-specific bibliography with checked printed pages and source limits, a CC BY 4.0 license notice, and a SHA-256 manifest. The critical proofs are `proof/obstruction.md` and `proof/prime.md`; the assemblies and checklists are in `proof/counterexample.md` and `proof/prime.md`.

GPT-6.1 Sol, in OpenAI Codex under human direction, developed the proof and drafted this text; a separate GPT-6.1 Sol session in a fresh context performed an adversarial review. Claude planned the work, checked key steps against the sources, and reviewed and edited the final text. No human expert has certified the work.

19.title: Independent verification of the geometric half of Theorem A (§§3–5, Appendices A–B): six local points repaired
19.excerpt_md: **中文摘要：** 本投稿对定理 A 的几何部分（§3–§5、§6.1、附录 A–B）及 §6.2 中定理 C 的证明做了独立的逐步核验，并对照原文核对了所引 [17]（Schultens 2010 及 Kapovich 附录）的陈述。
19.body_md:
**中文摘要：** 本投稿对定理 A 的几何部分（§3–§5、§6.1、附录 A–B）及 §6.2 中定理 C 的证明做了独立的逐步核验，并对照原文核对了所引 [17]（Schultens 2010 及 Kapovich 附录）的陈述。

**结论：** 未发现改变定理 A 或（按 §6.2 所证形式、即 $D_{\ell,a_0}$ 非空时）定理 C 之陈述的错误。发现六处局部问题 G1–G6（G4、G6 仅为隐含步骤），均给出修补；另有六处表述错误 M1–M6，均可局部修正，不影响证明结构。其中 M5（定理 C 第二族的陈述与 §6.2 所证集合不符）已由投稿 #10 先行指出。定理 B 及 Prop. 5.2、§6 的条件推导已由投稿 #10 在 Lean 中形式化；本文未检查定理 B 及该 Lean 代码，但另行重推了 Prop. 5.2 的局部下降与 §6.1–6.2。

**最实质的修补：**
- G1：附录 A 在边界顶点用 Hopf 引理，需一阶系数有界；论文所写的“各片直到边界光滑”（p.23、p.25）不能从定义 A.1（仅 $C^1$）推出。本文把 p.24 的极小曲面恒等式用于坐标：$\Delta_Wx^k=\mathrm{tr}_W\mathrm{Hess}\,x^k$，从而一阶系数有界（仅用 $C^1$）。
- G2：为在 $z$ 出现前固定输出顶点又能避开 $Z$，须同时缩小圆角宽度，而不只是推离尺度。
- G5：宽度的取法缺少两条约束（其一保证输出与 $S$ 不交），另有一个常数须对两对扇形对称地取。

**外部依赖：** 除标准结果外，只依赖论文列出的输入：[17] Thm A.5（即 (U)；[17] 的证明仅一段（$\mathcal J$ 的曲线或相等或不交，故“[7] 的论证照样适用”），公共边界叶另见 p.886 与其 Lemma 2 情形 2（p.891））、[17] Prop. A.1 与 Cor. A.3（即 (Fin)）、Hass–Scott Thm 6.12（含 (27)）、Kakimizu 连通性定理 [10]。

## 0. Scope and verdict

**Paper.** The competition PDF (48 pp.), SHA-256 `34f17d7d99780d3fd3626d9e5d7b35d6aa76661c404f191b6df341b300c0c06f`; page numbers refer to it.

**Scope.** Everything Theorem A uses besides Theorem B (§3, §4, §5, §6.1, Appendix A, Appendix B), and the proof of Theorem C in §6.2.
- Theorem B, and the conditional deduction of Prop. 5.2 and of §6, are formalised in Lean by submission #10. I did not re-check Theorem B or that Lean code; the local descent of Prop. 5.2 and §§6.1–6.2 were re-derived directly (§2 below).
- Appendix C (unused by the paper) is out of scope; for Theorem D only Lemmas 6.1–6.2 and the per-torus changes were read.

**Method.** Within this scope each step of the paper's own arguments was re-derived, every constant of Appendix B.1 recomputed, the order of choices in §B.4 checked, and every statement cited from [17] compared with its printed text (J. Topol. 3 (2010) 883–900, with Kapovich's appendix).

**Verdict.**
1. No finding changes the statement of Theorem A, or that of Theorem C in the form proved in §6.2 (for $D_{\ell,a_0}$, under the non-emptiness proviso stated there).
2. There are **six local points, G1–G6** (G4, G6 only implicit steps), each repaired in §3 below: G1 and G5 supply a missing argument or constraint; G2 completes an insufficient proof; G3 corrects an intermediate formula; G4 and G6 make explicit what the paper's own lemmas give.
3. There are **six misstatements, M1–M6** (§4 below), each corrected locally, none affecting a proof's structure. One of them, M5, is in the statement of Theorem C.

## 1. Audit of what is cited from [17]

Each of the following matches the printed text of [17].
- **Statements.** Def. 3 (strictly convex boundary; $\mathcal J$ a smooth foliation by closed curves; the appendix opens with smooth curves, later (p.899) fixes "a $C^1$-foliation"); Thm 4 (stated in [17] to be Thm A.5) = (U)(i); Thm A.5 = (U)(ii); Thm 2 = Cor. A.4 = (E)(ii); Prop. A.1 and Cor. A.3 = (Fin): for $\partial S\ne\varnothing$, $\mathcal M_a$ is compact in $C^1$ and a disjoint union of finitely many open-closed sets of mutually isotopic surfaces.
- **Hypotheses** (opening two paragraphs of the appendix): $M$ compact, $P^2$-irreducible, with smooth strictly convex boundary; $\mathcal J$ compact; $S$ connected; $f(S)$ incompressible; $f^{-1}(\partial_iM)$ a single component of $\partial S$. There is **no minimal-genus hypothesis**.
- **Stability.** The proof of Prop. A.1 uses stability only through Schoen's interior estimates (p.898 of [17]), as the paper says on p.27; this places $F'_i$ in $\mathcal M_a$ in Theorem A.6.

Remarks.
- **Only the distinct-vertex case of (U)(i) is used** (Lemma 4.3; Theorem 5.1(b) with $z\notin\{u,w\}$; compare "Only the two-surface clause of (U) is used", p.9). That case is [17, Thm A.5] with $n=2$.
- **Caveat on [17, Thm A.5].** Its proof in [17] is one paragraph: curves of $\mathcal J$ are equal or disjoint, so Freedman–Hass–Scott's cut-and-paste (the paper's [3]; [7] in [17]) preserves the boundary condition and "the arguments in [7] go through". [17] notes (p.886) that relative least area surfaces "can share components of their boundary" and that the Meeks–Yau trick "allows us to skirt this issue" (illustrated in its Lemma 2), but the proof of A.5, which defers to [7], does not spell out the shared-leaf case; and the paper itself says (p.19) that the bounded argument of [3, §7] "neither covers a common boundary leaf, nor a competitor that is not itself minimal". In my view, together with (27), this is the most delicate external input. Appendix B's (T2) estimates could supply the area bookkeeping for a shared leaf; the topological step of Freedman–Hass–Scott would still be needed.

## 2. What was verified

- **§3.** For $dr^2+\varphi^2g_\partial$, $\varphi=1-r$: $\nabla_X\partial_r=(\varphi'/\varphi)X$, $\mathrm{Hess}\,r=\varphi\varphi'g_\partial\le0$, $\mathrm{Hess}\,r(\partial_r,\cdot)=0$, so boundary-to-boundary geodesics have interior points with $r>0$; $\mathrm{II}=g_\partial>0$, $\mathrm{tr\,II}=2$.
- **§4.** Lemma 4.2 (same side: compressing disc or trivial arc; opposite sides: intersection $\pm1$, against linking duality); Lemmas 4.3–4.5 (the sphere $E\cup F\subset\mathrm{Int}\,M$; $P$ misses the ball); Lemma 4.8 (order type $\le\omega^2$); Lemma 4.9 (boundary count in $p^{-1}(\partial E(K))$; discarded components have $\chi\le0$).
- **§5.**
  - Prop. 5.2 (local descent).
  - Lemma 5.6: (15) by connectedness of $B_\gamma\setminus\gamma$; (16) and (17); $\varphi(a)\le\varphi(b)$, hence $\mathcal G(a)+\mathcal G(b)\le e$.
  - Theorem 5.1 (T0): $\tilde B_\downarrow,\tilde B_\uparrow$ use the opposite sectors $(\downarrow\downarrow),(\uparrow\uparrow)$, so they share $\alpha$ and $\theta$; (20) is the partition of $S_+\cup S_-$; the total is $\le A(u)+A(w)-2\varepsilon_0+C\sigma$, with $\varepsilon_0$ fixed before $\sigma$.
- **B.1.** $\Theta$ is even, $\Theta\ge|\cdot|$, $|\Theta'|\le1$, $\Theta'(0)=0$; $g>0$ and non-decreasing; $m=\cot\frac\alpha2\in[\tan\frac\theta2,\cot\frac\theta2]$; $F_s^2\le2\eta^2m'^2+8m^2\eta'^2$; $0\le E_1\le m'^2\eta^3$. With (35) three error terms are each $\le g_0/4$ and $8m^2\kappa^2=\frac29g_0$, so the bracket is $\ge\frac{37}{36}g_0$.
- **B.2–B.5.**
  - Lemma 5.5.
  - Prop. 5.7: Lax–Milgram; GT 8.15 (no sign condition); Lichtenstein; odd reflection; Vekua; $2\partial_z\hat v\equiv0$ would force $A=B$; (24) by GT 8.19.
  - Lemmas B.1–B.2, and Corollary B.4(1) (loss at most $4N\rho_2$).
  - The order of choices on p.37, $\text{scheme}\to\rho_0\to r_1\to\rho_2\to(\theta_1,\varrho_1)\to(\eta^{\rm geo}_1,\kappa_1)\to\eta_1\to c_\star\to\varepsilon_\ast\to\delta\to t\to\eta_2\to\hat B\to C\to\sigma$, has no cycle, also with the constants added in G3–G5.
- **Appendix A.**
  - Lemmas A.2–A.3. (A.3 is stated for smooth sheets but needs only $C^1$ up to the arc.)
  - Prop. A.5: at an interior vertex the covering degree is 1; at a boundary vertex $\Theta\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}$ by (29), then Hopf (G1), then $\Theta=\pi$, in both branches of the case split.
  - Theorem A.6 and Lemma A.7.
- **§6.** Theorem A. Theorem C for $D_\ell$, and for $D_{\ell,a_0}$ as defined on p.20 whenever it is non-empty (unions of fibres, downward closed).

## 3. Gaps and repairs

### G1. Hopf at a boundary vertex (Lemma A.4 in Prop. A.5)

**Issue.**
- GT Lemma 3.4 needs bounded first-order coefficients, but in graph coordinates $\Delta_W=g^{ij}\partial_{ij}-g^{ij}\Gamma^k_{ij}(g)\partial_k$ and $\Gamma(g)$ involves second derivatives of the graph.
- The text gives no reason: it calls the pieces "smoothly embedded up to [their] own boundary" (p.23; cf. p.25), which does not follow from Definition A.1 ($C^1$ only) or from (27), and never applies its identity $\Delta_Wu=\mathrm{tr}_W\mathrm{Hess}\,r$ (p.24) to coordinates.
- Second derivatives of a $C^1$ minimal sector need not stay bounded at a corner; compare the harmonic function $r^{\pi/\theta}\sin(\pi\vartheta/\theta)$ on a sector of angle $\theta\in(\pi/2,\pi)$.
- So "continuous coefficients" (p.25) is unproved at a boundary vertex, where the paper has only a "$C^1$ graph" (p.26); Lemma A.4 itself is stated for a $C^1$ map.

**Repair (needs only $C^1$ up to $p$).** Write $W=\Phi(U\cap B_\delta)$ with $\Phi(x)=(x,v(x))$; here $W$ is $S_0\cup\dots\cup S_j$, or $S_j$ alone.
1. On the part of $W$ over $\mathrm{Int}\,U$, where $W$ is smooth and $\vec H=0$, for $F\in C^2(M)$ we have $\Delta_W(F|_W)=\mathrm{tr}_W\mathrm{Hess}^hF$.
2. By the chain rule with $\langle\nabla^Wx^i,\nabla^Wx^j\rangle=g^{ij}$, $\Delta_W\psi=g^{ij}\partial_{ij}\psi+(\Delta_Wx^k)\partial_k\psi$.
3. Hence

   $$
   b^k=\Delta_Wx^k=-g^{ij}\,\Gamma^k_{ab}(h)\,\partial_i\Phi^a\partial_j\Phi^b ,
   $$

   which is bounded and continuous up to $p$.
4. $g^{ij}$ is continuous at $p$, so the operator is uniformly elliptic near $p$.
5. GT Lemma 3.4 applies to $-u$ on the disc $B\subset\mathrm{Int}\,U\cap B_\delta$ of the interior sphere condition. This proves Lemma A.4 as stated.

The sentences on pp.23 and 25 should say "$C^1$".

### G2. Avoiding $Z$ needs a smaller rounding width (Lemma 4.9(2); Theorem 5.1(b))

**Issue.**
- The paper shrinks only the push-off ("the push-off may be taken small enough to miss $Z$", p.12; "That the push-off scale depends on $Z$ is harmless", p.17). In (T1)/(T2) it chooses $t_z$ after $Z$ and shrinks the push-off (pp.36, 39), again without fitting the width to $Z$. (Lemma 4.9(2) itself claims only "some choice of representatives", so its statement is right; the proofs omit the width.)
- But the output is pushed off the rounded $\hat B$, which enters the wedge with a width fixed before $z$, and a minimiser $Z$ disjoint from $S_+\cup S_-$ can lie in that wedge near $\Gamma$.

**Repair.**
1. *The class does not depend on the width.* For admissible widths $\eta,\zeta$ the widths $(1-s)\eta+s\zeta$ are admissible, since both constraints in (12) are convex. So $s\mapsto\hat B((1-s)\eta+s\zeta)$ is a smooth isotopy, supported near $\Gamma$, and inside $\mathrm{Int}\,C$ by G5(ii).
2. Let $d_Z:=d(Z,S_+\cup S_-)$, or $d(Z,A_{t_z}\cup B)$ in (T1)/(T2). The covering map is 1-Lipschitz, so distances measured in the cover are $\ge d_Z$.
3. Round with $\lambda\eta$, $\lambda:=\min\{1,d_Z/(4\sup_\Gamma\eta\sqrt{1+m^2})\}$ (finite: $\eta$, $m$ are continuous on the compact $\Gamma$).
4. The modified part then has $|\xi|\le d_Z/4$ in (30) (see M3); as $\|h-\delta\|\le C_{\rm met}|\xi|\le g_0/24$ there by (35), it lies within $d_Z/2$ of $\Gamma$, so $\hat B(\lambda\eta)\cap p^{-1}(Z)=\varnothing$.
5. A push-off whose displacement is less than $d(\hat B(\lambda\eta),p^{-1}(Z))$ misses $p^{-1}(Z)$. It lies in the coarse class fixed before $z$, and the compression sequence is transported along the isotopy.

### G3. Lemma B.3(i),(ii) on the collar: $f$ versus $f_t$

**Issue.**
- "In the collar $\Gamma_t=\{f=-\varsigma t\}$" (p.34) holds only where $\chi\equiv1$ and $\psi_p\equiv0$.
- But $\mathcal C=L\times(0,r_0)$ (the collar of Lemma B.3) meets the transition band of the cut-off $\chi$ of (39), and may meet $D_p$, whose radius is not tied to $r_0$.

**Repair.**
1. Keep $\chi\equiv1$ near $r=0$, with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\mathrm{supp}\,\chi\subset\{r<r_0/2\}$, and $D_p\subset\{r>3r_0/4\}$. Put $\mathcal C':=L\times(0,3r_0/4)$, on which $f_t:=f+\varsigma t\chi$.
2. *(i)* On $I\times(0,r_1]$: $\varsigma f_t\ge\frac12a_0r>0$, for every $t>0$.
3. *(ii) in $\mathcal C'$.* Let $K_\chi=L\times\mathrm{supp}\,\chi'$ and $c_\chi=\min_{K_\chi}|df|>0$, by (25). For $t<\delta_\chi:=c_\chi/(2\sup|\chi'|)$, $f_t$ has no critical point in $\mathcal C'$, and the extremum argument runs with $f_t$.
4. Case C has $\gamma\subset\{r\le r_0/2\}\subset\mathcal C'$, so it is correct.
5. $\delta_\chi$ joins the minimum defining $\delta$ and restricts the $t$-range of Lemma B.3(iii).
6. Lemma B.2's collar case needs the same reading: by (ii) $f_t$ has no critical point in $\mathcal C'$.

### G4. Smoothing the width ramp (44)

**Issue.** After smoothing, $\eta'$ may be non-zero just inside $B_{\rho_2}(p)$ or just below $r_1/2$, where (12) still needs $|\eta'|\le\kappa$ and $\eta\le\eta_{\max}$. The same ramp is reused in (T1).

**Repair.**
1. The proof of Corollary B.4(2)–(3) already works on $\mathcal K\subset G''\cap\{r\ge r_1/4\}$; only its statement is narrower.
2. Once $\Gamma_t$ lies within $\min\{\rho_2/4,r_1/8\}$ of $A\cap B$, it gives the bounds on $\Gamma_t$ outside $\bigcup B_{3\rho_2/4}(p)$, within $\{r\ge3r_1/8\}$.
3. Smoothing at scale $<\min\{\rho_2/4,r_1/8\}$ keeps $\{\eta\ne\eta_2\}\supset\{\eta'\ne0\}$ inside that set.

### G5. Missing width constraints, and one constant

**(i) Sheet separation.**
- Chart (30) needs the tube to meet $\tilde B$ only in the two sheets through $x$; Lemma 5.4 assumes this (normal slice, p.14) but fixes no radius, and (T0)–(T2) do not check it.
- Add $\eta\sqrt{1+m^2}\le\frac12\min\{\mathrm{reach}(A_t),\mathrm{reach}(B)\}$.
- Uniformity in $t$ follows from $A_t\to A$ in $C^1$ and the $C^3$ bounds of Corollary B.4(3); build this bound into $\eta^{\rm geo}_1$ before $\delta$, with $\delta$ also below the threshold for $\mathrm{reach}(A_t)\ge\frac12\mathrm{reach}(A)$. Near $\mathcal T$ and $L$ ($\eta_2$ is chosen after $t$) positivity suffices; likewise in (ii).

**(ii) Distance to $S$.**
- Nothing in the width choices (p.17, (42), (48)) keeps the rounding of $\tilde B_\uparrow$ (toward $S_1$) or of $\tilde B_\downarrow$ (toward $S_0$) away from $S_0\cup S_1$.
- Yet Lemma 4.9(1) ("they lie in $C$", p.12) and hence Theorem 5.1(a) (adjacency to $x$) need it.
- Add $\eta\sqrt{1+m^2}\le\frac14d(S,S_+\cup S_-)$. In (T1)/(T2) use $\frac18d(S,A\cup B)$, built into $\eta^{\rm geo}_1$ (hence $\eta_1,\varepsilon_\ast$) before $\delta$, with $\delta$ also below the threshold for $d(S,A_t\cup B)\ge\frac12d(S,A\cup B)$. At the last step take $\sigma<\frac14d(S,\cdot)/\sup|X|$.

**(iii) Admissibility independent of the sector.**
- p.15 says the bounds see the sector only through $\theta$, "the same for all four sectors", so one $\eta$ serves frontiers and exchanged surfaces. This holds for the lower bounds of (11), except that $M'=\sup_\Gamma|m'|$ (p.31) uses one sector's slope $m$ and (T0) takes $\eta\le\min_\Gamma\eta_{\max}$ (p.17), which depends on the sector rounded.
- Define admissibility by the sector-free lower bounds $\underline\eta$, $\underline\kappa$ of (11), with one change on p.31: replace $M'=\sup_\Gamma|m'|$ by $\cot^2(\theta_\bullet/2)M'$, where $M'$ bounds $|m'|$ on $\{\theta\ge\theta_\bullet\}$ (as Cor. B.4(3) bounds it, uniformly in $t$), since an adjacent sector has slope $1/m$ and $|(1/m)'|=|m'|/m^2$. Then every entry of (35) and $\kappa$ is bounded below for both slopes. Take $\eta\le\underline\eta(\theta_0,\dots)$ in (T0), and build $\eta^{\rm geo}_1,\kappa_1,\eta_2$ from these bounds in (T1)/(T2). Then the claim on p.15 holds.

### G6. Independence of $t$ (§B.4, reused in §B.5)

**Issue.**
- $H_t$ carries the frontiers at $t_0$ to those at $t$ (p.36), but "small push-offs to admissible push-offs" is loose: $H_t(\hat B)$ is not a rounding of the new frontier. The conclusion does follow from the paper's lemmas: $T_t\simeq\tilde B_t=H_t(\tilde B_{t_0})\simeq T_{t_0}$ by Lemmas 5.4(3) (read as in M3) and 5.5.

**Repair.** State that chain, with G2 (step 1) for the width.

## 4. Misstatements (each corrected locally; no proof's structure changes)

- **M1 (Prop. 5.7(1), pp.19, 32).** "Isolated in $\mathrm{Int}\,A\cap\mathrm{Int}\,B$" should read "isolated in $\mathcal T$": by (24) the zeros of $f_p$ accumulate at $p$, while the same sentence shows that $p$ is the only critical point of $f_p$ in $D_p$, which is what is used.
- **M2 (strict-side claims).** p.29 says the new sheet lies in the open wedge "where $|\xi_2|<\eta$", and p.16 that "$\partial Q$ lies in the sector's interior". Both fail on the band where the $\chi$ of B.1 is $\equiv1$ near $1$, so $\Theta(t)=|t|$. Harmless: Lemma 5.4(2) itself states $\hat B\subset\overline U$ with a collar into $U$, and in Step 2 of Lemma 5.6 $D'\subset\partial Q$ on the band.
- **M3 (Lemma 5.4: (1), (3), (5), smoothness).**
  - The modification reaches $\eta\sqrt{1+m^2}$ from $\Gamma$, not $\eta$; p.30 itself writes $|\xi|\le\eta\sqrt{1+m^2}$. The fifth entry of (35) should therefore be $\varrho_\partial/(2\sqrt{1+m^2})$.
  - In (3), no diffeomorphism maps the smooth $\hat B$ onto the cornered $\tilde B$; read (3) piecewise smoothly (Definition A.1), which is all (5) and Lemma 5.6 use. Between two roundings G2 (step 1) gives a smooth isotopy.
  - Lemma 5.4 promises a $C^\infty$ $\hat B$ for a $C^1$ width, but by (31) $\hat B$ is only as smooth as $\eta$ (and as $m$ and the chart, smooth here). Take widths $C^\infty$: (35) leaves room, since $8m^2\kappa^2=\frac29g_0<\frac14g_0$.
- **M4 (Lemma 5.6, Step 2).** "Area$(B')\to\dots$ as the push-off tends to 0" and "$B'$ has a genuine corner" mix the smooth and piecewise smooth readings. Cleaner: take $B'=B_\gamma\cup D$; its corner is exactly $\gamma$, its area is exactly $\mathrm{Area}(B)-\mathrm{Area}(D')+\mathrm{Area}(D)$, and it is isotopic to $B$ across the ball bounded by $D\cup D'$.
- **M5 (Theorem C, p.2).**
  - The statement concerns "vertices of genus at most $\ell$ and relative area at most $a_0$, for every $a_0>0$", but the proof (p.20) treats $D_{\ell,a_0}=\{g<\ell\}\cup\{g=\ell,A\le a_0\}$.
  - The literal set need not be downward closed, and if $a_0<\min\{A(v):g(v)\le\ell\}$ (positive by Lemma 4.8(ii)) it is empty, hence not contractible (footnote 2, p.3), whereas for $\ell>g(K)$ the proved set $D_{\ell,a_0}\supseteq D_{\ell-1}\ne\varnothing$ is contractible. For $\ell=g(K)$ the sets coincide and §6.2 needs $D_{\ell,a_0}\ne\varnothing$ (p.20); "for every $a_0>0$" omits this.
  - First noted in submission #10, §5(b).
- **M6 (wording).** p.26: "increase area" should be "do not decrease area", for interior variations. p.25: "$U\subset S$ near 0" should be "the tangent cone of $U$ at $0$ is $S$".

## 5. What remains external, and conclusion

After G1–G6 no remaining gap was found in the paper's own argument for Theorem A. Besides standard results (elliptic theory from Gilbarg–Trudinger; Lichtenstein [9, Thm 4.1]; Vekua [18]; isotopy extension [20]; Seifert's algorithm [12]; irreducibility of $E(K)$; piecewise smooth isotopy of smooth surfaces implies smooth isotopy), it rests on four inputs, all named by the paper:
1. **[17, Thm A.5]** ((U) for distinct vertices), with the caveat in §1 above.
2. **[17, Prop. A.1, Cor. A.3]** ((Fin)). (E)(ii), cited as [17, Cor. A.4], is re-derived in Theorem A.6 from (E)(i) and (Fin).
3. **Hass–Scott 1988, Thm 6.12**, including the membership clause (27). The paper says plainly that this clause is "not reached by the argument printed for it" (p.23; see also Remark A.8).
4. **Kakimizu's connectedness theorem** [10, Thm A].

I did not re-prove these four inputs.

**Conclusion.** In my judgement the geometric half of the proof of Theorem A is correct once G1–G6 are repaired, relative to the inputs above. No statement of Theorem A changes, and Theorem C holds in the form proved in §6.2, that is, for $D_\ell$ and for every non-empty $D_{\ell,a_0}$.
- The least routine repairs are G1 (the p.24 identity, applied to $x^k$, bounds the drift Hopf needs) and G5(ii) (keep the outputs off $S$); G2 (shrink the rounding width, not only the push-off) is short but needed for (b).
- With submission #10 (Lean: Theorem B; conditionally Prop. 5.2 and §6), every internal step of Theorem A's proof is addressed by one of the two; neither re-proves the four inputs.

*AI disclosure.* Reading, re-derivation and drafting were done with AI assistance (Claude); the result was checked by several independent AI review agents (one compared every quotation with the rendered PDF). I have not verified every step by hand myself; all arguments are written out so that each can be checked.

21.title: Partial link extensions: Hopf fibre links, annular satellites, and connected sums
21.excerpt_md: This supplement concerns *Contractibility of the Complex of Incompressible Seifert Surfaces: The Knot Case of Kakimizu's Problem*, attribute…
21.body_md:
This supplement concerns *Contractibility of the Complex of Incompressible Seifert Surfaces: The Knot Case of Kakimizu's Problem*, attributed to Apex Intelligence, **the official competition version dated 11 September 2026, 48 pages**, with PDF SHA-256 `34f17d7d99780d3fd3626d9e5d7b35d6aa76661c404f191b6df341b300c0c06f`.

The Introduction, p. 2, leaves general links untreated; Theorem D uses linking-indecomposability. This **partial extension** proves contractibility for every oriented Hopf fibre link. For the balanced family, arbitrary finite inclusions are nullhomotoped by equivariant height interpolation, regular-fibre arc-flow averaging and region-potential common rounding in a perfect-matching polytope; unbalanced links are fibred and give a point. Annular satellites have three complete calculations: a cone under a single-boundary condition, one edge for torus companions, and a tree for $K_{7/19}$ beyond that condition. Banks closure organises these results with the four-fibre tree and the connected-surface extension under their declared inputs.

### 1. The object and the combined theorem

For an oriented link $L\subset S^3$, let $\phi:\pi_1(E(L))\to\mathbb Z$ send each actual positive meridian to $1$. Vertices are ambient-isotopy classes of oriented, componentwise incompressible spanning surfaces with no closed components and one prescribed oriented boundary on each labelled torus; boundaries may move. All genera, disconnected and non-minimal systems are included.

For connected lifts of the **whole open complements**, with $V_{S,j}=\tau^jV_{S,0}$, put

$$
D(S,R)=\max\{j:V_R\cap V_{S,j}\ne\varnothing\}
-\min\{j:V_R\cap V_{S,j}\ne\varnothing\},\qquad
\delta([S],[R])=\min_{S',R'}D(S',R').
$$

Distinct vertices with $\delta=1$ are edges of the flag complex $X(L)=IS_{\mathrm{cyc}}(L)$. Whole complements are connected with one common deck choice. For connected spanning surfaces this equals the original geometric-disjointness complex; disconnected assertions concern $X$.

**Combined partial extension.** Permitted non-split factors are:

- knots, using Competition Theorem A and the unknot argument;
- links with all incompressible spanning surfaces connected, under the multiple-boundary inputs in §5;
- all balanced Hopf fibre links $H_{2m}$, $m\ge1$;
- prescribed-class fibred links, including unbalanced Hopf fibre links;
- two oppositely oriented zero-framed parallels of a nontrivial (SB) companion;
- the specified parallels of $K_{7/19}$ and its mirror.

Every finite binary iterated oriented connected sum joining specified components in previously disjoint blocks has contractible $X$. If $r$ counts original nonfibred factors,

$$
r=0\Longrightarrow X(L)=\{*\},\qquad
r\ge1\Longrightarrow |X(L)|\cong
\prod_{J_i\ \mathrm{nonfibred}}|X(J_i)|\times\mathbb R^{r-1}.
$$

This is a choice-dependent realization homeomorphism with Banks's ordered triangulation. There is no negative exponent or universal all-minimal factor class; another factor requires its own contraction.

### 2. All Hopf fibre links: a finite-input proof

For balanced $H_{2m}$, $E=S^1_h\times P_{2m}$ and $\phi(h)=0$. The actual boundary is the signed fibre slope $h=\lambda_i^H+\mu_i^H$. Hatcher's essential-surface classification, pp. 20–22, excludes horizontal pieces; successive verticalisation fixing earlier cut faces gives $m$ positive-negative matching annuli. Projected relative-path double cosets and simultaneous straightening certify the vertex bijection under ambient isotopy; PL-code equality is decidable. All vertices have norm zero.

Normalisation identifies common arcs and excludes bigons, half-bigons and relative product regions. PS Proposition 3.2, pp. 1494–1495, makes the complete-block calculation the class minimum. Cutting along the entire second matching gives a connected $m$-holed sphere; its signed region potential satisfies

$$
\delta([F_a],[F_b])=\max H-\min H.
$$

All values are attained open-block indices, with one common deck shift. Crossings force three consecutive indices, so true simplices have simultaneous disjoint normal representatives. The six-hole converse and tetrahedron remain special structural results.

**Finite-input theorem.** Every finite $K\subset X(H_{2m})$ has its inclusion nullhomotoped to any fixed $M_*$ inside finite $Y\supset K\cup\{M_*\}$, without an intersection or radius cutoff.

Choose common PL arcs, bands and triangulation. Each matching defines a band circle map inducing $\psi$, with real lift $h_M$ normalised at one band-free point and satisfying $h_M(\tau z)=h_M(z)+1$. Convex heights remain equivariant and boundary-monotone of period change $\pm1$. Regular phases avoid vertex phases; each fibre has one endpoint per hole and opposite-sign interval ends. Deleting circles leaves legal matchings $A_r(h)$, without assuming complementary-block invariance.

First average arc indicators over the regular phase intervals:

$$
W_e(h)=\sum_J|J|\,\mathbf1_{\{e\in A_{r_J}(h)\}},\qquad r_J\in J.
$$

The positive arc classes come from disjoint fibres of the same map, giving an embedded bipartite support graph $G$ with its actual endpoint order. Every hole has incident weight one, hence $W(h)\in P_G$, where

$$
P_G=\{w\ge0:\sum_{e\ni v}w_e=1\text{ for every labelled hole }v\}.
$$

**Fixed-graph carrier.** Cap holes by radial stars and use connected complementary regions. Orient edges from negative to positive. For reference matching indicator $m$, circulation decomposition into simple cycles gives a region potential, unique up to one common constant:

$$
w=m+D_Gu,\qquad (D_Gu)_e=u_{\ell(e)}-u_{r(e)}.
$$

For $0\le\theta<1$, set $q_f^\theta=\lfloor u_f+\theta\rfloor$ and $m^\theta=m+D_Gq^\theta$. Common rounding preserves integer-endpoint bounds $-m_e\le u_\ell-u_r\le1-m_e$, so $m_e^\theta\in\{0,1\}$. Sector differences telescope, retaining each incident sum one. Thus every threshold gives a legal matching $M_\theta$, including disconnected graphs, bridges and non-disk regions.

For any two matchings in $G$, their difference potential descends across unused edges without losing values; cap-star sectors do not join distinct regions. In the complete complement of the second matching, its jumps across first-matching walls are exactly the complete-block jumps. Common arcs stay cut boundaries. Its oscillation is therefore the class distance. Since $q^{\theta'}-q^\theta$ takes only $0,1$ for $\theta<\theta'$, threshold outputs form a true simplex. Their finite integral

$$
\mathcal S_G(w)=\int_0^1[M_\theta]\,d\theta
$$

has average arc indicator $w$. Reference changes are integral potential shifts; root changes rotate the threshold. Zero-weight edges occur in no output. After choosing a supported reference their potentials agree, so decoding commutes with deletion. Rules from different graphs agree on common zero faces even if their other edges cross.

On a true simplex, root-normalised integer matching potentials have pairwise oscillation at most one and form a coordinatewise chain. Relative to its least member they are binary; the rounded convex potential occupies each matching for precisely its original barycentric coefficient. Thus decoding recovers the input exactly. The induced matching complex triangulates $P_G$, without assuming it is one simplex.

A uniform height bound gives finitely many segment, order and gluing templates, retaining arc winding classes. Finite rational subdivision fixes phase order and affine weights. Colliding intervals lose vanishing weights; positive intervals retain their templates. Thus $W$ is continuous in a fixed finite arc-coordinate space and has finitely many support graphs. Fixed-graph decoders are similarly continuous and piecewise affine. Their compact polytopes glue on the certified zero faces, giving continuous $F=\mathcal S\circ W$ with finite output.

For an initial simplex, band height is $b_e+c_eu_e$ with $c_e=\sum_{M\ni e}\lambda_M\in[0,1]$. Its arc's phase-occupation length is $c_e$, giving $W(h_\lambda)=\sum\lambda_M\chi_M$ and $F(h_\lambda)=x$. Hence

$$
C_K(x,t)=F\left((1-t)\sum_{M\in\sigma}\lambda_Mh_M+t h_{M_*}\right)
$$

is the desired homotopy. One height family serves all faces. A terminating rational procedure is specified; full software implementation is not claimed. Compact sphere images lie in finite CW subcomplexes, so these inclusion nullhomotopies and Whitehead prove contractibility. The finite image $Y$ need not itself be contractible.

**Attribution.** Circle maps, regular fibres and averaging follow Hatcher 2008, second proof, pp. 5–6. Classical planar matching heights are background from Propp, arXiv:math/0209005v3 (2021), §3, Theorem 2, pp. 21–22; *Electronic Journal of Combinatorics* 32(4) (2025), #P4.26. The needed rounding and gluing are proved here. PS Theorem 1.1 already states the balanced-family conclusion; this independent proof avoids §§4–7 and retains §3.

For an unbalanced Hopf union, $k=\phi(h)=\sum_i\epsilon_i\ne0$; the Seifert horizontal product complement proves fibration, so $X$ is a point. A single fibre is the unknot. Therefore **all nonempty oriented Hopf fibre links have contractible $X$**.

### 3. Annular satellites: cone, edge and complete tree

For a nontrivial companion $C$, take its zero-framed parallels oriented $+C,-C$. Their exterior is

$$
M=P\cup_T Q,\qquad P=S^1_\lambda\times B,\qquad Q=E(C),
$$

with $B$ a pair of pants and $\lambda$ the preferred companion longitude. Total oriented linking vanishes on all of $\pi_1(Q)$; it is not the companion knot-fibration class. An inner-inner seam gives the incompressible norm-zero annulus $A$.

**(SB)** says that every connected orientable essential surface in $Q$, with nonempty boundary entirely of preferred-longitude slope, has one boundary circle. Essential means incompressible and boundary-incompressible.

**Cone theorem.** Under (SB), $\delta([A],v)=1$ for every other vertex. Essential minimum-$T$ cut pieces have longitudinal pattern annuli. An outer-outer annulus would close two single-boundary companion pieces, forbidden here. Only two reaching annuli remain unless the surface is $A$. Joint straightening supplies a disjoint annulus for this same representative.

In its whole complement, that annulus separates into two chambers: otherwise a once-crossing loop contradicts $\phi=0$ there. The complete lift has width one. Width zero for any representatives forces the annulus to be a whole component using both actual boundaries, so any remainder would be closed. Only $[A]$ has distance zero; flagness gives the cone.

**Exact edge theorem.** For torus companions and mirrors, the only other vertex is two oppositely oriented companion fibres with reaching collars. Longitudinal essential surfaces are horizontal; relative-class primitivity and the product complement force one boundary and a fibre. Joint fibre normalisation and compatible gluing absorb winding. Its complexity $\chi_-=2(2g(C)-1)>0$ exhibits a disconnected non-minimal vertex.

Hatcher–Thurston's Theorem 1 and Propositions 1–2, pp. 228–230, give the exact two-bridge criterion: (SB) holds precisely when every admissible zero-slope minus-continued-fraction carrier is all-even. An odd coefficient supplies an essential two-longitude neighbourhood double. The family $K_{(2m-1)/(4m-1)}$, $m\ge1$, and mirrors passes. For $m\ge2$, the nonmonic Alexander polynomial $mt^2+(1-2m)t+m$ proves nonfibredness, including $5_2=K_{3/7}$ up to handedness; no parallel-complex infinitude is claimed.

**Complete tree beyond (SB).** For $K_{7/19}$, the only zero-slope carriers are

$$
7/19=1+[-2,-2,2,-2]=[2,-2,-2,-3].
$$

HT parameter moves classify the whole longitudinal system as a pure parallel stack of genus-two single-boundary fibres $R$, or separating genus-three two-boundary surfaces $S$ of relative class zero. Mixed disjoint systems are impossible.

Every vertex is $A$, the unique disconnected $+R,-R$ assembly $G$, or a connected chain of $k$ copies of $S$. The chain has genus $3k$ and minimum torus intersection $2k$. Its canonical coordinates are $F(k,a,t)$, with $k\ge1$, $0\le a<2k$, $\gcd(2a+1,2k)=1$ and $t\in\mathbb Z$. The gcd condition excludes all closed components, and path orientations are forced. Product-annulus comparison and a middle-slab confinement argument prove that companion returns have zero meridional winding, so no twist coordinates are identified.

Joint replacement by nested waves gives a marked four-hole arc model. Essentialising the whole union preserves disjointness in one direction; simultaneous assembly proves the converse. Crossings force three complete layers, while disjointness with one whole surface connected gives width one. Only $G$ is disconnected, so this covers every distinct pair.

Pillowcase coordinates send a chain to $(p,2k)$, where

$$
p=2a+1+4kt,\qquad 0\le a<2k,
$$

and identify $A=1/0$. Chains are exactly the reduced odd-numerator fractions $p/k$, $k>0$, and their cyclic edges satisfy

$$
|pk'-p'k|=1.
$$

The annulus neighbours are all $k=1$ chains and $G$, which is a leaf. Of the two lower Farey candidates, exactly one numerator is odd. Unique parent descent reaches $A$; maximal denominators exclude finite cycles. The full graph is a tree, and flag completion adds no higher simplex. Root-path contraction is continuous in the weak simplicial topology. The linear family has $\delta(A,F_k)=k$, including the genus-six distance-two example. The annulus is not a cone vertex, while the entire complex is contractible. Reflection gives the mirror calculation.

### 4. Banks closure and all-fibre local insertions

Banks Theorem 10.3, arXiv:1109.0965v1, p. 22, gives the two-nonfibred-factor product. Its all-incompressible transfer uses cyclic widths; fibred absorption removes winding and preserves and reflects edges. Decomposing-annulus and product-disk arguments prove non-splitness and that a component sum is fibred exactly when both factors are. Binary-tree induction gives $r-1$. The product theorem belongs to Banks.

For balanced Hopf links,

$$
\pi_1(E(H_{2m}))=\mathbb Z\langle f\rangle\times F_{2m-1},\qquad\phi(f)=0.
$$

Choose a free basis $x,y_1,\ldots,y_{2m-2}$ with values $1,0,\ldots,0$. The free kernel has basis $\{x^ny_jx^{-n}:n\in\mathbb Z,\ 1\le j\le2m-2\}$. For $m\ge2$ it has infinite rank, excluding a compact spanning fibre's finitely generated group. Thus these balanced factors are nonfibred. For $m=1$, projection of the annular base onto its circle gives the prescribed annular fibration, so $H_2$ is fibred and $X(H_2)$ is a point.

Let $I$ index nonfibred knots among $2m$ local insertions. For $m\ge2$,

$$
|X(H_{2m}\#_1K_1\cdots\#_{2m}K_{2m})|
\cong |X(H_{2m})|\times\prod_{i\in I}|X(K_i)|\times\mathbb R^{|I|}.
$$

Here $r=1+|I|$. For $H_2$ the base is fibred, so $r=|I|$: $I=\varnothing$ gives a point, and $|I|\ge1$ gives $\prod_{i\in I}|X(K_i)|\times\mathbb R^{|I|-1}$. No negative exponent is used. Fibred knots add no winding coordinate. The products use Banks; contraction of arbitrary nonfibred knot factors also uses Competition Theorem A.

For every nontrivial two-parallel satellite here, the injected $\pi_1(T)=\mathbb Z^2$ lies in $\ker\phi$, since total oriented linking vanishes on the companion group. A compact spanning fibre with boundary has free group and cannot contain it. In particular the $K_{7/19}$ parallel factor and its mirror are nonfibred.

### 5. Connected surfaces, the four-fibre tree and Seifert scope

The independent connectivity bound uses the rational Alexander rank:

$$
b_0(F)-1\le r_\phi(L),\qquad
r_\phi(L)=\dim_{\mathbb Q(t)}\left(H_1(\widetilde E_\phi;\mathbb Q)
\otimes_{\mathbb Q[t,t^{-1}]}\mathbb Q(t)\right).
$$

Whole-surface equivariant Mayer–Vietoris proves it. Rank zero forces connected spanning surfaces and non-splitness. For two components, all-connected means not a boundary link; compression cannot merge boundary-bearing components.

Under the target's connected multiple-boundary geometric inputs and Theorem B, $X$ and its nonempty full subcomplexes downward closed in complete lexicographic complexity $(g,A)$ are contractible. Arbitrary rectangular caps are not included. The proof retains the local repairs and §6.3, p. 22, length correction. Exact zero-linking braid certificates are supplied; attainment, disjointness, compactness, regularity and local estimates remain inherited.

The stronger four-fibre calculation gives an induced Farey tree:

$$
V(X(H_4))=\{p/q:\gcd(p,q)=1,\ q>0\text{ odd}\},\qquad
p/q\sim p'/q'\iff |pq'-p'q|=1.
$$

PS §3 certifies the class minimum; unique descent to the integer line proves it is a tree.

In a Seifert exterior, $k=0$ gives vertical annuli and reduced $X=MS$; the independent Hopf proof covers the whole balanced family. The general exceptional-fibre $k=0$ case remains unproved here. At $k\ne0$, the horizontal product complement gives the prescribed fibration and a point. Boundary and filling classifications are in the repository.

### 6. The PS certificate and its consequence

The self-contained `proof/ps-counterexample.md` uses eight balanced Hopf fibres, each with Banks's nonfibred genus-one knot locally inserted. Four taut classes satisfy the **published** Definition 4.1, including its torus deletion, and

$$
\pi_A(B)=P_-,\qquad\delta(A,B)=\delta(S,P_-)=2,
$$

with $\delta(A,S)=\delta(B,S)=\delta(A,P_-)=\delta(B,P_-)=1$. The independent direction rule gives $B<_A S$. This refutes Lemma 6.1's ordered and adjacent-or-equal conclusions, p. 1499, and Lemma 6.5's radius-one vertex conclusion, p. 1501. Computing $\pi_A(S)=\pi_A(P_-)=A$ makes the induced flag four-cycle finite and $A$-convex, contradicting Theorem 7.2, pp. 1503–1504.

Banks coordinates and a separate nonparallelism/whole-block calculation certify the class distances. Torus deletion merges chambers and changes the complete lifted wall. The cycle nevertheless fills in a finite $[0,1]^{12}$ subcomplex with 6,144 vertices, including a filling in the minimum layer. **Theorem 1.1's whole-complex statement is not refuted.** Its disconnected proof uses the failed Lemma 6.1 and Theorem 7.2; Lemma 6.5 enters §8 directly. The knot case is unaffected, and no general replacement contraction is supplied.

### 7. Dependencies and literature boundary

The positive proofs avoid PS's projection and general contraction, while retaining §3 and the Banks transfer's §5 order interfaces, including its subscript correction. The satellite tree uses Banks's expressly extended all-incompressible width criterion. Competition Theorem A and the connected-surface analytic package remain inputs.

A literature search on 7 October 2026 located no erratum to PS 2012. Schultens, *Topology Proceedings* 50 (2017), and *AGT* 18 (2018), use weighted, free-boundary frameworks with connected complement; the Seifert proof is restricted to closed spaces. No automatic transfer, two-dimensional counterexample, general satellite/JSJ gluing or all-link contraction is asserted.

Full proofs, source editions and pages, dependencies, certificates and SHA-256 manifest are in the [evidence repository](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p01-seifert-links-partial) at revision `c92d4b58bdc2d483bca50aa55e38894db6fa2042`.

GPT-6.1 Sol, in OpenAI Codex under human direction, developed the proof, ran the computations where applicable, and drafted this text; a separate GPT-6.1 Sol session in a fresh context performed an adversarial review. Claude planned the work, checked key steps against the sources, and reviewed and edited the final text. No human expert has certified the work.

23.title: A partial Lean 4 formalization of the full paper
23.body_md:
# Seifert surfaces: partial Lean formalization

A **partial** Lean 4 formalization of *Contractibility of the Complex of
Incompressible Seifert Surfaces: The Knot Case of Kakimizu’s Problem*
(Apex Intelligence, 11 September 2026).

**20 of 46 original assertions are verified; 26 remain open.** Theorem B is
complete. Headline Theorems A, C and D remain open. Start with
[MainTheorems.lean](MainTheorems.lean): one public entry imports all 20 accepted
originals and their proof dependencies in one Lean project. See the
[all-46 result checklist](docs/PAPER_RESULTS.md) for exact statements and scope.

Proof development stopped at canonical revision
`a2bf8eb443d6e3a8656c3893709a30ad920e153d`. This release preserves the accepted
public statements and their reviewed proof content; packaging adds no original
result credit. Some proof dependencies are restored closed proof terms from the
previously checked development. These are repository-local textual source,
submitted to Lean’s normal kernel, rather than newly derived mathematical proofs.

## Main and supporting results

Theorem B proves contractibility of the weak geometric realization of every
exchange complex, without finite-vertex or finite-descending-link hypotheses.
Lemma 2.2 supplies an injective well-ordered complexity. Lemma 2.4 proves
heredity for the qualified full subcomplexes and descending links.

The same entry includes the push-off and tangency results 5.5/5.7, the link
connectedness and compression results 6.1/6.2, the conditional minimal-surface
results A.2–A.5 and A.7, the intersection estimates B.1–B.3, and the barrier and
conformal-structure results C.6–C.9 and C.11.

A.2/A.5 require an attained minimizer in the specified class; A.7 assumes the
supplied A.6 minimizer. C.6/C.11 require a full Lemaire minimizer. C.9 retains
the manuscript’s L2′/L2″ compatibility alternatives. These implications do not
establish the open minimizer-existence or headline results. Corollary 2.3 remains
open as an original: the qualified nonempty-downset support receives zero
additional original credit.

```lean
import MainTheorems

#check SeifertSurfaces.exchange_complex_contractible
#check SeifertSurfaces.OriginalEndpoints.original_5_5
#check SeifertSurfaces.OriginalEndpoints.AppendixAOriginal.A5_original
#check SeifertSurfaces.AppendixC.Original.paper_C9
```

## Build and verification

Install [elan](https://github.com/leanprover/elan), Git and Python 3, then run
from the repository root:

```sh
lake exe cache get
lake build MainTheorems
python3 tools/verify.py
```

Lean is pinned to **4.35.0-rc3**, Mathlib to
`3f6737de4761ec7bf368491fe9faccc991ebd6ca`, and the Lake manifest pins transitive
packages. Runtime compilation uses repository-local project source and these
pinned dependencies. It requires no historical project object, original
workspace, or independent verification environment.

The public verifier checks source custody hashes, scans Lean tokens and recognized
serialized declaration payloads, builds the common entry, and audits exactly
**25 original declaration heads plus one qualified support head** from
[RECEIVING_MANIFEST.json](tools/RECEIVING_MANIFEST.json). Their axiom sets stay
within `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. It then executes the 15
literal/operative receiving scripts and the actual-common kernel audit with
its logical result validator: exactly 507 records and 48 required safe-operative
equalities, including the safe-to-partial reference boundary. This one public
command is the authoritative receiving verification pass.

`python3 tools/verify.py --sources-only` checks custody, source tokens and
recognized serialized payloads without compiling. Payload scanning rejects
serialized axioms and `sorryAx` in the recognized forms. Closed expressions
still require the normal Lean kernel and complete root axiom audit; scanning
alone is not proof verification.

[VERIFICATION.json](docs/VERIFICATION.json) records the final receiving checks
and exact bounded fidelity receipts. [BUILD_STATUS.md](docs/BUILD_STATUS.md)
explains restored proof terms and the source-build boundary. The pinned Mathlib
cache is reused; this release does not claim an independent source rebuild of
Mathlib.

## Source layout

| Location | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| [seifert-surfaces/unified/](seifert-surfaces/unified/) | Common proof-source tree and selected shared provider owners. |
| [seifert-surfaces/core/](seifert-surfaces/core/), [seifert-surfaces/conformal/](seifert-surfaces/conformal/) | Preserved baseline copies; current compilation uses the unified tree. |
| [seifert-surfaces/historical/](seifert-surfaces/historical/) | Documentary original/provider sources and compact provenance; excluded from the public import closure. |
| [docs/](docs/) | Result checklist, exact declaration inventory, custody hashes, contexts and verification receipts. |
| [tools/](tools/) | Public verifier and root axiom audit entry. |

Historical provider sources may retain unaccepted sibling placeholders. The
archive is not globally claimed complete, buildable or placeholder-free.
Compiled project objects, old caches and large historical audit dumps are not
release inputs. Historical exporter reads are offline provenance only; missing
historical elaborator metadata is not represented as fully restored.

[SOURCE_ISSUES.md](SOURCE_ISSUES.md) preserves manuscript qualifications;
[FORMALIZATION_ISSUES.md](FORMALIZATION_ISSUES.md) records Lean interface issues.
[THIRD_PARTY.md](THIRD_PARTY.md), [NOTICE](NOTICE) and the provider license files
preserve source attribution. The copied Apache license applies to the named
provider sources; this release assigns no blanket license to the Seifert work.

The repo is available at [rational-intelligence/seifert-surfaces](https://github.com/rational-intelligence/seifert-surfaces)

13.title: A complete Lean 4 formalization of the full paper
13.body_md:
# Curve complex formalization

A Lean 4 formalization of the complex of essential curves that pairwise
intersect at most once, with contractibility in genus two as its main result.
The development follows *The Complex of Curves Pairwise Intersecting at Most
Once Is Contractible in Genus Two* (Apex Intelligence, 11 September 2026),
including the four numbered results in Section 1.2.

Start with [MainTheorems.lean](MainTheorems.lean): one public entry module imports
all four original theorem declarations and their necessary proof dependencies.

## The mathematical object

For a closed surface S, C₁(S) is the flag simplicial complex whose vertices are
ambient-isotopy classes of essential simple closed curves. A finite collection
of distinct vertices spans a simplex when every pair has geometric intersection
number at most one. The topological conclusions below concern its geometric
realization with the weak topology.

The more general `curveComplex S d` uses intersection bound `d`; thus C₀(S)
is the disjointness complex and C₁(S) allows one intersection. See
[SourceRealization.lean](curve-complex/CurveComplexGenusTwo/Foundations/SourceRealization.lean)
for the complex and its realization.

## Main results

The first three declarations live in `CurveComplexGenusTwo.SourceTopology`.
They take a surface `S` with a topology and a two-dimensional real charted-space
structure, together with the explicit `IsGenus S g` hypothesis. This predicate
records nonemptiness, a closed-surface structure, and the integral homology
conditions defining the genus; see
[Genus.lean](curve-complex/CurveComplexGenusTwo/Dictionary/Genus.lean).

| Article | Result | Lean declaration and proof source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.1 | C₁(S) is contractible when S has genus two. | [`c1_contractible_genusTwo`](curve-complex/Theorems/MainTheorem11ProofOriginal12Consumer.lean) |
| 1.2 | C₁(S) is integrally acyclic in genus two: positive-degree homology vanishes and the degree-zero augmentation is an isomorphism. | [`c1_acyclic_genusTwo`](curve-complex/CurveComplexGenusTwo/Topology/ActualOriginalArticle/Main12OriginalCanonicalImportsHaasConditionalV15.lean) |
| 1.3 | C₁(S) is simply connected for every genus g ≥ 2. | [`c1_simplyConnected_allGenus`](curve-complex/Theorems/SourceTopologyMainBound.lean) |
| 1.4 | A supplied genus-two hyperelliptic model gives the unique full-preimage arc/circle dictionary for essential curve classes. | [`headline_hyperelliptic_dictionary`](curve-complex/CurveComplexGenusTwo/Topology/ActualOriginalArticle/MainTheorem14OriginalComplete86.lean) |

The fourth declaration is
`CurveComplex.HyperellipticModel.headline_hyperelliptic_dictionary`.
For a supplied `HyperellipticModel E S`, it identifies the disjoint union of
marked non-loop arc classes and 3|3 circle classes on the quotient surface
with all essential curve vertices on E. The correspondence is induced by
literal full preimages: arcs give curves with connected complement, while
3|3 circles give curves with disconnected complement. Its conclusion is a
unique equivalence of these classes, with the stated complement properties.

## Mathematical foundations

The supporting development connects concrete surface geometry to the topology
of the curve complex:

- **Surfaces and curves:** surface classification, Jordan curves, Schoenflies,
  essential curves, ambient isotopy, and geometric intersection numbers.
- **Geometric constructions:** proper arcs, simultaneous position, local disk
  and band arguments, covering spaces, and hyperbolic surface geometry.
- **Topology and algebraic topology:** simplicial realizations, CW structures,
  path homotopies, singular homology, and Hurewicz/Whitehead arguments.
- **Hyperelliptic geometry:** the supplied branched-cover model and the
  full-preimage correspondence between quotient arcs/circles and curves.

The genus-two contractibility proof combines the simple-connectivity and
integral-acyclicity results through the development's CW machinery. Its short
final assembly can be read directly in the linked Theorem 1.1 source.

## Source layout

[MainTheorems.lean](MainTheorems.lean) is the public entry point. The supporting
sources are grouped under [curve-complex/](curve-complex/):

| Directory | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| [`CurveComplexGenusTwo/`](curve-complex/CurveComplexGenusTwo/) | Curve-complex foundations, dictionary, topology, and CW/homotopy machinery. |
| [`ClassificationOfSurfaces/`](curve-complex/ClassificationOfSurfaces/) | Surface-classification infrastructure. |
| [`CurveTopology/`](curve-complex/CurveTopology/) | Curve and arc complexes, carriers, and finite geometric constructions. |
| [`CoveringSpaces/`](curve-complex/CoveringSpaces/) | Covering-space and branch-chart constructions. |
| [`HyperbolicGeometry/`](curve-complex/HyperbolicGeometry/) | Hyperbolic charts and geometric bridges. |
| [`SurfaceGeometry/`](curve-complex/SurfaceGeometry/) | Local surface geometry, arc alignment, and disk/band arguments. |
| [`Theorems/`](curve-complex/Theorems/) | Main contractibility and simple-connectivity proof assemblies. |
| [`vendor/schoenflies-lean/`](curve-complex/vendor/schoenflies-lean/) | Local Schoenflies dependency. |

## Build and verification status

Install Lean through elan, then run from the repository root:

```sh
lake update
lake exe cache get
lake build
```

The toolchain is pinned to **Lean 4.35.0-rc3** in
[lean-toolchain](lean-toolchain), and Mathlib to revision
`3f6737de4761ec7bf368491fe9faccc991ebd6ca` in
[lakefile.toml](lakefile.toml). The default Lake target is `MainTheorems`;
Schoenflies is resolved as a local source dependency.

The proof-source closure is free of `sorry` and `admit`. The four original
endpoints have passed bounded compiler/kernel checks, axiom audits using exactly
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, and `Quot.sound`, and unchanged-statement checks
with the accepted object cache. A fresh full source build, declaration cleanup,
and final comparison are still in progress; the commands above describe the
intended build workflow, rather than a claim that this full rebuild has finished.

## References and attribution

The mathematical source is *The Complex of Curves Pairwise Intersecting at Most
Once Is Contractible in Genus Two* (Apex Intelligence, 11 September 2026),
Section 1.2 for the four main results. Lean and Mathlib provide the underlying
proof language and library. See [THIRD_PARTY.md](THIRD_PARTY.md) for the vendored
Schoenflies revision, license, and dependency attribution.

To cite this formalization, refer to *Curve complex formalization*, specifying
the revision used: [EonMath/curve-complex](https://github.com/EonMath/curve-complex/).

3.title: A stratumwise strong deformation retraction for the genus-two curve complex
3.excerpt_md: **Paper and claim.** This contribution concerns Theorem 1.1 of [Apex Intelligence, *The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once…
3.body_md:
**Paper and claim.** This contribution concerns Theorem 1.1 of [Apex Intelligence, *The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once is contractible in genus two*](https://math.apexin.net/papers/curve-complex-genus-two.pdf), the 35-page PDF dated 11 September 2026, SHA-256 `d1eadd01f94e9af17ee9f5fb2ee1b05b326430f37296309fd9417340ea366fd4`. We explicitly strongly deform the full arc complex $A$ onto $X$, replacing the spectral sequence and acyclicity argument. The genus-two main theorem then needs neither Theorem 7.7 nor its Harer input; the geometric cone lemmas remain essential.

**Boundary.** The contribution is the block decomposition, explicit relative homotopies and their gluing. Retained inputs are the arc/curve correspondence, Theorem 6.8, bad-vertex filtration and unique decomposition, and Sections 9-10. Necessary shared repairs are supplied in Section 5. The companion validation and its enumeration are not inputs. No new genus range, surface type, equivariance or simplicial collapse is claimed; significance is for expert review.

## 1. The retained combinatorial structure

Use the paper's Definitions 2.3-2.5 and Convention 2.1. The sphere has six marked points $B$, fixed pointwise in isotopies. Vertices of $A=A(S^2,B)$ are essential arc classes, with loops allowed. Simplices are finite systems with pairwise disjoint interiors and distinct classes. The complex $X$ has non-loop vertices; two different vertices are adjacent when they admit disjoint interiors and have different endpoint pairs. Remark 2.6, via Theorem 3.13, gives $X\subseteq A$.

A bad face is a loop vertex or a pair of non-loop vertices with the same endpoint pair (Definition 8.2). Write $\operatorname{bv}(\sigma)$ for the vertices belonging to bad faces of $\sigma$. For $p\ge0$ set
$$
Y_p=\{\sigma\in A:|\operatorname{bv}(\sigma)|\le p\},\qquad
\mathcal S_p=\{S\in A:|S|=p,\ \operatorname{bv}(S)=S\},
$$
$$
L_S=\{\tau\in\operatorname{lk}_A(S):\operatorname{bv}(S\cup\tau)=S\}.
$$
The $Y_p$ and $L_S$ are subcomplexes by monotonicity (Lemma 8.3). Lemma 8.5 gives $Y_0=X$ and $Y_{12}=A$; the bound for all of $A$, including loops and multiple edges, is justified in Section 5. 

By Lemma 8.6, a simplex with $p>0$ bad vertices decomposes uniquely as $S\sqcup\tau$, with $S=\operatorname{bv}(\sigma)\in\mathcal S_p$, $\tau\in L_S$: every witnessing bad face lies wholly in $S$. Lemma 9.15 and Lemma 10.8, with Corollary 10.9, give a vertex $a_S\in L_S$ such that
$$
\tau\in L_S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\tau\cup\{a_S\}\in L_S.
$$
Thus $L_S$ is a simplicial cone with an actual vertex, not just the complex containing the empty simplex. Choose each $a_S$ without equivariance. We never assume $L_{\varnothing}=X$ contractible.

## 2. The attaching blocks

For $p\ge1$ and $S\in\mathcal S_p$, let $\Delta(S)$ be the full simplex on the $p$ vertices in $S$, and put
$$
B_S=\Delta(S)*L_S,\qquad D_S=\partial\Delta(S)*L_S.
$$
All joins here are abstract simplicial joins, followed by geometric realization with the weak CW topology. The vertex sets $S$ and $L_S$ are disjoint by the definition of link. The boundary consists of the proper subsets of $S$. In particular, for $p=1$ it is $\{\varnothing\}$, and the abstract-join convention gives $D_S=L_S$; no topological join with an empty space is being used.

Every simplex of $B_S$ is $R\sqcup\tau$ with $R\subseteq S$ and $\tau\in L_S$. It belongs to $A$ since it is a face of $S\sqcup\tau$. Monotonicity and membership of bad vertices in the current simplex give
$$
\operatorname{bv}(R\sqcup\tau)\subseteq
\operatorname{bv}(S\sqcup\tau)\cap(R\sqcup\tau)=R.
$$
If $R\subsetneq S$, this simplex lies in $Y_{p-1}$. If $R=S$, its bad-vertex set is exactly $S$, so it does not lie in $Y_{p-1}$. Consequently
$$
B_S\cap Y_{p-1}=D_S,\qquad
