Y_p=Y_{p-1}\cup\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal S_p} B_S.
$$
For the second equality, use the unique decomposition of every simplex outside $Y_{p-1}$. If a simplex outside $Y_{p-1}$ belongs to both $B_S$ and $B_T$, the preceding calculation identifies both $S$ and $T$ with its bad-vertex set. Therefore
$$
B_S\cap B_T\subseteq Y_{p-1}\quad(S\ne T).
$$
These identities hold on realizations too: a point belongs to a subcomplex exactly when its support simplex does.

## 3. An explicit relative homotopy on each block

Write $e_v$ for the coordinate vector of a vertex. A point $x\in|B_S|$ has finitely supported barycentric coordinates $\lambda_v(x)\ge0$ of total sum one; absent coordinates are zero. Define
$$
m_S(x)=\min_{s\in S}\lambda_s(x),
$$
$$
H^S_t(x)=x-tm_S(x)\sum_{s\in S}e_s
             +ptm_S(x)e_{a_S},\qquad 0\le t\le1.
$$
Each new $S$-coordinate is nonnegative since $tm_S\le\lambda_s$. As $a_S\notin S$, the removed total mass $ptm_S$ is added back exactly; the coordinates still sum to one.

If the support of $x$ is $R\sqcup\tau$, its image has support contained in $S\cup\tau\cup\{a_S\}$. This is a simplex of $B_S$ because $\tau\cup\{a_S\}\in L_S$. Thus the formula remains in $|B_S|$. It starts at $x$. At $t=1$ at least one coordinate indexed by $S$ is zero, so the image lies in $|D_S|$. A point already in $|D_S|$ has a missing $S$-coordinate, hence $m_S=0$, and is fixed at every time. For $p=1$, this transfers the bad vertex's weight to $a_S$ and fixes $L_S$.

For continuity, restrict to any closed simplex of $B_S$. There $m_S$ is the minimum of finitely many affine functions, and the image of its product with $I$ lies in the one finite simplex obtained by adjoining $S$ and $a_S$. The formula is continuous there. Hatcher's *Algebraic Topology*, Theorem A.6 and the preceding discussion (pp.523-524), identify the weak topology on these closed-cell prisms with the ordinary product topology because $I$ is compact. Thus $H^S:|B_S|\times I\to|B_S|$ is jointly continuous, even though the complex can be infinite and not locally finite.

## 4. Simultaneous retraction and the main theorem

On $|Y_{p-1}|\times I$ use the identity, and on $|B_S|\times I$ use $H^S$. Distinct blocks overlap inside $Y_{p-1}$, hence inside both of their $D$-subcomplexes; both formulas are the identity there. They therefore define a single map
$$
H^{(p)}:|Y_p|\times I\longrightarrow |Y_p|.
$$
Every closed simplex of $Y_p$ lies in $Y_{p-1}$ or in a block $B_S$. On its prism the map is continuous, with image in a finite simplex as above (or unchanged). Apply Theorem A.6 again to obtain joint continuity. This checks continuity without a locally finite cover assumption. We obtain a strong deformation retraction $r_p=H^{(p)}_1:Y_p\to Y_{p-1}$. If $\mathcal S_p$ is empty, the decomposition says $Y_p=Y_{p-1}$ and we take the identity homotopy.

Retract in the order $12,11,\ldots,1$. Explicitly let $R_0=\mathrm{id}_A$ and, for $k=0,\ldots,11$, put $R_{k+1}=r_{12-k}R_k$. On the time interval $[k/12,(k+1)/12]$ use
$$
F_t(x)=H^{(12-k)}_{12t-k}(R_k(x)).
$$
The endpoints agree and the twelve closed time intervals give a continuous homotopy by finite pasting. All stages fix $X=Y_0$ pointwise. Hence $F$ is a strong deformation retraction of $|A|$ onto $|X|$.

Hatcher's revised *On Triangulations of Surfaces*, Theorem (a), applies to the sphere with six interior marked points and says $A$ is contractible. Its marked disc and annulus exceptions do not apply. If $C:A\times I\to A$ is a contraction and $r=R_{12}$, then $(x,t)\mapsto r(C(x,t))$, for $x\in X$, is a contraction of $X$: it starts at $r(x)=x$ and ends at the constant $r(C(x,1))$. Finally Proposition 6.1 and Theorem 6.8 identify $X\cong K'$ and strongly deform $K=C_1(S_2)$ onto $K'$. Contracting $K'$ after that homotopy contracts $K$.

The new retraction and closing argument avoid spectral sequences, homology and Hurewicz-Whitehead. The Farey justification below still uses Whitehead upstream. Theorem 7.7 remains an independent general-genus result. The geometry of Sections 9-10 remains essential.

## 5. Shared repairs and retained inputs

These necessary shared inputs are part of this proof; no additional contribution is claimed.

**Arcs (3.8-3.13).** Lemma 3.8 says “an arc” although the preceding notation $\alpha^\circ$ was defined for essential arcs. Embedded compactification requires distinct ideal ends; prove 3.9 first and read 3.8 conditionally. An inessential loop enclosing no other mark has equal ends. For an essential loop based at $b$, shrink cusps so distinct lifted closed horoballs are disjoint. Equal ideal ends put the deck element of the truncated loop, closed along a cusp boundary, in its cyclic parabolic stabilizer. Its homology is then both $\kappa m_b$ and $\sum_{q\in T}m_q$, with $T$ and $B\setminus(T\cup\{b\})$ nonempty. In $\mathbb Z^B/\langle\mathbf1_B\rangle$ the coefficient of $\mathbf1_B$ would be both one and zero. Non-loop ends have different cusp labels. Lemma 3.10 uses compactification with distinct limiting ends and the Jordan crosscut theorem.

In 3.12 prove simplicity before isotopy. The geodesic joining the ends has trivial stabilizer: an element fixing both is trivial in the cyclic parabolic stabilizer; an exchanging element has trivial square, so torsion-freeness excludes it. Crossing a distinct translate would force the corresponding lifts of the original embedded arc to cross. The projected geodesic's radial cusp tails compactify to an embedded arc or based loop. As in Remark 3.3, extend cusp conformal charts over the marks and transport the metric to the stipulated smooth sphere by a diffeomorphism matching the marks; these tails are smooth there.

Nearest-point interpolation is uniformly proper: projection of $a+ib$ onto the imaginary axis has height $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\ge b$, and horoballs are convex. Interpolate the final directed parameter to an increasing homeomorphism of $\mathbb R$ to obtain an embedded parametrization, still with uniformly proper tails. For non-loops, choose a uniform tail cutoff and small endpoint discs; other marked-point discs avoid the compact middle homotopy. Radial retraction of the punctured discs to their boundaries gives a continuous truncated homotopy. Remove its initial/final noninjective tail parametrizations by endpoint-fixed homotopies, cancel angular endpoint tracks by collar rotations, and apply Epstein 3.1 to proper arcs with fixed boundary endpoints. Restore rotations and fill discs fixing centers. For loops use Epstein 4.1 on $S^2\setminus(B\setminus\{b\})$, fixing $b$; essentiality and orientability exclude discs and Möbius bands. His Appendix A1-A2 supplies the tame/PL setting. Compactness of isotopies fixing marks preserves lifted ideal pairs, proving uniqueness.

In 3.13 every geodesic crossing has alternating ideal ends and forces an original crossing; distinct lifts cannot count the same crossing. This bounds the canonical count by every finite representative count. Shared ideal ends give no interior crossing, and essential loops have distinct ends. The fixed geodesics thus realize all pairwise minima simultaneously. Matching Hatcher's p.1 arc-system complex uses the standard system-isotopy fact presupposed by his definition: disjoint systems with the same component classes have the same system-isotopy class. We declare this literature input; we do not claim the definition proves it.

**Dictionary and intersections (4.1-5.7).** Retain Lemmas 4.1-4.6, 4.10 and Theorem 4.11. In 4.6 minimize finite intersection/chord complexity, not the number of all curve points inside a disc. For isotopic intersecting lift components use Farb-Margalit Proposition 1.7. Epstein Lemma 2.4 gives annuli between disjoint isotopic essential circles. Cutting along a nonseparating core and ordering three additional parallel circles gives three annuli and a two-boundary genus-one piece; the paper correctly uses only the outer exchanged annuli. For arcs choose $N(\alpha)\cap B=\{p,q\}$. Its covered endpoint discs and edge strip form an annulus with core $\pi^{-1}(\alpha)$ and one collar on each side. Align cores by ambient isotopy (Farb-Margalit 1.11), choose a smaller product collar inside both neighborhoods, and push their boundaries through the collars. Their boundary multicurves are isotopic. Disc-arc uniqueness below completes the reduction.

For Fact 3.6's needed input use Margalit-Winarski pp.1,6, $\operatorname{SMod}(S_2)=\operatorname{Mod}(S_2)$. The six-point double cover, determined by nontrivial meridian monodromy, is conjugate to their hyperelliptic model. Surface classification and fiber-preserving mapping-class representatives carry invariant model curves to invariant representatives of every class; uniqueness makes their closed geodesics invariant. Haas-Susskind's original article was not inspected.

Fiber counting gives $2j+e$; $u=z^2$ gives regular lifts $z(s)=s\sqrt{c(s^2)}$. In 5.3 a small tapered rotation of the sign of the nonzero radial angle difference separates equal departure directions without new crossings. For 4.11's surjectivity and 5.5's lower bound, projected geodesics are regular at branch points: the cone conformal structure extends (Remark 3.3); in a conformal coordinate $\iota z=-z$ and $\pi=h(z^2)$ with $h$ a local conformal coordinate change. Centered arclength gives an odd smooth parametrization $z(s)=s a(s^2)$, $a(0)\ne0$, and its quotient is regular in $t=s^2$. This calculation is independent of the bijection. Thus 5.5 applies to distinct non-loop classes and 5.7 yields Proposition 6.1.

**Farey links (6.4-6.8).** Lemmas 6.4-6.5 exclude two separating vertices in a simplex. Same-side isotopy annuli and bigons cannot contain the essential separating circle (an annulus would identify it with its nonseparating core), so gluing creates neither new isotopies nor smaller intersections. Slopes and $|ps-qr|$ follow from Farb-Margalit pp.27,29, with homotopy-to-isotopy from 1.10.

The abstract Farey realization includes ideal vertices and is not literally $\mathbb H^2$. Adjacent primitive vectors form a basis and their only common neighbors are their sum/difference up to sign. Outside the triangle $0,1,\infty$, recursively insert mediants in its three boundary intervals. In an endpoint basis every interior rational has coprime positive coordinates $(m,n)$; subtracting the smaller from the larger decreases $m+n$ and locates it uniquely in the recursion. This exhausts vertices and adjacent triangles; disjoint nested intervals prevent branch identifications, so the triangle dual is a tree. A finite connected dual subtree is a triangle disc, each leaf adding a new third vertex on its unused side. Every finite subcomplex lies in such a disc. By Hatcher A.1 compact images lie in finite subcomplexes; sphere maps contract in discs, and Whitehead gives contractibility. In the abstract join, compact images lie in $G_1*G_2$ for finite $G_i$, contained in finite discs $D_i$; $D_1*D_2$ is contractible. The same argument proves the join contractible. Theorem 6.8's original relative-star gluing now applies using Hatcher 0.16, 0.20 and A.6. Its continuity argument is correct; Whitehead remains upstream.

**All of $A$ (8.5).** Include all six marks as vertices of a simplex's graph, even isolated ones. For $E$ edges its regular neighborhood has $\chi=6-E$; complementary planar pieces satisfy $\sum\chi(R_i)=E-4$ and $\sum\ell_i=2E$, counting edge-band sides. Non-discs have $\chi\le0$. Every disc has $\ell_i\ge3$. Length zero, or one non-loop edge traversed twice, would exhaust the sphere with an isolated vertex/edge neighborhood, excluding the other marks. Length one is an inessential loop; two distinct non-loop edges give an empty bigon. Two loops at one base point bounding a length-two disc are based homotopic, hence isotopic as unoriented arcs by Epstein 4.1. A loop and a non-loop cannot make a length-two closed walk; a loop's two sides lie in different sphere regions. Thus $E-4\le2E/3$ and $E\le12$.

**Cones (9.1-10.9).** Retain the object/gap construction: distinct objects meet in at most one mark, each has at least two Jordan disc gaps, and a nonfree gap contains a smaller one (9.1-9.10). Minimal gaps inside two different gaps of one object give two disjoint free gaps; 9.11 proves they are faces of the whole graph. Their boundary marks occur once and come from one object (9.12). An empty free gap gives an inessential loop or isotopic bounding arcs. Both therefore contain untouched marks; since $S\ne\varnothing$, $V'\ge1$ and their counts sum to at most $6-V'\le5$. One is a clean free face $\Delta$ with $k=1$ or $2$ (9.13-9.15).

For 4.9, 10.2 and 10.4, disc-arc uniqueness holds with two interior endpoints, or one boundary endpoint and the sole interior mark. Put two arcs in finite transverse position, with distinct endpoint directions, by PL/smooth perturbation fixing boundary and endpoints. With $m$ crossings their union has $V=m+2,E=2m+2,F=m+2$. Faces have positive even degree; at most one bigon would imply $2E\ge4F-2$, impossible. At most one face contains the outside of the disc, so an interior empty bigon exists. For $m>0$ its corners cannot both be the original endpoints. Pushing across its empty disc removes two crossings, or one if an endpoint is a corner, rotating about that fixed endpoint and fixing the boundary. Supports contain no other mark. At $m=0$ slide across the empty disc. Moves with two interior endpoints have compact support. The empty-bigon use in 9.14 takes a slightly larger disc around the closure.

Lemma 10.1 makes $L_S$ full and flag, with each canonical arc in one face. Cleanliness excludes boundary-to-boundary arcs (10.5). For $k=1$, uniqueness gives a nonempty simplex of arcs from the interior mark to boundary marks. For $k=2$ choose the unique class $r$ between the two interior marks. Given a boundary-to-interior vertex $w$, take a short segment opposite its canonical radial cusp tail and an embedded PL arc in the connected slit disc $\Delta\setminus w$ from the other interior mark to the segment's far end. Stop at its first meeting with the segment; their truncated union represents $r$ and meets $w$ only at the common endpoint. This supplies 10.6's straightening without misusing Epstein 3.1 at interior endpoints. The apex class is fixed, its representative may vary with $w$. Its interior avoids $\Gamma_S$ and an endpoint is untouched, so it is allowable. Vertices in other faces are disjoint and cannot have its endpoint pair. Flagness gives the actual simplicial cone required above (10.8-10.9).

## 6. Public references and disclosure

[Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf): Proposition 0.16 and Corollary 0.20, pp.15-16; Proposition A.1, p.520; product discussion and Theorem A.6, pp.523-524; Whitehead Theorem 4.5, p.346. [Hatcher, revised *On Triangulations of Surfaces*](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Papers/TriangSurf.pdf): arc-system conventions p.1, Theorem (a) p.2. [Epstein, *Curves on 2-Manifolds and Isotopies* (1966)](https://archive.ymsc.tsinghua.edu.cn/pacm_download/117/6005-11511_2006_Article_BF02392203.pdf): Lemma 2.4 p.87, Theorems 3.1/4.1 pp.89/91, Appendix A1-A2 pp.105-106. [Farb-Margalit, *A Primer on Mapping Class Groups*](https://euclid.nmu.edu/~joshthom/teaching/ma589/farbmarg.pdf): Propositions 1.3, 1.6-1.7, 1.10-1.11; Corollary 1.9; slopes pp.27,29; surface classification pp.37-38. [Margalit-Winarski, *The Birman-Hilden Theory*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.03448v1), pp.1,6. Page numbers are printed pages except the revised arc paper. These are literature inputs, not independently reproved theories.

**AI disclosure.** Claude proposed the retraction; GPT-6 Astra supplied the formula. Codex drafted the text. Fresh GPT contexts checked mathematics and claim boundaries. Claude, a different model family, then checked this manuscript's construction and closing argument. For v1.2, a DeepSeek-based review agent raised wording points; Claude and GPT adjudicated them, Codex made the edits and a fresh GPT context checked them. No human expert certification is claimed.

22.title: Higher Connectivity, Fixed Points, and an Equivariance Obstruction for Curve Complexes

22.body_md:
**Paper and contribution.** This supplement concerns Apex Intelligence, [*The Complex of Curves Pairwise Intersecting at Most Once Is Contractible in Genus Two*](https://math.apexin.net/papers/curve-complex-genus-two.pdf), the 35-page competition PDF dated 11 September 2026, SHA-256 `d1eadd01f94e9af17ee9f5fb2ee1b05b326430f37296309fd9417340ea366fd4`. We extend its Theorem 1.3 (printed p. 2; proved as Theorem 7.7, p. 24) to an explicit higher-connectivity range. In genus two we prove a fixed-space comparison theorem, deduce fixed-point contractibility using Hensel–Osajda–Przytycki, and prove that the ordinary retraction of Theorem 6.8 (p. 22) cannot have a full-mapping-class-group-equivariant counterpart, even as a set map.

Complete proofs, including the equivariant arc retraction, cone repairs and system-isotopy input, are in the [evidence repository](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-connectivity-fixed-points) at revision `f91b75f7fa8e31147c395c713f602a4e8f7955cb`. Realizations have the weak CW topology, curves and arcs are unoriented, and mapping classes are orientation preserving unless stated otherwise. Fixed points are geometric, including barycenters of permuted simplices.

## 1. Higher connectivity

Let $S_g$ be closed, connected and orientable, and let $C_d(S_g)$ be the flag complex on all essential simple closed curve isotopy classes, with adjacency $i(a,b)\le d$. Separating classes are included.

**Theorem H.** For integers $g\ge2$, $d\ge1$, $k\ge1$,

$$
d\binom{k+1}{2}\le2g-2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|C_d(S_g)|\text{ is }k\text{-connected}.
$$

Thus $C_1(S_g)$ is 2-connected for $g\ge3$ and 3-connected for $g\ge4$, and

$$
\mathrm{conn}\,C_1(S_g)\ge
\left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{16g-15}-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
$$

The case $d=1,k=1$ recovers Theorem 1.3. For general $d$, $k=1$ gives simple connectivity when $d\le2g-2$. The higher-dimensional step is a compatible homotopy of every sufficiently low-intersection finite image into $C_0$, fixing all its vertices.

**Essential boundary lemma.** A nonempty finite system of essential embedded circles with transverse double intersections and no triple points has an essential regular-neighborhood boundary whenever its total intersection count $I$ is at most $2g-2$. The system need not be connected. If $z$ components are isolated circles, give each an artificial vertex and edge; then

$$
V=I+z,\qquad E=2I+z,\qquad \chi(N)=\chi(G)=-I.
$$

If every boundary circle were inessential, its unique disk side could contain no component of $N$: every such component contains an original circle essential in $S_g$. This excludes both the incident component and any other component hidden inside that disk. Consequently all complementary components are disks. A sufficiently small neighborhood is proper, so their number $F$ is positive and

$$
2-2g=-I+F,\qquad I\ge2g-1,
$$

a contradiction. This directly proves essential boundary, including the equality case, disconnected systems and isolated circles.

**Compatible finite replacement.** Let $L\subset C_d(S_g)$ be a finite subcomplex satisfying

$$
I_\sigma=\sum_{\{v,w\}\subseteq\sigma}i(v,w)\le2g-2
\qquad(\varnothing\ne\sigma\in L).
$$

Choose one representative per distinct vertex using closed geodesics, which are simultaneously pairwise minimal (Farb–Margalit, Corollary 1.9 and the following paragraph, p. 33). Separate multiple intersections inside disjoint small disks by generic small perturbations preserving every pairwise crossing count; the repository supplies this local argument. After perturbation, $I_\sigma$ is the actual double-point count of the common representative graph $G_\sigma$.

Choose regular neighborhoods by descending induction on dimension so that

$$
\tau\subsetneq\sigma\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
N_\tau\subset\mathrm{int}(N_\sigma).
$$

For a shared face, the finite intersection of the interiors of all previously chosen coface neighborhoods still contains its entire graph. A sufficiently thin regular neighborhood inside that intersection gives the required choice, once for each face. Choose an essential component $c_\sigma$ of each boundary. For a singleton its class is the original vertex. The rule $r(\sigma)=[c_\sigma]$ defines a simplicial map $r:\mathrm{sd}L\to C_0$: boundaries of nested neighborhoods are disjoint along every inclusion chain. Repeated boundary classes merely collapse a simplex.

To construct the homotopy, let $P_\sigma$ be the full subcomplex of $C_d$ on

$$
W_\sigma=\sigma\cup
\{[c_\tau]:\varnothing\ne\tau\subseteq\sigma\}.
$$

The vertex $[c_\sigma]$ is disjoint from every vertex in $W_\sigma$. Flagness makes $P_\sigma$ a finite cone; it does not require boundaries of incomparable faces to be disjoint. Also $P_\tau\subseteq P_\sigma$ for faces. Both the original inclusion and the subdivided replacement lie in the corresponding carrier. For a singleton the carrier is a point. Inductively extend the prescribed bottom, top and side maps of each simplex prism into its cone carrier, keeping the whole prism boundary fixed. Each shared face is processed once, so the extensions agree. This gives a homotopy of the inclusion to a map through $C_0$, fixed on all original vertices. No link-connectivity assertion is used.

For a based map $S^j\to|C_d|$, $1\le j\le k$, take a based simplicial approximation (Hatcher Theorem 2C.1, p. 177, and the fixed-vertex observation, p. 179). Its image simplices and their faces form a finite $L$ of dimension at most $j$; do not replace it by the full complex on all image vertices. Every face satisfies

$$
I_\sigma\le d\binom{\#\sigma}{2}
\le d\binom{j+1}{2}\le2g-2.
$$

The replacement moves the map into $C_0$ through a based homotopy. Harer's *The Cohomology of the Moduli Space of Curves*, definition of $Z_g^0$ on p. 170, Lemma 3.6 on p. 171 and Theorem 4.1 on p. 176, gives $|C_0(S_g)|\simeq\bigvee S^{2g-2}$, hence $(2g-3)$-connectivity. Our range has $k\le2g-3$: for $k=1$ this follows from $g\ge2$; for $k\ge2$ use $k+1\le\binom{k+1}{2}\le2g-2$. Thus every such sphere map is null-homotopic. Path connectivity follows because $C_0$ contains all vertices and every point joins to a vertex inside its simplex. This proves H.

**Method and priority.** Harer Lemma 4.3 (pp. 178–179) already uses a very similar regular-neighborhood boundary replacement, subdivision and homotopy. Here that method is applied with nested finite neighborhoods and cone carriers to obtain the stated threshold-dependent bound. The target paper says on p. 2 that Souto [8] stated Theorem 1.3 without proof. We have not obtained Souto's note and do not claim that higher connectivity was never stated. The bound's optimality and higher-genus contractibility are not established.

## 2. The equivariant arc input, with its proof included

Put $K=C_1(S_2)$ and let $K'$ be its full nonseparating subcomplex. On the six-marked hyperelliptic quotient $(S^2,B)$, let $A$ be the full essential arc complex, loops allowed, and let $X$ have non-loop vertices with disjoint interiors and different endpoint pairs required for adjacency (target Definitions 2.3–2.5, p. 5). Proposition 6.1 (pp. 20–21) identifies $X\cong K'$.

We prove a $G=\mathrm{Mod}^{+}(S^2,B)$-equivariant strong deformation retraction $|A|\searrow|X|$, allowing permutations of the marks. The repository includes its complete proof and the following geometric dependencies.

For a nonempty all-bad simplex $S$ (bad faces are loops or repeated-endpoint pairs), set

$$
L_S=\{\tau\in\mathrm{lk}_A(S):\mathrm{bv}(S\cup\tau)=S\}.
$$

The object/gap lemmas in target §9, especially Lemmas 9.11, 9.15 and Corollary 9.12 (pp. 30–31), supply good Jordan-disc faces having one or two interior marks and one or two boundary marks, each appearing once. Every good face prescribes unique arc classes: from its sole interior mark to each boundary mark, or between its two interior marks. Disc-arc uniqueness is proved by empty-bigon elimination fixing the boundary and marks, so Epstein's boundary-interval theorem is not applied directly to two interior endpoints. With two interior marks, a slit-disc construction makes the fixed joining class disjoint from any allowed boundary-to-interior class; cleanliness excludes boundary-to-boundary arcs. For vertices in other faces, disjoint interiors and the untouched interior endpoint give both adjacency conditions. Thus every prescribed class cones off the whole $L_S$, repairing the required use of target Lemmas 10.4–10.8 (pp. 32–34).

Take the finite nonempty union $Q_{S,\Gamma}$ of prescribed classes from all good faces, removing repetitions. The included system-isotopy proof aligns cusp half-edge order and integral winding, then applies Epstein 3.1 and Farb–Margalit Lemma 2.9 to truncated arcs with distinct boundary endpoints. It gives a common ambient isotopy fixing $B$ between representative systems. This transports all good faces and their unique classes, proving $Q_{S,\Gamma}=Q_S$ independently of the graph.

Transport by any mapping class gives $Q_{gS}=gQ_S$, without assuming an invariant auxiliary metric. Since every member is a full-link cone vertex and $L_S$ is flag, $\tau\cup Q_S\in L_S$ for every $\tau\in L_S$. Its natural barycenter is

$$
c_S=\frac1{|Q_S|}\sum_{a\in Q_S}e_a,\qquad c_{gS}=gc_S.
$$

The bad-vertex filtration has $Y_0=X$, $Y_{12}=A$; the repository proves the bound including loops, multiple edges and disconnected systems. Unique bad-set decomposition gives blocks $B_S=\Delta(S)*L_S$ with lower-layer intersection $D_S=\partial\Delta(S)*L_S$. Distinct blocks intersect in that layer. For $p=|S|$, use

$$
m_S(x)=\min_{s\in S}\lambda_s(x),\qquad
D_t^S(x)=x-tm_S(x)\sum_{s\in S}e_s+ptm_S(x)c_S.
$$

Coordinates remain nonnegative and sum to one, with support in $S\cup\tau\cup Q_S$. At $t=1$ one $S$-coordinate vanishes; on $D_S$ the homotopy is the identity. The formula commutes with the group action. Gluing the blocks and twelve layers gives the equivariant retraction. Each closed simplex prism has image in one finite simplex; Hatcher's product criterion (pp. 523–524) gives joint continuity without local finiteness.

Birman–Hilden gives

$$
1\longrightarrow\langle\iota\rangle\longrightarrow
\mathrm{Mod}^{+}(S_2)\xrightarrow{\Theta}
\mathrm{Mod}^{+}(S^2,B)\longrightarrow1.
$$

See Margalit–Winarski, arXiv:1703.03448v1, pp. 1–2, 6. The deck kernel is central and fixes every curve class: each curve type has an invariant model, and surface classification makes each type a mapping-class orbit. Fiber-preserving representatives make the dictionary equivariant. Thus, for any subgroup $H$ and $\bar H=\Theta(H)$,

$$
|K'|^H\cong|X|^{\bar H},\qquad
|A|^{\bar H}\searrow|X|^{\bar H}.
$$

Restriction works for every subgroup because a jointly continuous equivariant homotopy preserves its geometric fixed points.

## 3. No full-group-equivariant map to the core

**Theorem O.** No $\mathrm{Mod}^{+}(S_2)$-equivariant map $|K|\to|K'|$ exists, even as a set map. The same holds for $\mathrm{Mod}^{\pm}(S_2)$.

Choose a separating class $\sigma$ and $H=\mathrm{Stab}(\sigma)$. The source has the $H$-fixed point $e_\sigma$. A target fixed point would have a finite nonempty $H$-invariant support simplex, forcing each of its nonseparating vertices to have finite orbit. Every nonseparating class $c$ instead has infinite $H$-orbit. If it crosses $\sigma$, powers of $T_\sigma\in H$ are distinct because

$$
i(T_\sigma^n c,T_\sigma^m c)=|n-m|\,i(\sigma,c)^2>0
\quad(n\ne m)
$$

(Farb–Margalit Proposition 3.2, p. 69). If $c$ is disjoint from $\sigma$, it lies in one of the two one-holed tori. Choose a curve $d$ there meeting it once; $T_d$, extended by the identity, fixes $\sigma$ and again gives an infinite orbit. The closed-surface intersection is one by its single-crossing representative and algebraic intersection $\pm1$. Hence $|K'|^H=\varnothing$, which obstructs the map. An extended-group-equivariant map would restrict to the impossible orientation-preserving one. No continuity was used.

## 4. Fixed-space comparison

**Theorem F.** For every $H\le\mathrm{Mod}^{+}(S_2)$, put $Z_H=|K'|^H$.

If $Z_H\ne\varnothing$, it is a strong deformation retract of $|K|^H$. If $Z_H=\varnothing$, then $|K|^H$ is empty or one separating vertex.

Here is the fixed-link and attachment argument. For a separating $\sigma$, target Lemma 6.6 (pp. 21–22) identifies its link with $\mathcal F_1*\mathcal F_2$, the Farey complexes on the two one-holed tori. The repository proves contractibility of the abstract Farey realization via its triangle-dual tree: every finite subcomplex lies in a finite triangle disk; Hatcher A.1 and Whitehead then apply. It includes the rational vertices and is not literally the hyperbolic plane.

For any $J\le\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb Z)$, its Farey fixed set is: the whole contractible complex for $J=1$; a unique edge midpoint or triangle barycenter for nontrivial finite $J$; or empty or one rational vertex for infinite $J$. Indeed, the pointwise stabilizer of two rational lines is trivial (primitive generators can only be multiplied by $\pm1$, with equal signs forced by determinant one). A subgroup preserving at least two rational slopes therefore embeds in a finite permutation group. Finite nontrivial subgroups have a unique hyperbolic fixed center in a Farey edge or triangle and no fixed rational vertex; these give the stated abstract midpoint or barycenter. Infinite subgroups can only fix a support of size one. In particular, preserving any finite nonempty set of rational slopes gives a nonempty contractible Farey fixed set, even if those slopes do not span a simplex.

Let $N\le H$ be the subgroup preserving both sides of an $H$-fixed $\sigma$; it has index one or two. Its projective homology images are $J_i\le\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb Z)$; set $A_i=|\mathcal F_i|^{J_i}$. If both sides are preserved, the fixed link is their join when both are nonempty, the sole nonempty factor when only one is nonempty, and empty when both are empty. These are the actual barycentric endpoint cases. If $s\in H$ exchanges the sides, the fixed link is homeomorphic to $A_1$ by

$$
x\longmapsto\tfrac12x+\tfrac12sx.
$$

Equal side masses are necessary; $s^2\in N$ and $sNs^{-1}=N$ give sufficiency. Twice the first-side coordinates give the continuous inverse on subdivided fixed cells. Thus every nonempty fixed link is contractible, and for finite groups it is always nonempty, including side exchange.

To handle arbitrary $H$, a curve $c$ crossing $\sigma$ determines nonempty finite slope sets $P_i(c)$ from its cutting arcs in each torus. Each arc is essential by minimal position and has primitive nonzero relative homology, since a dual closed curve crosses it once. The canonical map $H_1(T_i)\to H_1(T_i,\partial T_i)$ is an isomorphism. Apply Farb–Margalit Lemma 2.9 (pp. 61–62) to the two-curve systems $(\sigma,c)$ to see that the slope sets are independent of minimal representatives. The resulting ambient isotopy acts trivially on $H_1(S_2)=H_1(T_1)\oplus H_1(T_2)$, so cannot exchange the summands and is trivial on each. Naturality gives $P_i(nc)=\rho_i(n)P_i(c)$. A finite $N$-orbit of $c$ therefore supplies a finite nonempty invariant slope set on each side, hence a nonempty fixed link, also in the side-exchange case.

If $Z_H$ is nonempty, choose its true support simplex $\Omega$. For any fixed separating $\sigma$, a member $c\in\Omega$ either is disjoint from $\sigma$, in which case its whole finite $H$-orbit lies in the link simplex and its barycenter is fixed, or crosses $\sigma$, in which case the cutting-slope argument applies. Thus all attaching fixed links are nonempty and contractible.

Target Lemma 6.4 and Corollary 6.5 (p. 21) ensure at most one separating vertex in any simplex. A fixed point outside the core therefore has a unique, individually fixed separating vertex in its support. Its fixed star is the cone on its fixed link. Distinct stars meet only inside the core. After barycentric subdivision, fixed spaces are CW subcomplexes of chains of $H$-invariant faces; this also holds for infinite $H$. A nonempty contractible fixed link is a strong deformation retract of its cone by Hatcher 0.16 and 0.20 (pp. 15–16). Choose these relative homotopies and glue them with the identity on $Z_H$. Every closed fixed cell lies in the core or one star; the closed-cell-prism criterion gives joint continuity. This proves the first case of F.

If $Z_H$ is empty, any positive nonseparating mass in a fixed point could be normalized to a point of $Z_H$. Only individually fixed separating vertices remain. There cannot be two: distinct separating curves intersect by Lemma 6.4, and cutting one relative to the other yields a nonempty fixed link in $K'$, a contradiction. This proves F's second case.

## 5. Fixed-point corollaries and scope

Use Hensel–Osajda–Przytycki, [*Realisation and Dismantlability*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.0513v1), **arXiv:1205.0513v1, 2 May 2012**. Theorem 3.1 (p. 8) gives a finite subgroup an invariant nonempty clique in the full arc graph. Theorem 10.1 (pp. 27–28) says the full arc-complex geometric fixed set for any subgroup is empty or contractible. Here $(S^2,B)$ has punctured Euler characteristic $2-6=-4$, and all hypotheses hold. Its definitions permit essential loops, ignore shared endpoints in disjointness, and allow marked-point permutations. Single-arc homotopy-isotopy and simultaneous representatives identify that complex with $A$, not $X$. The exact interface and inspected version are recorded in the repository; no filling claim is needed from Theorem 3.1.

For finite $F\le\mathrm{Mod}^{+}(S_2)$, its sphere image fixes the barycenter of a finite nonempty arc clique. HOP makes $|A|^{\Theta(F)}$ contractible; the equivariant retraction transfers this to $|K'|^F$, and Theorem F transfers it to $|K|^F$. Both are nonempty and contractible. For arbitrary $H$, HOP and the arc retraction make $Z_H$ empty or contractible; Theorem F gives the same dichotomy for the full fixed set.

These spaces need not be simultaneously empty for infinite groups: $H=\mathrm{Stab}(\sigma)$ has $|K'|^H=\varnothing$ and $|K|^H=\{e_\sigma\}$. This explains the obstruction despite the contractibility of every nonempty fixed set. The separately chosen fixed-space retractions do not provide a full-group-equivariant retraction. Fixed-point conclusions here are limited to orientation-preserving subgroups. Infinite vertex stabilizers also preclude concluding that the full complex is a model for proper actions. The corollaries extend the target-specific fixed-point analysis; they do not improve HOP's theorem for arc complexes. Independent literature novelty and contribution significance remain for expert assessment.

**AI disclosure.** GPT-6.1 Sol, in OpenAI Codex under human direction, developed the proof and drafted this text; a separate GPT-6.1 Sol session in a fresh context performed an adversarial review. Claude planned the work, checked key steps against the sources, and reviewed and edited the final text. No human expert has certified the work.

2.title: Validation of the original augmented spectral-sequence step in the genus-two paper
2.excerpt_md: This submission checks Proposition 8.7, Theorem 8.9 and the homological argument in Theorems 11.1–11.2 of Apex Intelligence, *The complex of…
2.body_md:
This submission checks Proposition 8.7, Theorem 8.9 and the homological argument in Theorems 11.1–11.2 of Apex Intelligence, *The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once is contractible in genus two*, dated 11 September 2026, [original paper](https://math.apexin.net/papers/curve-complex-genus-two.pdf), printed pp.25–27 and 34. The 35-page PDF has SHA-256 `d1eadd01f94e9af17ee9f5fb2ee1b05b326430f37296309fd9417340ea366fd4`; the public PDF and the copy examined have this same hash.

The original spectral-sequence step is correct under its stated geometric inputs. This submission verifies its augmentation, chain splitting, signs, degreewise bounded convergence and collapse, with the algebraic details given below. It neither substitutes another proof nor depends on another submission's acceptance. The convergence calculation and limiting zero-column identification clarify correct steps, rather than identify errors.

## 1. Definitions and accepted inputs

Let $B$ be six marked points of $S^2$, and let $A=A(S^2,B)$ be the paper's essential arc complex, including loop arcs. Simplices are finite systems of distinct isotopy classes admitting representatives with disjoint interiors. Isotopies fix the marked points and may rotate endpoint directions. The complex $X$ retains the non-loop systems with no repeated endpoint pair, identified with the flag complex of Definition 2.5.

A bad face of a simplex $\sigma$ is either a singleton loop vertex or a pair of distinct non-loop vertices with the same endpoint pair. Write $b(\sigma)=\operatorname{bv}(\sigma)$ for the set of vertices belonging to such faces. Define

$$
Y_p=\{\sigma\in A:|b(\sigma)|\leq p\},\qquad
\mathcal S_p=\{S\in A:|S|=p,\ b(S)=S\},
$$

$$
L_S=\{\tau\in\operatorname{lk}_A(S):b(S\cup\tau)=S\}.
$$

The link condition means $S\cap\tau=\emptyset$ and $S\cup\tau\in A$. We accept these inputs from the paper:

1. **Monotonicity and the zero stratum:** $b(\rho)\subseteq b(\sigma)$ whenever $\rho\subseteq\sigma$, with $b(\emptyset)=\emptyset$ and $Y_0=X$ (Lemmas 8.3 and 8.5). The identification with the paper's flag complex includes its simultaneous-representative input.
2. **Unique decomposition:** if $|b(\sigma)|=p$, then $\sigma=S\sqcup\tau$ uniquely, where $S=b(\sigma)\in\mathcal S_p$ and $\tau\in L_S$. Deleting a vertex of $\tau$ preserves the bad set $S$, whereas deleting a vertex of $S$ leaves at most $p-1$ bad vertices (Lemma 8.6).
3. **Global size bound used in the paper:** Lemma 8.5(iv) uses the standard fact that maximal arc systems give generalized triangulations to obtain at most twelve arcs per simplex and $Y_{12}=A$. The spectral-sequence convergence argument below does not use this bound; the remaining geometric inputs are accepted as stated.
4. **Ambient contractibility:** $|A|$ is contractible. The accepted identification with Hatcher's arc complex includes the isotopy conventions for entire disjoint systems. In [Hatcher, *Triangulations of Surfaces*, revised version](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Papers/TriangSurf.pdf), the definitions on p.1 allow coincident arc endpoints, and Theorem (a), p.2, applies to this marked sphere: it is outside the exceptional disc and annulus cases. This is the literature input used by Fact 7.2.
5. **Positive links:** for every $p\geq1$ and $S\in\mathcal S_p$, $L_S$ is a cone with an actual apex vertex (Lemma 9.15, Lemma 10.8 and Corollary 10.9). This includes nonemptiness, not merely a formal empty simplex.

Their geometric proofs and the Budget/cone construction are not recertified here. The face-deletion rules follow from the definition: every bad witness lies wholly in $S$, so removing a vertex outside $S$ destroys no witness, while monotonicity forbids new bad vertices after deleting a vertex of $S$.

## 2. Augmentation and the relative chain splitting

Use integral oriented simplicial chains and the weak topology on realizations. Distinguish the empty simplex $\emptyset$, the complex $\mathcal E=\{\emptyset\}$, and the void complex $\mathcal O$, which contains no simplices. As in Convention 8.1, $\emptyset$ is a simplex of every non-void complex, in particular of $A$. For a non-void complex $K$, its augmented complex $\widetilde C_*(K)$ has $\widetilde C_{-1}(K)=\mathbb Z\langle\emptyset\rangle$, sends each vertex to $\emptyset$, and is zero below degree $-1$. In contrast, $\widetilde C_*(\mathcal O)=0$ in every degree. In particular,

$$
\widetilde H_{-1}(\mathcal E)=\mathbb Z,\qquad
\widetilde H_{-1}(K)=0\quad\text{if }K\text{ has a vertex}.
$$

The definition of $Y_p$ gives $Y_{-1}=\mathcal O$, since even the empty simplex has zero bad vertices. The definitions of $\mathcal S_p$ and $L_S$, with $Y_0=X$, give $\mathcal S_0=\{\emptyset\}$ and $L_{\emptyset}=X$. Monotonicity makes every $Y_p$ a subcomplex. Moreover $L_S$ is a subcomplex: for $\tau'\subseteq\tau\in L_S$, monotonicity gives $b(S\cup\tau')\subseteq S$, while the bad witnesses inside $S$ give the reverse inclusion.

For $p\geq1$, the quotient

$$
\widetilde C_n(Y_p,Y_{p-1})
=\widetilde C_n(Y_p)/\widetilde C_n(Y_{p-1})
$$

is free on oriented $n$-simplices with exactly $p$ bad vertices. For each $S\in\mathcal S_p$ fix an order $s_1,\ldots,s_p$. Order the remaining vertices after them. The unique decomposition gives a graded-group isomorphism whose $S$-component is

$$
\Phi_S\langle s_1,\ldots,s_p,t_0,\ldots,t_{n-p}\rangle
=\langle t_0,\ldots,t_{n-p}\rangle.
$$

Reordering the $t$-vertices changes both sides by the same sign; convert any other ordering of $\sigma$ to the displayed order with its permutation sign. This defines the map on oriented chains. Since $|\sigma|=p+|\tau|$, the degree shift is $p$ and $\dim\tau=n-p$.

Deleting an $s_i$ lowers the bad-vertex count and hence gives zero in the degree-$(n-1)$ relative quotient. Deleting $t_j$ stays in the same $S$-component and has sign $(-1)^{p+j}$. Therefore

$$
\Phi_S\partial=(-1)^p\partial\Phi_S,
$$

and the chain splitting is

$$
\bigl(\widetilde C_*(Y_p,Y_{p-1}),\partial\bigr)
\cong
\bigoplus_{S\in\mathcal S_p}
\bigl(\widetilde C_{*-p}(L_S),(-1)^p\partial\bigr).
$$

When $\tau$ is a vertex, its deletion leaves $S$, corresponding to $\partial\langle t_0\rangle=\emptyset$ in $L_S$. When $\tau=\emptyset$, $S$ has dimension $p-1$ and maps to degree $-1$ of its component; all faces of $S$ vanish in the relative quotient. This augmentation term must be retained.

For $p=0$ the quotient is exactly $\widetilde C_*(X)$, including degree $-1$, because the denominator is zero. Replacing $Y_{-1}$ by $\mathcal E$ would kill the augmentation generator and make the zero column compute ordinary, rather than reduced, homology.

The sets $\mathcal S_p$ may be infinite. Chains have finite support, so the maps and their inverses use algebraic direct sums. Kernels and images are computed componentwise: for a boundary with finitely many nonzero components, choose primitives in those components only. Thus homology commutes with these direct sums. Multiplying a differential by $(-1)^p$ changes neither its kernel nor its image.

## 3. The first page and degreewise bounded convergence

Set $C_* =\widetilde C_*(A)$ and $F_pC_* =\widetilde C_*(Y_p)$ for every $p\geq0$, and set $F_pC_*=0$ for $p<0$, without truncating at twelve. This is a filtration by subcomplexes. Every $m$-simplex has at most $m+1$ bad vertices, so $F_pC_m=C_m$ for $m\geq-1$ and $p\geq m+1$. This includes the augmentation generator in degree $-1$; chain groups below degree $-1$ vanish. Thus the filtration is bounded and exhaustive in each chain degree. The homological spectral sequence has

$$
E^1_{p,q}=H_{p+q}(F_pC_*/F_{p-1}C_*)
\cong\bigoplus_{S\in\mathcal S_p}\widetilde H_q(L_S;\mathbb Z),
\qquad E^1_{0,q}=\widetilde H_q(X;\mathbb Z),
$$

$$
d^r:E^r_{p,q}\longrightarrow E^r_{p-r,q+r-1}.
$$

The row $q=-1$ is present. The first page is zero for $p<0$ or $q<-1$, and so are all subsequent pages. No first-quadrant convergence assumption is made.

To check convergence directly, put $n=p+q$ and, for $r\geq0$, write

$$
Z^r_{p,n}=\{x\in F_pC_n:\partial x\in F_{p-r}C_{n-1}\}.
$$

Thus $Z^0_{p,n}=F_pC_n$. The usual cycle representatives of the filtered-complex construction give, for $r\geq1$,

$$
E^r_{p,q}=
\frac{Z^r_{p,n}}
{Z^{r-1}_{p-1,n}+\partial Z^{r-1}_{p+r-1,n+1}},
$$

with differential represented by $x\mapsto\partial x$. Both denominator terms are contained in the numerator; the first accounts for lower-filtration representatives and the second for boundaries already detected. At $r=1$ this is precisely the homology of the associated graded complex. Taking the kernel modulo image of the displayed differential yields the same quotient with $r$ replaced by $r+1$.

Fix a total degree $n\geq-1$. Only $0\leq p\leq n+1$ need be considered. Write $Z_n(C)=\ker\partial$ and $B_n(C)=\operatorname{im}\partial$, and take an integer $r\geq n+3$. Then $p-r<0$ and $p+r-1\geq n+2$, so the three groups in the quotient become

$$
Z^r_{p,n}=F_pC_n\cap Z_n(C),\qquad
Z^{r-1}_{p-1,n}=F_{p-1}C_n\cap Z_n(C),
$$

$$
\partial Z^{r-1}_{p+r-1,n+1}=F_pC_n\cap B_n(C).
$$

For the last equality, $F_{p+r-1}C_{n+1}=C_{n+1}$, and its defining condition on a possible primitive is exactly $\partial y\in F_pC_n$. Hence these groups have stabilized, and

$$
E^\infty_{p,q}
=\frac{F_pC_n\cap Z_n(C)}
{(F_{p-1}C_n\cap Z_n(C))+(F_pC_n\cap B_n(C))}
\cong\frac{\mathcal F_pH_n(C)}{\mathcal F_{p-1}H_n(C)},
$$

where

$$
\mathcal F_pH_n(C)=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_n(F_pC_*)\longrightarrow H_n(C_*)\bigr).
$$

Indeed, a cycle in $F_pC_n$ maps into $\mathcal F_{p-1}H_n(C)$ exactly when it differs from a cycle in $F_{p-1}C_n$ by a boundary in $C_*$. This proves the last isomorphism. The induced homology filtration begins at zero and reaches all of $H_n(C)$ at $p=n+1$. This degreewise bounded convergence argument does not use $Y_{12}=A$; no inverse limit, completed chain group, or finite-rank assumption is involved. When $n=-1$, only $p=0$ needs consideration.

## 4. Collapse and the exact zero-column conclusion

Each accepted positive link $L_S$ is a cone with a vertex, so $\widetilde H_q(L_S;\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $q\geq-1$. Nonemptiness is specifically needed at $q=-1$: the formal complex $\mathcal E$ would contribute a copy of $\mathbb Z$ there. Thus $E^1_{p,q}=0$ for $p\geq1$.

For every $r\geq1$, a differential leaving column zero has target in a negative column; a differential entering it has source in column $r$, which is zero. All other columns are already zero. Inductively every differential vanishes, and $E^1=E^\infty$.

The algebraic reduced groups used here agree with reduced singular homology of the realizations. [Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Theorem 2.27, p.128](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf) identifies simplicial and singular homology for all delta-complex pairs, including infinite complexes. The comparison sends each vertex to its characteristic singular simplex and respects augmentation, so it also gives the reduced identification. The accepted contractibility of $|A|$ therefore gives $H_q(C_*)=\widetilde H_q(A;\mathbb Z)=0$.

In column zero the convergence statement is especially precise: since $\mathcal F_{-1}H_q(C)=0$,

$$
E^\infty_{0,q}=\mathcal F_0H_q(C)
=\operatorname{im}\bigl(\widetilde H_q(X;\mathbb Z)
\longrightarrow\widetilde H_q(A;\mathbb Z)\bigr)=0.
$$

Combining this with the first-page identification and collapse proves

$$
\widetilde H_q(X;\mathbb Z)\cong E^1_{0,q}
=E^\infty_{0,q}=0\qquad(q\geq-1).
$$

This proves the original homological conclusion. Identifying the limiting zero column as this image makes the paper's subquotient statement precise without changing its validity.

## 5. Scope and verification provenance

If the separate homotopy equivalence $C_1(S_2)\simeq X$ of Theorem 6.8 is accepted, acyclicity transfers to $C_1(S_2)$. This submission does not verify that equivalence, the geometric inputs, the finite Budget enumeration, or simple connectivity. Acyclicity alone does not prove contractibility. The result verifies the original homological module, not the entire manuscript or other surfaces.

OpenAI Codex prepared this focused submission. Claude Opus 5.5, a different model family, reviewed the original spectral-sequence steps and the previous separated version (v1.1). A fresh GPT context reviewed the earlier separated text; earlier GPT reviews of broader materials are separate evidence. For v1.2, Codex revised the convergence argument to use degreewise boundedness and clarified its dependence on the accepted inputs. A new GPT session reviewed the v1.2 changes and their affected context; this was not a new review of the geometric inputs or computation. For v1.3, a further AI review by a DeepSeek-based agent raised presentation points; Claude and GPT adjudicated them, Codex made the three resulting clarifications, and a fresh GPT context reviewed them. AI-assisted checks are not human expert certification or formal proof verification. The significance of this focused validation and any award eligibility remain for the organizers to assess.

1.title: Exhaustive finite validation of the six-point Budget lemmas in the genus-two curve-complex paper
1.excerpt_md: This submission contributes a reproducible finite verification of Lemmas 9.11, 9.14, 9.15 and Corollary 9.16 in Apex Intelligence's [*The co…
1.body_md:
This submission contributes a reproducible finite verification of Lemmas 9.11, 9.14, 9.15 and Corollary 9.16 in Apex Intelligence's [*The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once is contractible in genus two*](https://math.apexin.net/papers/curve-complex-genus-two.pdf), dated 11 September 2026. The target is the 35-page PDF with SHA-256 `d1eadd01f94e9af17ee9f5fb2ee1b05b326430f37296309fd9417340ea366fd4`.

The completed computation found 191 oriented hosts, 782,145 nonempty subsets and 11,504 purely bad witnesses representing 658 types. Every Budget assertion passed. The contribution is this exhaustive audit and reconstruction specification; the paper's lemmas and standard surface topology are not claimed as new results.

## 1. Precise claim and dependencies

Let $B$ be six marked points of an oriented sphere. A legal arc system is a finite collection of pairwise non-isotopic essential arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors, including loops. Isotopies fix the marks; endpoint rotations are allowed. A nonempty system $S$ is *purely bad* in Definition 8.2 precisely when each non-loop arc has another arc of $S$ with the same unordered endpoint pair; loops are automatically bad.

Types are taken up to orientation-preserving homeomorphism, allowing permutation of the six marked labels. Mirrors merge only if an orientation-preserving isomorphism exists. These are not the infinitely many fixed-mark isotopy classes. All tested properties are invariant under the stated equivalence, so the completeness inputs below ensure coverage of every fixed-label system.

Inputs are embedded representatives of disjoint systems, the usual essential-arc and empty-disc isotopy conventions, the independent bound $E\leq12$, and generalized triangulation extension. Their topological justification below makes the cutoff inspectable. Neither truncated enumeration nor program agreement independently proves these inputs; the observed ten-edge maximum cannot justify the cutoff at twelve.

Excluded are the spectral sequence, whole contractibility theorem, hyperelliptic dictionary, intersection formula, arc-complex dimension statements other than the bound $E\leq12$ derived in Section 2, and geometric Cone lemma. Experiment 1B was not performed: zero new exact intersection samples. The finite audit stops at Section 9's Budget assertions; it does not certify Section 10.

## 2. Why the finite host space suffices

The reduction uses no Budget conclusion. Generalized triangulations allow loops, repeated triangle vertices or sides and self-folding, as in [Hatcher, *Triangulations of Surfaces*, revised version, pp. 1–2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Papers/TriangSurf.pdf). These are standard topological inputs.

**Edge bound.** Include all six marks, even unused isolated marks, in a regular neighborhood $N$ of a legal $E$-edge system. The compact complementary pieces $R_i$ satisfy

$$
\chi(N)=6-E,\qquad \sum_i\chi(R_i)=E-4,\qquad \sum_i\ell_i=2E,
$$

where $\ell_i$ counts edge sides on the boundary, with repetitions. The pieces are planar; a non-disc piece has Euler characteristic at most zero. Every disc piece has at least three edge sides. Indeed, length zero would leave a sphere with only one isolated vertex; length one would bound an inessential loop. At length two, distinct non-loop edges form an empty bigon and are isotopic. Two same-basepoint loops bounding the mixed two-sided region give the same conclusion after normalizing that region to a disc at the basepoint. A loop and a non-loop cannot form a closed two-step boundary walk. The same non-loop edge traversed twice would be an isolated one-edge component whose disc complement leaves no place for the other marks; the two sides of a loop are separated on the sphere. Thus, if $D$ is the number of disc pieces,

$$
E-4\leq D\leq\frac{2E}{3},\qquad E\leq12.
$$

Empty-disc isotopy slides one side to the other, supported near the disc with endpoints fixed and rotations allowed. For same-basepoint loops normalize the mixed region at the basepoint, slide and reglue. This does not classify arbitrary loop isotopy classes by enclosed marked sets.

**Extension.** Starting from a nonempty legal system, add a legal disjoint arc whenever possible. The independent bound above makes this process terminate at a maximal system $T$. Any unused mark could be joined inside its complementary region to an existing boundary vertex; the new endpoint ensures a new isotopy class. If $T$ were disconnected, a complementary region incident to two components would admit an arc joining them, again a new class. Hence $T$ uses all six marks and is connected, so its complementary regions on the sphere are open discs.

Cut these discs open along their boundary walks, retaining repeated labels and sides. Empty monogons and digons are excluded by essentiality and distinctness; a face traversing a single edge twice would force the whole connected graph to be that edge. If a face has at least four sides, draw a diagonal between nonadjacent corners. Repeated labels may make the diagonal a loop, which is allowed. An allegedly inessential diagonal would cut off an empty disc whose original edges must themselves be inessential loops. An allegedly isotopic diagonal would form an empty bigon or, for same-basepoint loops, an empty normalized mixed disc with an existing edge. Any original edge inside that disc would be an inessential loop or parallel to its boundary edge. Legality excludes these possibilities; with no interior original edges, the two corners would have been adjacent. Thus the diagonal is legal, contrary to maximality. This is the local content of generalized triangulation extension, including repeated boundary labels and self-folding.

Consequently the host has

$$
V=6,\qquad 3F=2E,\qquad V-E+F=2,
\qquad E=12,\quad F=8.
$$

Conversely, a connected sphere map with six vertices and triangular faces is legal. If an edge or pair of edges bounded an empty monogon or digon, normalize it to a triangulated disc with boundary length $b\in\{1,2\}$ and no interior vertices. Euler characteristic and triangle-side counting would require $b-3<0$ interior edges. The normalized empty mixed region between same-basepoint loops is covered by the same count. Thus every host subset is legal, and every legal system appears as a subset of at least one host. This reduction uses none of Lemmas 9.11, 9.14, 9.15 or Corollary 9.16.

## 3. Generate all oriented hosts

The following specification permits reconstruction without any particular canonical-labeling library.

The dual host is a connected cubic sphere map with eight vertices and twelve edges, allowing loops, multiple edges and bridges. Choose a spanning tree, cut its five other edges into ten stems, and root at one stem. The oriented tree is then an ordered full binary tree with eight internal nodes. Its neighborhood and exterior are discs, so the cut edges are a noncrossing perfect matching of the ten stems in exterior-boundary order. Conversely every such tree and matching glues in the exterior disc to produce a cubic sphere map. Thus all target maps occur without relying on flip-graph connectivity.

Generate ordered trees recursively:

$$
\mathcal T_0=\{\text{empty}\},\qquad
\mathcal T_n=\bigcup_{i=0}^{n-1}
\{(L,R):L\in\mathcal T_i,\ R\in\mathcal T_{n-1-i}\}.
$$

At each internal node assign three darts in the cyclic order (parent, left, right), defining a permutation $\tau$. Pair parent/child slots along tree edges using $\alpha$; temporarily fix the root parent slot and every empty child slot. Read these ten stems in the unique orbit of $\tau\circ\alpha$. Generate all noncrossing matchings recursively by pairing position zero with each odd-numbered position and independently matching the two remaining even intervals. Replace the fixed stems by the matching pairs and set

$$
\sigma=\tau\circ\alpha,\qquad
\varphi=\sigma\circ\alpha=\tau.
$$

Here $\alpha$ pairs edges, $\sigma$ cycles are vertices and $\varphi$ cycles are triangular faces. Check these permutation identities, connectedness and six vertex cycles for every construction. There are

$$
C_8C_5=1430\cdot42=60{,}060
$$

raw constructions. Deduplicate by rooting at each of the 24 darts, breadth-first relabeling in the fixed successor order $[\alpha(d),\sigma(d)]$, and minimizing the concatenated relabeled permutation arrays. Equal codes are exactly oriented map isomorphisms: a rooted isomorphism preserves the traversal, and equal arrays exhibit the inverse correspondence. Never invert $\sigma$. The result is 191 hosts.

In each host order its twelve edge pairs by their smaller dart and traverse every nonempty bit mask from 1 through 4095. Test pure badness only by counting selected non-loop endpoint pairs; each must occur at least twice. Each selected loop forms its own object. Do not prune by used-mark count, gap count, freeness, cleanliness or any Budget conclusion.

## 4. Reconstruct regions and test the assertions

For any retained edge set $Q$, compute $R(Q)$ as follows. Begin with the eight host triangles and merge across every edge outside $Q$, including self-joins. Each component is an open complementary region. Represent it by three disjoint kinds of atoms:

- its open triangles;
- the open edges outside $Q$ incident to those triangles;
- the marked vertices unused by $Q$ whose incident triangles belong to that component.

All incident sectors of an unused vertex merge, since all its incident edges are outside $Q$. A used vertex is on a region's boundary exactly when a selected dart at that vertex has the region on one of its sides. Restrict each vertex cycle of $\sigma$ to retained darts, giving $\sigma_Q$. The cycles of $\sigma_Q\circ\alpha$ are boundary walks; attach each to the component of its adjacent host triangle. Retain every boundary walk of each region. A region need not be a disc when $Q$ is disconnected. The interior marked-point count $k$ is the number of vertex atoms.

Retaining all boundary groups and unused marks preserves disconnected nesting. A slit edge can change an open region without changing its triangles, so all equality and disjointness tests use the complete three-kind atom sets.

Legality is also checked directly on hosts and rechecked on retained representatives. A loop must have another mark on each side in $R(\{e\})$. Two non-loop edges with the same endpoints must have marks on both sides in $R(\{e,f\})$. Two loops at the same basepoint may not have an unmarked mixed digon whose boundary uses one side of each. These are essentiality and empty-disc tests independent of the Budget assertions; host subsets inherit legality.

For a pure system $S$, the objects are single loops and entire repeated non-loop endpoint families. The gaps of an object $O$ are the regions $R(O)$. Another object $O'$ is contained in the closure of a gap $g$ if and only if every open edge atom of $O'$ belongs to $g$; its endpoints then belong to the closure automatically. A gap is free if no other object satisfies this test. This computes the definition directly, without assuming Lemma 9.8. In counting $k(g)$, include all marks in the gap, including any used by other objects.

For each gap, compare its full atom set with each region of $R(S)$ to decide whether it is a face of the whole system. Let $X(g)$ be its actual boundary-mark set and let $\mathcal F$ be the repeated non-loop endpoint pairs of $S$. Test cleanliness by checking that every distinct pair in $X(g)$ belongs to $\mathcal F$; do not assume the boundary has at most two marks. A good face must simultaneously be a whole-system face, a free gap, clean, and have $k(g)\in\{1,2\}$.

The recorded predicates are:

1. Lemma 9.11: at least two free gaps have pairwise disjoint complete atom sets, and every free gap equals a whole-system face.
2. Lemma 9.14: every free gap has $k(g)\geq1$.
3. Lemma 9.15: at least one good face exists.
4. Corollary 9.16: the actual number $V'$ of marks used by $S$ satisfies $V'\leq4$.
5. Auxiliary Corollary 9.13: every free gap is clean, checked separately for diagnostic purposes.

## 5. Exact type deduplication and independent checks

For each subset construct a four-colored directed graph with six mark nodes, selected dart nodes, selected edge nodes and complementary-region nodes. Each dart points to its endpoint mark, its edge, its side-region (the component of its host $\varphi$-face), and the next selected dart at its vertex. Each unused mark points to its containing region. The four target colors distinguish the four dart relations.

Define a canonical certificate as the lexicographically least adjacency matrix over all permutations within each color, prefixed by the four color sizes. Brute-force canonicalization is sufficient in principle; the implementation uses `pynauty==2.8.8.1`. Edge membership recovers $\alpha$, dart successors recover the oriented rotation, and region incidence groups all boundary walks and locates unused marks. These data determine the regular neighborhood and its genus-zero complementary surfaces, hence the oriented embedding up to the stated equivalence. In particular, disconnected components are not classified merely by an unordered list of their separate rotations.

Full certificates decide equality; SHA-256 only labels records. Different canonical-labeling implementations can produce different bytes and identifiers for the same types, predicates and counts.

An independent Whitehead-move closure from an explicit octahedron made 1,924 transitions. Separate canonicalization confirmed the same 191 hosts and empty set differences. The tree/stem proof supplies coverage; list agreement alone does not.

The main predicates use union-find and half-edge boundary walks; the separate implementation uses dual-graph BFS and its own atom/object calculations. They share definitions and encoding conventions, not region or predicate functions. Before deduplication a supplementary audit checked all 11,504 pure witnesses, comparing ten fields: combined and separate 9.11 predicates, 9.13, 9.14, 9.15, 9.16, free-gap count, good-face count and $V'$. All 115,040 comparisons agreed; every conclusion passed.

The audit also checked atom conservation, Euler relations, 658 full record reconstructions, 658 deterministic dart relabelings and five hand-built positive/negative legality examples. It calls the existing predicates and is not a third independent implementation or host generator.

**Cross-model reimplementation and host census.** After this text was frozen, Claude, a different model family, reviewed the reduction and wrote two standard-library scripts without importing any module above. The first checks the host list independently of every generator: the 191 hosts are valid, pairwise non-isomorphic oriented triangulations, and

$$
\sum_{h}\frac{24}{|\mathrm{Aut}^+(h)|}=4096,
$$

where $\mathrm{Aut}^+(h)$ is the group of orientation-preserving map automorphisms, computed by rooted relabeling. The right side is the number of rooted planar cubic maps with eight vertices (OEIS A002005, $a(4)$). Every valid host contributes a positive amount and all oriented hosts together sum to $a(4)$, so none is missing. A brute-force count of rooted cubic sphere maps with two and four vertices, allowing loops and multiple edges, reproduces $a(1)=4$ and $a(2)=32$, confirming that the sequence counts exactly these duals.

The second script is a third predicate implementation written directly from Definitions 8.2 and 9.1–9.4. On all 782,145 subsets it reproduces the 11,504 purely bad witnesses, their edge-count distribution $(504,1218,2121,2607,2375,1599,765,255,54,6,0,0)$ and used-mark distribution $(1310,5916,3718,560,0,0)$, with zero failures of 9.11, 9.13, 9.14, 9.15 and 9.16. It rechecks host legality directly: 1,465 loop and repeated-pair tests find no empty monogon or digon. Controls show that the predicates discriminate: 459 witnesses have no good face with $k=1$, 560 use four marks, and 7,515 lack three pairwise disjoint free gaps. It shares only the host data and the paper's definitions with the implementations above.

## 6. Results and evidential limits

| Quantity | Completed result |
|---|---:|
| Tree/stem constructions | 60,060 |
| Oriented hosts | 191 |
| Nonempty host subsets | 782,145 |
| Rejected solely as not purely bad | 770,641 |

The type counts by edge count $E=1,\ldots,12$ are

$$
(2,10,26,69,114,164,142,95,30,6,0,0).
$$

The type counts by used-mark count $V'=1,\ldots,6$ are

$$
(32,238,303,85,0,0).
$$

The $V'=5,6$ ranges contained 295,711 and 165,188 candidates: all underwent the pure-badness test, none passed, and none was pruned using Corollary 9.16. Of the 658 types, 170 are disconnected with multiple-boundary regions, 647 contain loops and 464 contain multiple same-basepoint loops. Counts for one through four components are 488, 151, 18 and 1. 11.title: Conditional Lean verification of genus-two 1-curve complex contractibility: arc retraction and arc–curve correspondence
11.excerpt_md: This **Key Verification** submission concerns Apex Intelligence's *The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once is contractible…
11.body_md:
This **Key Verification** submission concerns Apex Intelligence's *The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once is contractible in genus two* (11 September 2026; competition paper 2, 35-page PDF), SHA-256 `d1eadd01f94e9af17ee9f5fb2ee1b05b326430f37296309fd9417340ea366fd4`. In Lean 4 and Mathlib **v4.35.0-rc3**, the development verifies a conditional form of Theorem 1.1 for $C_1(S_2)$, constructs a strong deformation retraction of the actual six-marked-sphere arc complex $A$ onto $X$, proves Proposition 6.1 within the development from the listed inputs, and connects $A\to X\to K'\to K$. License: **Apache License 2.0**. Repository: [iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-lean](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-lean), commit `b285b9389f003cf28919d0a5c364220e8cd6fb4a`. Verification of this commit: a [GitHub Actions run](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-lean/actions/runs/36949145313) on a fresh runner (results uploaded as an artifact) and local clean-copy and fresh-clone builds (§6).

**Key premises and proved conversions** (input labels as in `docs/DEPENDENCIES.md`). C5s (`BigonSurgeryWithSpectators`) and S (`TorusSlopes`) still carry key geometry. The Hatcher instance `ContractibleSpace Topo.MarkedSphere.A.Realization` remains a premise about this exact object/topology. C4d (the local core of Lemma 10.4), HR (the arc recovery of Lemma 4.10(ii)) and L/N (the subsurface identification and intersection preservation used in Lemma 6.6) are now derived conditionally from smaller disk, braid, twist, bigon and annulus theorems (§4); two-point side selection, arc recovery and subsurface localization are proved internally. C1e is proved outright. The replacement standard inputs still lack unconditional Lean instances and require the recorded source bridges.

## 1. The verified statements

The sphere is the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^3$ with six labelled marks. Arcs are embedded intervals between distinct marks or embedded based circles for loops, with unmarked interiors and Definition 2.3's empty-disc essentiality. Vertices are mark-fixing ambient-isotopy classes.

Faces of `Topo.MarkedSphere.A` admit simultaneous interior-disjoint representatives, loops included. `Topo.MarkedSphere.X` is flag on non-loop classes, adjacent for interior-disjoint representatives with distinct endpoint pairs. It is not generally full in $A$. Finite realization proves its inclusion and $Y_0=X$.

`Topo.GenusTwo.Space` is the octagon quotient with edge word $aba^{-1}b^{-1}cdc^{-1}d^{-1}$. Its essential circles (not bounding embedded discs) define ambient-isotopy vertices of `Topo.GenusTwo.K`, with adjacency $i(a,b)\leq1$. `Topo.GenusTwo.KPrime` ($K'$) is the full nonseparating subcomplex. Curve isotopies act on the whole surface. Model-certification limits appear in §7.

For a generic complex $\mathcal C$, its realization has finite nonnegative barycentric weights of mass one supported on a face, with **weak topology** final from closed simplices. Continuity out is checked there, without local finiteness. The empty face contributes no points.

The main theorem is

```lean
Topo.CurveComplexContractibility.genus_two_contractible
```

with conclusion

```lean
ContractibleSpace Topo.GenusTwo.K.Realization
```

under 43 explicit parameters: 14 sphere, 11 cover/twist, current-$A$ contractibility and 17 curve/disk/annulus inputs. C4d, HR, L/N and C1e are derived internally; so are Proposition 6.1, Budget, Cone, realization, flagness, the bound and Theorem 6.8. No parameter directly supplies Proposition 6.1, a dictionary bijection, an adjacency equivalence, Budget, Cone, the uniform bound or Theorem 6.8; C5s, S and the current-$A$ contractibility remain explicit premises. `Topo.CurveComplexContractibility.genus_two_contractible_direct` retains the intermediate 34-input interface.

Mathlib's `ContractibleSpace` means homotopy equivalence to a point, equivalently a continuous contraction. The construction

```lean
Topo.CurveComplexContractibility.real_strongDeformationRetraction_X_standard
```

uses only the 14 sphere inputs, without Hatcher. For the natural inclusion $j:|X|\hookrightarrow|A|$, it supplies jointly continuous $H:|A|\times[0,1]\to|A|$ with

$$
H(x,0)=x,\qquad H(x,1)\in j(|X|),\qquad H(j(y),t)=j(y).
$$

The endpoint $r:|A|\to|X|$ is continuous in the target's own weak topology and $rj=\mathrm{id}$. Current-$A$ contractibility gives

$$
|A|\text{ contractible}\Longrightarrow|X|\text{ contractible}
\Longrightarrow|K'|\text{ contractible}\Longrightarrow|K|\text{ contractible}.
$$

The latter implications use the constructed simplicial equivalence $X\cong K'$ and strong deformation retraction $K\to K'$.

## 2. Correspondence with the paper

Pages refer to the identified PDF; constructions use the stated inputs.

1. **Theorem 1.1 (p. 2).** `Topo.CurveComplexContractibility.genus_two_contractible` gives conditional contractibility of the fixed-model $1$-curve complex.

2. **Definitions 2.3/2.5 (p. 5), §8 zero stage.** `Topo.MarkedSphere.simultaneous_realization`, `arcComplex_flag` and `stage_zero_eq_X` prove zero-intersection realization, flagness and $Y_0=X$ from tameness, general position, bigon criterion and C5s.

3. **Theorem 1.4 (p. 2), Theorem 4.11 (p. 17), non-loop/nonseparating part.** `Topo.GenusTwoDictionary.nonloopDictionaryEquiv` and `psiArcClass_bijective` use cover/mapping-class/twist inputs, with HR derived. The $3\mid3$-circle/separating-curve part is not covered.

4. **Proposition 6.1 (pp. 20–21).** `Topo.ClassicalCurveContractibility.proposition61_of_classical` and `psi_adjacency_iff` construct the bijection, both adjacency directions and actual simplicial equivalence using one compatible cover. The main proof supplies the derived HR; no dictionary or adjacency equivalence is assumed.

5. **Lemma 6.4 (p. 21).** `Topo.GenusTwoInputs.separating_independent` follows from general position, parity, separating cuts, annulus isotopy and torus dichotomy.

6. **Lemma 6.6 (pp. 21–22).** `Topo.GenusTwoInputs.farey_links` identifies actual links with Farey $*$ Farey, using derived L/N and slope input S. `Topo.Farey.contractible` and `Topo.Complex.contractible_join` prove the contraction and join step.

7. **Corollary 6.5, Proposition 6.7, Theorem 6.8 (pp. 21–22).** `Topo.Complex.strongDeformationRetract_deletion` and `Topo.GenusTwoInputs.theorem68_from_classical` prove deletion, relative cone deformation and infinite gluing; the surface application uses derived L/N and remaining curve inputs.

8. **§9 (pp. 27–31), Budget (p. 31).** `Topo.Budget.Map.budget`, `used_le_four` and `Topo.CurveComplexContractibility.real_budget_for_layer` prove ribbon/actual-stratum Budget. Sphere inputs construct dictionaries, object planarity and legality; no Budget provider is a parameter.

9. **§10 (pp. 31–34), Lemma 10.4 (p. 32).** The C4d conversion in §4, `TwoPatch.core_uniform`, `WeakChart.cone` and `Topo.CurveComplexContractibility.real_coneHypothesis` give core identification and actual-link apices from disk inputs, patches/charts and localization.

10. **§§8–11 (pp. 25–35), replacement route.** `Topo.BadFiltration.strongDeformationRetraction` and §1's sphere construction yield $A\to X$ from actual Budget/Cone and a proved bound. Hatcher enters only for contractibility.

11. **Proposition 6.2 (p. 21).** `Topo.CurveComplexContractibility.face_card_le_1920` and `bad_card_le_1920` prove a coarse bound, without $12$, dimension $11$ or facet classification.

12. **Uncovered:** full §§3–5 hyperbolic/geodesic theory and intersection formula; §7 all-genus Theorem 1.3; §8 relative chains, spectral sequence and convergence.

The Mathlib-only `Statements.lean` states deletion, joins, Farey contractibility, punctured-disc path classification and ribbon Budget; `Topo/StatementVerification.lean` proves them with their displayed premises. The topology, counting and actual-object constructions are the substantive verified core.

## 3. Where the route differs

**Direct deformation.** Within a face, a vertex is bad if it is a loop or shares its endpoint pair with another vertex of that face. $Y_n$ allows at most $n$ bad vertices per face. Actual Budget/Cone, layer/block identities and relative deformations retract $Y_n$ onto $Y_{n-1}$, fixing the latter. Finite composition gives $A\to Y_0=X$.

Budget produces disjoint free, clean gaps; $V'$ counts marks met by the stratum:

$$
1\leq k(g_1),k(g_2),\qquad k(g_1)+k(g_2)\leq6-V'\leq5.
$$

One gap has one or two marks and proved Jordan boundary geometry. Cone/gluing gives joint continuity across infinitely many blocks; separating-vertex deletion gives $K\to K'$. This replaces §8's spectral sequence and Hurewicz–Whitehead route.

**Coarse bound.** For every actual face,

$$
|\sigma|\leq1920,\qquad |\operatorname{bv}(\sigma)|\leq1920.
$$

Euler/counting and empty-low-degree-face exclusions give $30$ edges per endpoint family; $2^6=64$ endpoint subsets give $1920$. This covers loops, parallel edges and unused marks. A finite bound suffices; $12$ and dimension $11$ are not established.

**Topological conventions.** Representatives are continuous embeddings with local topological transverse crossings. Isotopies are jointly continuous homeomorphism families fixing the marks. Comparison with the paper's smooth representatives and tangent-line convention remains external.

**Intersection numbers** lie in $\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$ (`ℕ∞`), with infinity for an empty candidate spectrum; nonempty spectra have attained natural minima. Proposition 6.1 treats zero/one-crossing pairs via coordinates and cover charts, without Theorem 5.5's full formula $i(\widetilde a,\widetilde b)=2\widehat j(a,b)+e(a,b)$.

## 4. Classical inputs and their review

`docs/DEPENDENCIES.md` records uses, sources, review status and conversion limits; `docs/PARAMETER-TYPES.md` prints the definitions; `docs/REVIEWS.md` summarizes each independent model review with its reservations. The standard premises below remain unproved Lean inputs.

**Sphere group (14):** graph topology, relative isotopy, point transport, general position, bigon/spectator surgery, plus `DiskArcStraightening` and `TwoStrandBraidGeneration`. `Topo.OpenEdgeFlatness.openEdgeLocalFlatness` proves C1e outright; the two disk inputs give C4d.

C4i requires **every strictly interior arc parameter to avoid all six marks at every time, with fixed endpoints**. Split based-loop isotopy separates nullhomotopy-to-empty-disc from nonzero based-homotopy-to-isotopy (Epstein §1.7, §4.1, Appendix A1 and compact-support extension). It supports the proved loop legality. Mixed-endpoint isotopy retains spoke winding.

**C4d.** `Topo.TwoPointDiskTwist.diskInteriorEndpointIsotopy_of_schoenflies_braid` uses single-arc boundary-relative Schoenflies normalization and generation of the two-marked-disc mapping class group by a concrete half twist. Normalization compares the arcs by a boundary-fixed homeomorphism; a half-twist-power correction makes it isotopic to the identity, while preserving the standard core. Core preservation, conjugation and transport to the real disc are proved. Exactly two interior marks suffice: no homotopy premise is needed.

**Cover/twist group (11):** compatible cover, homotopy lifting, symmetry, coordinates, Birman–Hilden, zero/one-crossing pair coordinates, collar E, twist comparison TC, `HalfTwistSquareNormalForm` and `NonzeroDehnTwistPowerRigidity`. Branch-point extension and assembly are proved conditionally.

**HR.** `Topo.TwoPointDiskTwist.halfTwistRigidity_of_square_power_schoenflies_braid` uses the two disk inputs, a single half twist's square normal form and nonzero twist-power rigidity for circles. Squaring equal or inverse half-twist classes gives boundary-twist-power equality; circle rigidity yields boundary isotopy. The project proves side transport and the two-versus-at-least-three mark count that prevents side interchange, then recovers the arc in the same two-point disc. Lemma 4.10(ii)'s recovery is thus derived internally. Collar, twist, certificate and descent constructions still depend on the other listed inputs.

Independent review judged all four premises true. Source bridges still require precise relative planar-arc/outer-boundary justification, the concrete braid generator, quotient-to-collar conversion with unit square exponent up to sign, and collar-sign/relative ambient-isotopy conversion. Epstein A1 does not state the whole single-arc interface; mark exchange alone does not certify the square factor.

Sources include Farb–Margalit's disk/braid and twist results and Epstein's extension tools. **E has no directly matching theorem in the cited sources. TC covers nonorientable surfaces and requires a local-annulus argument beyond the book's orientable version.** Chart compatibility and reversing-mapping-class bridges remain in the ledger.

**Curve/disk/annulus group (17).** Seven retained inputs are general position G, parity P, separating cuts C, annulus isotopy A, torus dichotomy T, incompressible essentiality I and slopes S. Two are closed-surface `BigonCriterion` and `ClosedCurveBaer`. Eight smaller inputs are `BoundaryPreservation`, `InteriorGeneralPosition`, `InteriorBigonCriterion`, `DiskSchoenflies`, `InteriorCurveBaer`, `DisjointIsotopicAnnulus`, `AnnulusCircleClassification` and `ParallelCopy`.

`Topo.StandardSubsurfaceCurves.incompressibleIsotopy_of_bigon_annulus` derives L; `subsurfaceIntersection_of_bigon` derives N. Proved bigon localization excludes the essential cut circle from the disc and puts the whole disc in the original side; pullback certifies ambient minimality of intrinsic minimal representatives. Nonperipherality and annulus classification keep a comparison annulus from crossing the cut, giving same-side intrinsic isotopy. Transport uses free homotopy and closed-surface Baer.
