L/N share proved lemmas; neither calls the other target theorem. Both conversions also use polygon regularity, Jordan–Schoenflies, the closed-surface `BigonCriterion` and `ClosedCurveBaer`, and incompressible essentiality; L uses all eight subsurface inputs, N only `DiskSchoenflies`, `BoundaryPreservation`, `InteriorGeneralPosition` and `InteriorBigonCriterion`. In the main assembly, polygon regularity comes from the compatible-cover witness.

Independent review judged the eight premises true. Bridges remain for intrinsic-boundary certification, simultaneous tameness, ambient-class/homotopy identification and empty-bigon extraction. Boundary-contact disc Schoenflies needs planar containment; peripheral interior Baer uses Epstein 2.1 beyond Farb–Margalit's narrower convention. Subsurface localization is proved.

**Remaining key content.** Six inputs of the intermediate interface carry content of the paper's own lemmas or key geometry: C4d (Lemma 10.4's local core), HR (Lemma 4.10(ii)'s arc recovery), C5s, L, N and S. Four of them—C4d, HR, L and N—are now derived. C5s supplies local supported cancellation, strict crossing decrease and spectator-crossing injections; descent, relative realization and flagness are proved downstream. S supplies the one-holed-torus slope equivalence and determinant formula, requiring puncture/fill and intersection-preservation bridges; Farey contraction is proved. Their geometric instances remain unproved.

**Hatcher (1):** revised Theorem (a), paper Fact 7.2, covers this six-marked sphere with loops. Its current-$A$ object/topology bridge and Lean instance remain unproved, as does the whole input bundle.

## 5. Remarks arising from the formalization

**Lemma 10.4's endpoint conversion.** Lemma 10.4 (p. 32) invokes Lemma 4.9's planar arc fact (p. 16). Epstein Theorem 3.1, pp. 89–90, has boundary endpoints, requiring conversion for interior marks; Lemma 4.9 also offers change of coordinates. The proved normalization/braid argument supplies boundary-fixed isotopy with two interior marks, without a homotopy assumption, from its two stated standard premises. This agrees with the statement of Lemma 10.4; only the cited justification needs the conversion.

**Arc recovery and localization.** Theorem 4.11's non-loop injectivity (p. 17) passes through $2\mid4$ circles and Lemma 4.10(ii). Two-point-side selection/core recovery and Lemma 6.6's bigon/annulus confinement are now proved. The slope identification remains S.

## 6. Checks

With pinned toolchain and locked dependencies installed, reproduction is offline:

```sh
lake --no-cache build
python3 verification/verify.py
```

The verifier checks frozen hashes, statement imports, shortcuts, build coverage, paths, machine types/input definitions, parameters and axioms; it also replays all 7,248 project declarations through the kernel in a fresh environment and runs 23 negative regression tests that must fail. Its whitelist is exactly `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`, not evidence that mathematical premises are true or jointly satisfiable. It writes `verification/results/summary.json` and fails nonzero.

`Statements.lean` has frozen SHA-256

```text
eb5b982a387d4ceb71c66c0b8db1a69d66049c87cfe0f51ea6befc3bda8b73fa
```

Frozen digests are not refreshed automatically. For commit `b285b93`, the verifier passed in the release tree, in a source-only copy without project build cache, and in a fresh clone of this repository built from scratch; dependency artifacts were reused and Mathlib was not rebuilt. The [GitHub Actions run](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-lean/actions/runs/36949145313) ran the same verifier on a fresh Linux runner and passed; its results are uploaded as an artifact.

## 7. Scope

The fixed octagon is proved compact, connected and Hausdorff with two-dimensional charts. Full orientation/genus certification and transport to arbitrary closed orientable genus-two surfaces are unfinished; `ChartedSpace ℂ` alone is insufficient. The smooth/topological bridge remains external.

Simultaneous realization covers **pairwise zero intersection**, also relative to a fixed representative subsystem, not general simultaneous minima. Uncovered portions include the $3\mid3$ correspondence, full §5 formula, §7 all-genus Theorem 1.3 and §8 spectral sequence. The bound is $1920$, without dimension $11$. Smaller standard inputs and C5s/S/Hatcher remain explicit premises. The entire paper is not verified.

**AI disclosure.** GPT-6.1 Sol wrote the Lean code in OpenAI Codex under human direction; GPT-6 Astra and Claude planned the route. Claude independently rebuilt each stage and checked statements and axioms. Fresh GPT contexts performed adversarial reviews of the inputs, release and an earlier draft of this note. GPT-6.1 Sol drafted the English submission; Claude revised the text of this version. No human expert certification is claimed.

12.title: Conditional Lean verification of genus-two 1-curve complex contractibility from reviewed classical inputs
12.excerpt_md: This **Key Verification** concerns Apex Intelligence's *The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once is contractible in genus tw…
12.body_md:
This **Key Verification** concerns Apex Intelligence's *The complex of curves pairwise intersecting at most once is contractible in genus two* (11 September 2026; 35-page PDF), SHA-256 `d1eadd01f94e9af17ee9f5fb2ee1b05b326430f37296309fd9417340ea366fd4`. Lean 4/Mathlib **v4.35.0-rc3** proves, from listed inputs, fixed-model Theorem 1.1 for $C_1(S_2)$, an actual-sphere strong deformation retraction $A\to X$, Proposition 6.1 and one-holed-torus slopes. License: **Apache License 2.0**. Repository: [iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-lean-v2](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-lean-v2); commit: `7563547869244c4c7a9b27c175892d3b75e951a1`; CI record: [GitHub Actions run](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p02-curve-complex-lean-v2/actions/runs/37180699232) (§5).

**Scope and premises** (labels in `docs/DEPENDENCIES.md`). The 40 inputs are sourced textbook statements or standard consequences/extensions, independently reviewed in their exact models. **No project-specific proof obligation or Hatcher contractibility premise is an input.** S, C5s, $A$ contractibility and C4d/HR/L/N are project-derived; C1e has no premises. Retained classical inputs have **no unconditional Lean instances**; source/model limits remain (§§4, 6). Reviews are not Lean proofs or expert certification. This is fixed-model conditional verification, not full-paper verification. Closed-torus classification and S in existence form are equally strong under the bridge premises (§4).

## 1. The verified statements

On the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^3$ with six labelled marks, arcs are embedded intervals between distinct marks or embedded based circles, with unmarked interiors and Definition 2.3's empty-disc essentiality. Vertices are mark-fixing ambient-isotopy classes. Faces of `Topo.MarkedSphere.A` admit simultaneous interior-disjoint representatives, loops included. `Topo.MarkedSphere.X` is flag on non-loop classes: adjacency requires interior-disjoint representatives with distinct endpoint pairs. It is not generally full in $A$. Finite realization proves inclusion and $Y_0=X$.

`Topo.GenusTwo.Space` is the octagon quotient with word $aba^{-1}b^{-1}cdc^{-1}d^{-1}$. Circles not bounding embedded discs define ambient-isotopy vertices of `Topo.GenusTwo.K`, adjacent for $i(a,b)\leq1$. `Topo.GenusTwo.KPrime` ($K'$) is its full nonseparating subcomplex. Isotopies act on the whole surface; certification limits are in §6.

Realizations have finite nonnegative barycentric weights of mass one on a face, with **weak topology** final from closed simplices, without local finiteness. The empty face gives no points.

Main theorem:

```lean
Topo.CurveComplexMain.genus_two_contractible
```

Conclusion:

```lean
ContractibleSpace Topo.GenusTwo.K.Realization
```

Its **40 explicit parameters** are classical inputs (§4). S, C5s, $A$ contractibility, Proposition 6.1, Legal/Budget/Cone, realization, flagness, dimension/X facets, Theorem 6.8, dictionary bijection, adjacency equivalence and surgery/descent are internal results. README prints types and uses.

Mathlib's `ContractibleSpace` is homotopy equivalence to a point, equivalently a continuous contraction. The sphere construction gives a strong deformation retraction, using derived C5s without Hatcher or closed-torus classification. For $j:|X|\hookrightarrow|A|$, jointly continuous $H:|A|\times[0,1]\to|A|$ satisfies

$$
H(x,0)=x,\qquad H(x,1)\in j(|X|),\qquad H(j(y),t)=j(y).
$$

The endpoint $r:|A|\to|X|$ is continuous in $|X|$'s own weak topology and $rj=\mathrm{id}$. With the project-derived $A$ instance,

$$
|A|\text{ contractible}\Longrightarrow|X|\text{ contractible}
\Longrightarrow|K'|\text{ contractible}\Longrightarrow|K|\text{ contractible}.
$$

The last two steps use $X\cong K'$ simplicially and a strong deformation retraction $K\to K'$.

## 2. Correspondence with the paper

Pages refer to the identified PDF; all surface results use the listed premises.

- **Theorem 1.1 (p. 2):** fixed-model conditional contractibility.
- **Definitions 2.3/2.5 (p. 5), §8 zero stage:** zero-intersection simultaneous realization, flagness and $Y_0=X$.
- **Theorems 1.4/4.11 (pp. 2, 17):** non-loop/nonseparating dictionary; $3\mid3$-circle/separating part excluded.
- **Proposition 6.1 (pp. 20–21):** `Topo.ClassicalCurveContractibility.proposition61_of_classical` gives bijection, both adjacency directions and simplicial equivalence from one compatible cover and derived HR.
- **Lemma 6.4 (p. 21):** separating independence from G/P/C/T and Baer-derived annulus isotopy.
- **Lemma 6.6 (pp. 21–22):** actual links are Farey $*$ Farey by derived L/N/S; Farey/join contractions proved.
- **Corollary 6.5, Proposition 6.7, Theorem 6.8 (pp. 21–22):** deletion, relative cone deformation and infinite gluing.
- **§9, Budget (pp. 27–31):** actual-stratum Budget via ribbon dictionaries, planarity and legality.
- **§10, Lemma 10.4 (pp. 31–34):** actual-link apices via C4d, Jordan patches/charts and localization.
- **§§8–11 (pp. 25–35):** replacement strong deformation retraction $A\to X$.
- **Fact 7.2 (p. 23):** finite discrete Hatcher surgery proves actual-$A$ contractibility, not the cited theorem itself.
- **Proposition 6.2/Lemma 8.5(4) (pp. 21, 25–26):** verified sharp size $12$, dimension $11$, X facets and $Y_{12}=A$.

Mathlib-only `Statements.lean` freezes independent deletion, joins, Farey contractibility, punctured-disc path classification and ribbon Budget; `Topo/StatementVerification.lean` proves the displayed statements with their premises.

## 3. Proof route and conventions

**Direct deformation.** In a face, a vertex is bad if it is a loop or shares its endpoint pair with another vertex. Write $\operatorname{bv}(\sigma)$ for these vertices; $Y_n$ allows at most $n$ per face. For positive n, actual Budget/Cone, layer/block identities and relative deformations retract $Y_n$ onto $Y_{n-1}$, fixing it. Finite composition gives $A\to Y_0=X$.

For a nonempty bad stratum, Budget gives disjoint free, clean gaps; $k(g)$ counts marks inside $g$, and $V'$ counts marks met by the stratum:

$$
1\leq k(g_1),k(g_2),\qquad k(g_1)+k(g_2)\leq6-V'\leq5.
$$

One gap has one or two marks and proved Jordan boundary geometry. Gluing gives joint continuity across infinitely many blocks; separating-vertex deletion gives $K\to K'$. This replaces the paper's §8 spectral sequence and final Hurewicz–Whitehead step; those arguments are not verified.

**Finite Hatcher surgery.** Fix an actual essential non-loop base arc $\beta$ with its interval witness. For any simplicial vertex map from a finite source complex into $A$, the minimal-position premise supplies representatives jointly minimal with $\beta$, disjoint on compatible pairs. Complexity sums minimal crossing ranks over source labels, counting repeated targets separately.

At positive complexity, a first crossing selects an essential raw branch. Classification by raw endpoints includes loop sources producing non-loop branches. Internal disk-side/push lemmas give a proper replacement avoiding relevant spectator carriers and marks, with variable width at shared endpoints. Square charts and an injection into retained physical crossings, omitting the first crossing, prove finite transversality and strict decrease. Proper homotopy plus arc/loop isotopy preserve essentiality.

Each affected old face together with the replacement remains a face. One-label replacement gives contiguous maps and jointly continuous barycentric homotopies. Natural-number descent gives a **finite chain** into the actual closed star of $\beta$, then its cone contraction. Every finite subcomplex inclusion into $|A|$ is nullhomotopic. The proved `Topo.Complex.contractible_of_finiteInclusionsNull` criterion extends maps skeletally to the simplicial cone and contracts the identity; the concrete base supplies nonemptiness, without an external Whitehead or CW premise.

This is **Hatcher's surgery flow in finite discrete form**, descending stepwise to a base-arc star, not the cited theorem or a continuous global flow. The three geometric specifications are internal, not final inputs. It proves exact-$A$ contractibility, including loops and its weak topology.

**Dimension and facets.** Each $A$ or $X$ face has at most $12$ vertices, attained by the octahedron's twelve edges. Thus $\dim A=\dim X=11$. X's facets are exactly isotopy classes of simple triangulations on all six marks, each of size $12$; $Y_{12}=A$. These use retained sphere inputs; not all A facets are classified. The contraction uses coarse bound $1920$ internally.

**Conventions.** Continuous embeddings, local topological crossings and jointly continuous ambient isotopies fixing sphere marks are used; comparison with smooth/tangent-line conventions remains external.

**Intersections** lie in `ℕ∞`: empty spectra give infinity; nonempty spectra attain natural minima. Proposition 6.1 handles zero/one-crossing pairs by coordinates/cover charts, without Theorem 5.5's distinct-non-loop formula $i(\widetilde a,\widetilde b)=2\widehat j(a,b)+e(a,b)$.

## 4. Classical inputs and their review

`docs/DEPENDENCIES.md` records sources/adaptations, `docs/PARAMETER-TYPES.md` definitions and `docs/REVIEWS.md` independent model reviews. Reviews provide neither Lean instances nor human expert certification.

**Sphere/disk inputs.** Graph topology, relative isotopy, point transport, general position, bigon criterion, Jordan–Schoenflies, proper disk-arc Schoenflies, `DiskArcStraightening`, `TwoStrandBraidGeneration` and finite simultaneous minimal position. C1e is proved without premises by `Topo.OpenEdgeFlatness.openEdgeLocalFlatness`.

**Derived interfaces.** `DiskAlexander` and `UnbranchedHomotopyLifting` are unconditional Lean theorems. `AnnulusIsotopy` is derived from retained `ClosedCurveBaer`; `DiskSchoenflies` and `BoundaryPreservation` from retained `JordanSchoenflies`. These three reduce independent premises; Baer and Jordan–Schoenflies stay assumed.

C4i fixes endpoints and keeps **every interior parameter off all six marks at every time**. `BasedLoopIsotopySplit` separates nullhomotopy-to-empty-disc from nonzero based-homotopy-to-isotopy (Epstein 1.7/4.1, A1 and compact-support extension). Loop legality uses no filling; mixed-endpoint isotopy retains spoke winding.

**C4d/HR.** Boundary-relative single-arc straightening and two-strand braid generation give C4d: a concrete half-twist power makes the comparison homeomorphism isotopic to identity while preserving its core. Core preservation and actual-disc transport are proved. Two interior marks suffice without homotopy. Paper Lemma 10.4 invokes 4.9; Epstein 3.1 has boundary endpoints, so does not alone give this conversion.

HR additionally uses `HalfTwistSquareNormalForm` and `NonzeroDehnTwistPowerRigidity`. Squaring equal or inverse half-twist classes identifies boundary circles; side transport and the two-versus-at-least-three mark count prevent side interchange. Core recovery proves Lemma 4.10(ii)'s arc step.

**Cover/coordinate/twist inputs.** Compatible cover, symmetry, coordinates, Birman–Hilden, zero/one-crossing pair coordinates, collar E, twist comparison TC and the two twist statements above. Homotopy lifting, branch extension and dictionary assembly are proved. Review judged the four disk/twist inputs valid. External adaptations concern planar arcs/outer boundaries, concrete braid generators, unit square exponent up to sign, collar signs/marked isotopy, charts and reversing mapping classes. A1 alone does not give the single-arc interface; mark exchange does not certify the square factor. **E has no directly matching theorem in its recorded sources; TC's nonorientable scope needs a local-annulus argument beyond Farb–Margalit.** These source/model qualifications add no final-theorem project obligations.

**Curve/subsurface inputs.** General position G, parity P, separating cuts C, torus dichotomy T, incompressible essentiality I and closed-surface bigon criterion/Baer; plus `InteriorGeneralPosition`, `InteriorBigonCriterion`, `InteriorCurveBaer`, `DisjointIsotopicAnnulus`, `AnnulusCircleClassification`, `ParallelCopy`.

**L/N.** Bigon confinement makes intrinsic minima ambiently minimal (N); nonperipherality and annulus classification confine the comparison annulus for same-side isotopy (L). Free homotopy and closed-surface Baer supply transport. Neither assumes the other. Both use polygon regularity from the cover, Jordan, closed-surface bigon/Baer and I. L uses six retained subsurface inputs; N uses the two general-position/bigon inputs. Both use the two Jordan-derived interfaces. All eight were reviewed true. External comparisons retain intrinsic-boundary source conversion, simultaneous tameness, class/homotopy identification and empty-bigon extraction. Boundary-contact Schoenflies needs planar containment; peripheral Baer needs Epstein 2.1's scope. Localization is proved.

**S: one-holed-torus slopes via a proved closed-torus bridge.** `ClosedTorusCurveBaer` and `ClosedTorusSlopes` in `Topo.CappedTorusBridge` concern only $(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$, without capping data. Baer identifies freely homotopic essential circles by ambient isotopy; slopes classifies unoriented essential isotopy classes by primitive integer vectors modulo sign, with absolute-determinant intersection formula in `ℕ∞`.

The project proves the capped polygon's standard-torus homeomorphism, bidirectional essentiality, punctured homotopy/retraction and class equivalence. Intersection equality follows by moving a transverse pair off the **entire closed filling disk**, then pulling back with transversality/counts preserved, including empty spectra. `Topo.CappedTorusBridge.torusSlopes_of_closedTorus` returns exactly S from Jordan, T, interior Baer, Jordan-derived boundary preservation, closed-torus Baer and a chosen closed classification.

Under Jordan, T and interior/closed-torus Baer, with derived boundary preservation, review checked `ClosedTorusSlopes ↔ Nonempty TorusSlopes`: source relocation does **not** reduce logical strength. Topological Baer uses Epstein (1966) 2.1+A1; Farb–Margalit 1.10–1.11 are smooth secondary references. Classification uses Farb–Margalit 1.4–1.5/§1.2.3 and Epstein 1.7. `CT-TopologicalDeterminantLowerBound` is unformalized, not a separately stated source theorem: local indices $\pm1$ sum to the determinant. Linear representatives give the upper bound; translation handles the diagonal. Review judged this valid. It belongs to the classical slopes interpretation, not an extra parameter/project obligation. Both closed-torus inputs lack Lean instances.

**C5s: proved controlled surgery.** `Topo.PLBigonSurgery.bigonSurgeryWithSpectators_of_classical` derives the exact interface from `JordanSchoenflies` and `ProperDiskArcSchoenflies`, using proved `DiskAlexander`, including moving loops, loop spectators, shared endpoints and half-bigons. The project constructs the disk/safe target, then realizes replacement by a mark-fixing ambient isotopy, identity outside the prescribed open set. Final crossings with original fixed curves are surviving old crossings, with finite transversality, strict decrease and same-point spectator injections. Spectators need not be pointwise fixed; crossing counts need not decrease throughout time.

`ProperDiskArcSchoenflies` extends exact parametrized correspondence between proper disk intervals with matching ordered boundary endpoints to a boundary-fixed homeomorphism. This standard relative Schoenflies consequence splits into two Jordan disks, extends specified boundary maps and glues (Epstein A1 supports the construction; 3.1 gives an isotopy alternative, not the interface verbatim). `DiskAlexander` proves the Farb–Margalit Lemma 2.1 interface (pp. 47–48), with time reversal and exact endpoint homeomorphism. Boundary fixation gives neither a fixed collar nor support-closure avoidance. Neither disk statement selects replacements or controls crossings; proper-arc Schoenflies has no unconditional Lean instance.

**Finite simultaneous minimal position.** `Topo.MarkedSphere.JointMinimalPosition.FiniteSimultaneousMinimalPosition` supplies representatives of any finite family of distinct unoriented proper-homotopy classes of homotopically essential embedded arcs, including based loops: pairwise finite-transverse and minimal against all finite-transverse competitors. Endpoints are fixed points, not germs; interiors avoid all marks during proper homotopy. Triple points are allowed. No surgery, rank or contraction is supplied.

It is a **standard extension**, not a verbatim theorem, of Farb–Margalit Theorem 1.2, Propositions 1.3/1.6, Corollary 1.9 and the finite-family paragraph (pp. 21–33), with the unproved arc remark in §1.2.7 (pp. 35–36). Review supports ideal ends by lift/linking minimality, simple geodesics, cusp-tail finiteness and chart/homeomorphism transport. The boundary-fixed half-bigon caveat does not apply to puncture endpoints. This premise lacks a Lean instance; existing isotopy inputs let the project fix the base literally and derive minimal ranks/compatible disjointness. Surgery/descent are proved internally.

## 5. Checks and reproduction

With the pinned toolchain and locked dependencies installed, reproduction is offline:

```sh
lake --no-cache build
python3 verification/verify.py
```

The verifier checks frozen hashes, Mathlib-only imports, forbidden shortcuts/kernel overrides, builds, types, parameters and axioms, including private/generated declarations and fresh trust-zero proof replay with zero skips. Negative fixtures must fail; benign controls must pass. The whitelist is exactly `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`; it certifies neither premise truth nor joint satisfiability. Failure exits nonzero.

Separate dependency scans cover constructor fields, inductive siblings and parameter-type closure, with hidden-premise fixtures/controls. They must exclude the five internally derived inputs, S/C5s, surgery specifications and $A$ contractibility as main inputs.

**Local verification: PASS** for the release tree: 11,571 project declarations, fresh trust-zero replay with zero skips. A clean copy rebuilt the project from an empty project cache, reusing installed dependencies rather than rebuilding Mathlib. The CI workflow runs the verifier and uploads its results.

## 6. Scope and AI disclosure

The compact, connected, Hausdorff octagon carries a complex analytic manifold structure under its conformal atlas, with positive real transition-derivative determinants (orientation). Its Mathlib finite CW structure has $1,4,1$ cells in dimensions $0,1,2$; Euler characteristic is $-2$. Contractibility transfers under the same 40 inputs plus a supplied space/topology and homeomorphism to the model. General closed orientable genus-two surface classification remains external.

Simultaneous realization proves **pairwise zero intersection**, also relative to fixed representatives. General finite pairwise minimal position is a reviewed classical premise; it is not independently proved in Lean, and does not assert triple-point-free representatives. Uncovered: full §§3–5 hyperbolic/geodesic theory, $3\mid3$ correspondence and §5 formula; §7 all-genus Theorem 1.3; §8 relative chains, spectral sequence, convergence and homology argument. Only the reviewed classical inputs are premises. The entire paper is not verified.

**AI disclosure.** GPT-6.1 Sol wrote the Lean code in OpenAI Codex under human direction. GPT-6 Astra and Claude planned the route; Claude independently checked the stages, including rebuilds, statements and axioms. Fresh GPT and Claude contexts reviewed the inputs; GPT and Claude adversarially audited the release package; Claude checked this text against it. GPT-6.1 Sol drafted this submission; Claude reviewed and edited the final text. No human expert has certified the work.

18.title: A complete Lean 4 formalization of the full paper
18.body_md:
# Convex Nivat formalization

A Lean 4 formalization of *The Convex Nivat Conjecture: A Complexity Lower Bound
for Star Configurations, and a Reduction from Low Convex Complexity to Star
Configurations* (Apex Intelligence, 12 September 2026).

Start with [MainTheorem.lean](MainTheorem.lean), the single public entry point.
The headline theorem is **`ConvexNivat.convexNivat`**, Theorem B / 8.18.

## Main theorem

Let `ξ : ℤ² → A` be a configuration over any finite alphabet. If some nonempty
finite lattice-convex set `S` satisfies

**Pξ(S) ≤ |S|,**

then `ξ` has a nonzero global period: there is `v ≠ 0` such that
`ξ(z + v) = ξ(z)` for every lattice point `z`.
Here `Pξ(S)` counts all patterns occurring on translates of `S`, and
lattice-convex means that `S` contains exactly the lattice points of its real
convex hull. Periodicity means one nonzero period, not necessarily two
independent periods.

The declaration and its rectangular corollary are in
[OriginalMain.lean](convex-nivat/Reduction/ConvexNivat/OriginalMain.lean).
For an `n × k` rectangle with `n,k ≥ 1`, the condition is `Pξ(n,k) ≤ nk`.

```lean
import MainTheorem

#check ConvexNivat.convexNivat
#check ConvexNivat.nivatRectangles
```

## Supporting mathematics

The development retains the paper's 49 precise original results in sections
0–8 and Appendix D. [The result index](docs/PAPER_RESULTS.md) maps the source
headings to their Lean declarations. Introductory aliases, definitions and
supporting helper lemmas are counted separately from those results.

- **Star configurations:** Theorem A / 7.3, `ConvexNivat.theoremT`, proves
  `Pθ(S) ≥ |S| + 1` for every nonempty finite lattice-convex window of a star
  configuration. See [the proof](convex-nivat/Star/ConvexNivat/MainTheorem.lean).
- **Algebra and spectrum:** Laurent difference operators, annihilators,
  exceptional spectra, Newton polygons and affine dimension bounds.
- **Geometry and dynamics:** lattice convexity, zonotopes, sectors, orbit
  closures, nonexpansive directions and periodicity propagation.
- **Two periodic components:** Appendix D's finite-field convex theorem and
  its finite-range abelian-group version are retained. Appendix D supplies
  a result used in Proposition 8.14.

The final convex-Nivat proof uses the independently verified `NivatTrial`
provider through [ExternalNivatAdapters.lean](convex-nivat/Reduction/ExternalNivatAdapters.lean).
The star proof and intermediate paper statements are also retained. In
particular, the exact 8.7 minimal-counterexample contract is discharged using
the provider's full theorem. This is an alternative proof route; the repository
does not claim to reconstruct Colle's original geometric proof.

## Source layout

All mathematical code is collected under [convex-nivat/](convex-nivat/),
with subdirectories grouped by mathematical subject. Lake preserves the existing Lean
module names through the source-directory configuration, so declaration and
import identities remain stable.

| Directory | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| [Foundations/](convex-nivat/Foundations/) | Configurations, finite patterns, lattice and period definitions. |
| [Algebra/](convex-nivat/Algebra/) | Laurent actions, finite differences, annihilators and decomposition. |
| [Spectral/](convex-nivat/Spectral/) | Fourier spectra, cyclotomic arguments, polynomial quotients and dimension bounds. |
| [Geometry/](convex-nivat/Geometry/) | Lattice convexity, zonotopes and polygon geometry. |
| [Star/](convex-nivat/Star/) | Star configurations, sector arguments, observables and Theorem A. |
| [Dynamics/](convex-nivat/Dynamics/) | Orbit closures, nonexpansive directions, periodicity propagation and two-component results. |
| [Reduction/](convex-nivat/Reduction/) | Paper reduction interfaces, external-provider adapter and the main theorem. |
| [vendor/nivat-trial/](convex-nivat/vendor/nivat-trial/) | Pinned independent convex-Nivat proof provider. |

The release omits 150 modules outside the retained source-result import
closure, including unused Colle reconstruction routes and experimental
scaffolds. The 447 retained original modules keep their complete source text.
No helper inside a retained module was deleted merely because a text search
found no reference: attributes, instances and proof automation can use such
helpers implicitly. `lake build` reaches every retained mathematical module.

## Build and verification

Install [elan](https://github.com/leanprover/elan) and Git, then run:

```sh
git clone git@github.com:EonMath/convex-nivat.git
cd convex-nivat
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake env lean tools/Verify.lean
```

The toolchain is pinned to **Lean 4.35.0-rc3**, and Mathlib to revision
`3f6737de4761ec7bf368491fe9faccc991ebd6ca`. The committed Lake manifest fixes
transitive package revisions. All dependencies are obtained from their pinned
repositories; no original workspace, absolute local source path or prebuilt
project artifact is required.

The release was built from source on 6 October 2026: all 448 mathematical
modules passed, using cached Mathlib dependencies and freshly compiling every
project and vendored module. The build took about 15 minutes on the development
machine; smaller CI runners can take longer. The 9,110 project declarations,
including private and generated declarations, passed the axiom audit. All 765
retained historical statement guards passed. The complete kernel types and
proof values of the main theorem, rectangular corollary and star theorem match
the accepted pre-cleanup versions. Remaining diagnostics are inherited linter
warnings, not proof holes.

`MainTheorem` is the default Lake target. The verification tool checks the
transitive axioms of project and vendored declarations. The accepted base is
`propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`; cited results are proved, not
left as additional mathematical axioms. GitHub Actions runs the same build and
verification commands.

## Source issues

[SOURCE_ISSUES.md](SOURCE_ISSUES.md) records one confirmed invalid inference
in Appendix C.3: nonvanishing for one operator factor does not prove
nonvanishing for the full product. The general nonextension assertion in
Remark 3.1′ has a separately proved witness, retained in this repository.

Appendix B's seven announcements omit exact statements and are expressly
outside the proof chain. Appendix C's original experiment scripts and outputs
were not supplied to this development, so those exact runs are not claimed
as reproduced. These limitations do not supply assumptions or outstanding
proof obligations for the main theorem. Historical translation defects are
listed separately from manuscript findings.

## References and attribution

The supplied manuscript is identified by SHA-256
`7fd67831155f4226c010fd6af32de558b76643771e6be12dea4eebafa21745a8`.
The PDF is not required for compilation.

[THIRD_PARTY.md](THIRD_PARTY.md) records the exact revisions and distinct
license status of the reused `Nivat` and `NivatTrial` sources. The latter's
shipped files and hashes are listed in
[EXTERNAL_NIVAT_PROVENANCE.json](EXTERNAL_NIVAT_PROVENANCE.json).
Lean and Mathlib retain their upstream licenses.

To cite this formalization, refer to
[EonMath/convex-nivat](https://github.com/EonMath/convex-nivat), specifying the
commit used.

5.title: Validation of the reduction to star configurations in the convex Nivat paper
5.excerpt_md: This note validates Section 8 and Appendix D of Apex Intelligence, *The Convex Nivat Conjecture: A Complexity Lower Bound for Star Configura…
5.body_md:
This note validates Section 8 and Appendix D of Apex Intelligence, *The Convex Nivat Conjecture: A Complexity Lower Bound for Star Configurations, and a Reduction from Low Convex Complexity to Star Configurations*, taking Theorem A (Theorem 7.3) as an input. It does not revalidate Sections 0–7, improve the lower bound, or certify the entire paper.

Source: [official PDF](https://math.apexin.net/papers/convex-nivat.pdf), published 2026-09-12, SHA-256 `7fd67831155f4226c010fd6af32de558b76643771e6be12dea4eebafa21745a8`. Text version: **v1.0**. Page references are printed pages of this PDF unless an external source is named. No executable certificate or hosted repository is needed.

## 1. The verified implication

For $\xi:\mathbb Z^2\to A$ with $A$ finite, write $X_\xi$ for its translation-orbit closure and $P_\xi(S)$ for its finite-window pattern count. Periodic means having a nonzero integer period; doubly periodic means having two independent periods.

Assume a counterexample exists. Among counterexamples encoded injectively into positive integers, choose $\xi$ of minimal integer periodic-decomposition order (Remark 8.3, p.20). Fix its nonempty finite lattice-convex window $S$ with $P_\xi(S)\leq|S|$. The verified output is a prime $p>\max A$ and a nonperiodic $\vartheta\in X_\xi$, read in $\mathbb F_p$, satisfying

$$
P_\vartheta(S)\leq P_\xi(S)\leq |S|,
\qquad \vartheta=\sum_{i=1}^m G_i,\quad m\geq2,
$$

Here the $G_i$ have pairwise nonparallel nonzero periods, none is doubly periodic, and each has two disjoint doubly periodic half-plane tails. This is Theorem 8.1 (p.19); Lemma 8.17 (pp.27–28) gives the star conditions (S1)–(S3). Theorem A supplies $P_\vartheta(S)\geq|S|+1$, yielding Theorem 8.18 (p.28).

The chosen counterexample need not retain an initial example's window. A point window forces constancy. For a segment of $n$ consecutive sites in primitive direction $v$, each $v$-line has at most $n$ length-$n$ words and period at most $n$: with $P(0)=1$, some $r<n$ has $P(r+1)=P(r)$, giving a constant sequence if $r=0$, otherwise a word graph of cycles of length at most $n$. Thus $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,n)v$ fixes every line. Regional extraction is consequently needed only for two-dimensional windows.

## 2. External dependency contracts and version limits

Checked sources: Kari–Szabados, *An Algebraic Geometric Approach to Nivat's Conjecture*, [arXiv:1605.05929v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.05929v1), manuscript dated 20 May 2016; Colle, *On periodic decompositions, one-sided nonexpansive directions and Nivat's conjecture*, [arXiv:1909.08195v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08195v4), 13 April 2022. The required conclusions were matched to these saved preprints. The Nivat paper cites 2020 and 2023 journal versions; their numbering and version changes were not directly verified. Links identify versions; no online lookup was made.

| Conclusion needed here | Assumptions in the checked source | Actual output and checked location |
|---|---|---|
| Integer annihilator: Theorem 8.4(a), p.20 | Kari–Szabados: finite-valued integer configuration, nonempty finite low-complexity window | Lemma 5, pp.5–6: a complex annihilator. Its finite integer linear system has a nonzero rational solution; clearing denominators gives an integer annihilator. No convexity needed. |
| Distinct-direction binomial product: Theorem 8.4(b), p.20 | Kari–Szabados: finite-valued integer configuration, nontrivial annihilator | Theorem 11 and Corollary 12, p.10: the required product. |
| Specified-period decomposition: Remark 8.3, Lemma 8.5, pp.20–21 | Integer configuration killed by a specified binomial product in distinct directions | Kari–Szabados, Lemmas 14–15 and proof of Theorem 13, pp.10–12: integer components with the exact periods, possibly unbounded; also Colle, Theorem 1.10(ii), p.5. |
| Both orientations one-sided nonexpansive: Theorem 8.6, p.21 | Colle: finite integer alphabet, nontrivial annihilator; each line has an orientation outside the one-sided nonexpansive set | Theorem 1.14, p.5: full periodicity; take the contrapositive. No equal-order premise. The Nivat citation is [2, Theorem 1.9]. |
| Nonperiodic closure point with two regional periods: Theorem 8.7, p.21 | Colle, Section 4.1: low convex complexity, minimal integer decomposition, equal order for nonperiodic closure points, and a line nonexpansive in both orientations | Proof of Lemma 4.5, pp.21–26: Case 1 uses a translate of the original configuration; Case 2 separately proves nonperiodicity in Claim 4.14. Both supply the region and two periods. The Nivat citation is [2, Lemma 4.6]. |
| Regional-period convention: Theorem 8.7, p.21 | Colle: lattice-convex region, two nonparallel unbounded edges with parallel periods, equality on overlaps | Orient the periods along the outward rays. Closed convexity gives $R+h\subseteq R$, making the overlap identities valid everywhere on $R$. |
| Row periodicity: Lemma D.7, p.35 | Bi-infinite finite-alphabet sequence with at most $n$ length-$n$ words | Morse–Hedlund, also Colle, Theorem 1.1, p.2: periodicity; accepted as a classical input. |

Fixed periods and integrality follow from Kari–Szabados' construction: Lemma 14 solves an inverse recurrence on each two-direction lattice coset; Lemma 15 successively removes prescribed factors. For $X^h-1$, the extreme coefficients $\pm1$ preserve integer values in both directions. No boundedness of the components is required.

Put $m=\operatorname{ord}(\xi)$. Its minimal decomposition has distinct directions because parallel terms merge. The product annihilator passes to every $\xi'\in X_\xi$ by locality, giving $\operatorname{ord}(\xi')\leq m$. A nonperiodic $\xi'$ is itself a low-complexity counterexample, so minimality gives the reverse inequality. This supplies Colle's equal-order premise; no minimality modulo $p$ is required.

For the regional-definition conversion, let $C$ be the closed convex region and suppose $x_0+sh\in C$ for every $s\geq0$. For any $x\in C$ and $t\geq0$,

$$
(1-t/s)x+(t/s)(x_0+sh)\in C\quad(s>t),
$$

The limit gives $x+th\in C$ for both outward periods. Both source cases supply global nonperiodicity separately from regional periodicity. Their output extraction was checked; the external papers and their earlier dependencies were not re-certified in full.

## 3. Global extension and the first half-plane

Lemma 8.2 (pp.19–20) extends regional full periodicity globally. For independent inward periods $a,b$ on a lattice-convex $R$, $g=a+b$ lies inside its recession cone $K_R$. Every $z$ satisfies $z+Ng\in R$ for large $N$. Set $\widetilde G(z)=G(z+Ng)$; forward periodicity makes this well-defined with both periods. On strict or weak half-planes, including irrational boundaries, use the positive inner product of $g$ with the normal instead.

In Lemma 8.8 (pp.21–22), let $G$ have period $kv$, where $v$ is primitive, and choose a lattice basis $(v,u)$. Write each differencing vector as $H_j=\alpha_jv+\beta_ju$ with $\beta_j\ne0$, and set

$$
\beta_- =\sum_{\beta_j<0}\beta_j,\quad
\beta_+ =\sum_{\beta_j>0}\beta_j,\quad L=\beta_+-\beta_-\geq1.
$$

Rows lie in $\mathbb F_p^k$. Each extreme row shift in $\prod_j(T^{H_j}-1)G$ comes from a unique subset, with coefficient an invertible signed horizontal shift, even in characteristic two. Vanishing for $t\geq c$ determines both adjacent rows from $L$ consecutive rows. The forward map on actually occurring states for $t\geq c$ is injective, hence a finite permutation, giving a transverse period from $t=c+\beta_-$ onwards. Global vanishing gives double periodicity. Backward determinacy is essential to periodicity from the stated threshold.

For Proposition 8.9 (pp.22–23), extend $\vartheta|R$ to $\widetilde\vartheta$ and choose $N_0\mathbb Z^2\subseteq\operatorname{Per}(\widetilde\vartheta)$. Put $H_j=N_0h_j$ and

$$
Q_i=\prod_{j\ne i}(T^{H_j}-1),\qquad D_i=Q_i\vartheta_i=Q_i\vartheta.
$$

Let $E_i$ be the subset sums of the product. Then $D_i=0$ where $z+E_i\subseteq R$. This eroded region contains $(y_0+K_R)\cap\mathbb Z^2$: push $y_0$ along $g$ to accommodate all shifts. Periodicity by $h_i=k_iv_i$ propagates zero along every discrete $h_i$-orbit meeting it.

If $\mathbb Rv_i$ meets the cone interior, every orbit enters it; $D_i=0$ globally and Lemma 8.8 gives double periodicity. Otherwise separation gives $K_R\subseteq\{\sigma_i\pi_i\geq0\}$, where $\pi_i=\det(v_i,\cdot)$ and $\sigma_i=\pm1$. Rays $g\pm\varepsilon v_i$ provide parallel slice segments growing linearly with positive height. Length at least $|h_i|$ meets every orbit $z+\mathbb Zh_i$ on the slice, including all nonprimitive residues. Thus $D_i$ vanishes on a half-plane; Lemma 8.8 gives the first periodic tail.

Corollary 8.10 (p.23) absorbs all doubly periodic components into one remaining term, enlarging its tangential period. At least two non-doubly-periodic terms remain, or the total would be periodic. The altered term remains non-doubly-periodic by subtraction of its background; its tail is still doubly periodic. Reapply Proposition 8.9 to this decomposition: the same cone is a sector of angle strictly between zero and $\pi$, with no component direction inside.

## 4. Appendix D: the independent two-component input

Theorem D.1 (statement p.33; proof p.36) gives a nonzero period of $\theta=\theta_1+\theta_2$ over $\mathbb F_p$ when its components have independent periods and $P_\theta(S)\leq|S|$ for nonempty finite lattice-convex $S$. It requires neither minimal decomposition nor double periodicity and uses neither the second-tail theorem nor Theorem A.

Write $h_1=c_1u$ with $u$ primitive, put $\pi=\det(u,\cdot)$, and orient $h_2$ so that $\Delta=\pi(h_2)>0$. The basic identity is

$$
\theta(z+sh_2)-\theta(z)=\theta_1(z+sh_2)-\theta_1(z),
$$

whose right side is $h_1$-periodic. Equality under $sh_2$ on $F$ therefore extends to $F+\mathbb Zh_1$. A strip $\operatorname{St}[a,b]$ has width $b-a$ and contains $b-a+1$ integer rows.

In D.3 (p.33), period $qu$ on a strip of width at least $\Delta$ gives $qh_1$ there. The difference $\psi=(T^{qh_1}-1)\theta$ has period $h_2$. For $m=\lfloor(\pi(z)-a)/\Delta\rfloor$, $z-mh_2$ lies in the strip; thus $\psi=0$ globally, including all nonprimitive phases.

Lemma D.5 (p.34) repeatedly deletes the shorter extreme row until the set is empty. The first transition from $P(D)-|D|\leq0$ to a positive value produces a balanced set $B$ with extreme row $E$ of size $n$ and

$$
P_\theta(B)\leq|B|,\qquad P_\theta(B)-P_\theta(B\setminus E)<n.
$$

For $n=1$, the row lower bound $n-1$ permits empty rows. Single-row $B$ is immediate. Otherwise both extreme chords have length at least $(n-1)|u|$; convexity gives this at every intermediate height, yielding at least $n-1$ lattice sites per integer row without presupposing nonemptiness.

For D.7 (pp.34–36), orient $E$ upwards and set $B_0=B\setminus E$. The pattern increment gives rightward and leftward rules using $0\leq k,k'<n$ top sites and the bottom pattern. Place $B$ in an ambiguity strip with $E$ on its top row; its witness $x\in X_\theta$ agrees below and differs on top. Agreement on a forward seed propagates right, then left, contradicting ambiguity. Let $\Gamma$ be bottom patterns along $iu$ translations, pulled back to $B_0$. Each has two extensions; hence $1\leq|\Gamma|\leq n-1$, excluding $n=1$.

Morse–Hedlund gives a common period $Qu$ on the finite bottom strip: each row has at most $n-1$ length-$n-1$ words. For single-row $B$, start with the empty strip and $Q=1$. When adding a row $y_i$, the bottom pattern depends on $i\bmod Q$. Keep the state

$$
\sigma_i=(i\bmod Q;y_i,\ldots,y_{i+K-1}),\qquad K=\max(k,k',1).
$$

Apply the forward rule at $i+K-k$ to obtain $y_{i+K}$; the backward rule gives $y_{i-1}$. Both adjacent states, including phase, are determined. The finite state set is permuted with period $Q'$ divisible by $Q$. Add rows until width $\Delta$ is reached, then use D.3. Zero-length seeds and an empty initial strip are covered.

Finally assume $\theta$ nonperiodic and enlarge $h_2$ so $\Delta\geq\operatorname{ht}(S)+1$. In the chosen orientation define

$$
D=\{\alpha h_1+\beta h_2:0\leq\alpha,\beta<1\}\cap\mathbb Z^2,
\qquad N=P_\theta(D)\geq1.
$$

Taking coordinate floors in $(h_1,h_2)$ gives $D+jh_2+\mathbb Zh_1=\operatorname{St}[j\Delta,(j+1)\Delta-1]$, retaining every nonprimitive residue. Reverse $D,N$ too if the balanced direction is reversed. The contrapositive of D.7 propagates agreement from a strip of width at least $\operatorname{ht}(B)-1$ upwards.

Choose a witness $z_0$ to the failure of the nonzero period $N!h_2$ *before* applying pigeonhole, and put $a=\lfloor\pi(z_0)/\Delta\rfloor-N$. Among the $N+1$ patterns on $D+(a+j)h_2$, some pair $0\leq j<j'\leq N$ agrees. With $s=j'-j$, the basic identity and upward uniqueness give

$$
\theta(z+sh_2)=\theta(z)\quad\text{for }\pi(z)\geq(a+j)\Delta.
$$

The fixed $z_0$ lies in this half-plane, all positive iterations stay there, and $s\mid N!$. Iterating $N!/s$ times contradicts the witness, including $N=1$. No global period was inferred from the half-plane identity alone. Corollary D.2 (p.33) follows since order two excludes periodicity and parallel terms merge. Remark D.9's abelian-group observation (p.36) is not a new claim here.

## 5. Two-component limits and the second half-plane

Orient the first tails as $U_j=\{\pi_j\geq t_j\}$. Each step chooses $N$ divisible by all $k_j$, with $N\mathbb Z^2$ in all known background period lattices. Thus $d\in N\mathbb Z^2$ parallel to $h_c=k_cv_c$ fixes $G_c$; if it points strictly into a known tail of $G_j$, then $T^{nd}G_j$ eventually equals that fixed background at each site.

For Proposition 8.14 (pp.24–25), choose $d$ fixing $c$, with $\pi_b(d)<0$, safe for every other component. Each subsequential limit of $T^{nd}G_b$ produces a total limit

$$
\Xi=(G_c+B)+G_b^\infty\in X_\vartheta\subseteq X_\xi,
\qquad P_\Xi(S)\leq P_\vartheta(S)\leq|S|,
$$

Here $B$ is doubly periodic, and membership in $X_\vartheta$ justifies the complexity comparison. The summands have independent periods, so D.1 gives a nonzero period $d_0$ of $\Xi$.

If $d_0$ is parallel to neither direction, $(T^{d_0}-1)(G_c+B)=-(T^{d_0}-1)G_b^\infty$ has both component periods. Lemma 8.13 (p.24) makes $G_c$ doubly periodic, a contradiction. If $d_0\parallel h_b$, a common multiple cancels the second summand with the same result. If $d_0\parallel h_c$, cancellation of the first gives $G_b^\infty$ a second independent period. Lemma 8.13 uses $(T^{pMd_0}-1)G=p(T^{Md_0}-1)G=0$ when $Md_0$ fixes the periodic difference. Characteristic $p$ acts on values; the integer displacement $pMd_0$ is nonzero.

For Lemma 8.15 (p.25), the unfinished indices define a cone containing $K_R$. With at least two indices its angle is less than $\pi$. From one boundary ray take the first component ray beyond it; another boundary's opposite ray guarantees a turn less than $\pi$. This fixes its own component, points out of the selected side, and stays inside all other unfinished sides except its own. Finished components have both tails. With one unfinished index, sign any other component direction into its missing side. These signs supply all safety conditions.

For Lemma 8.16 (pp.25–27), assume every subsequential limit of $T^{nd}G$ is doubly periodic, as supplied by 8.14. Let $G$ have period $kv$, $k\geq1$, $\det(v,u)=1$, $\pi=\det(v,\cdot)$, and $\delta=-\pi(d)>0$. Its limit set

$$
\Omega=\bigcap_{M\geq1}\overline{\{T^{nd}G:n\geq M\}}
$$

is nonempty, compact, invariant under $T^{\pm d}$, and consists of doubly periodic fields sharing $kv$. Finiteness requires a further argument.

The least positive transverse period height $\operatorname{Tr}(y)$, if bounded by $P$, permits only finitely many fields: reduce a period to $sv+tu$, $0\leq s<k$, $1\leq t\leq P$, and record $kt$ values. If $\Omega$ is infinite, choose $y_n\to\theta$ with $\operatorname{Tr}(y_n)\to\infty$ and a transverse period $\varpi$ of $\theta$. By $kv$-periodicity, box agreement becomes entire-row agreement: $y_n$ has a growing interval of $\varpi$-good rows, but not all rows are good.

Bad rows repeat at a positive transverse period of $y_n$, so both ends of its maximal good interval are finite. Move the lower end by $T^{qd}$ into rows $0,\ldots,\delta-1$. Reduce the adjacent bad site's horizontal coordinate by multiples of $kv$. It now lies in a fixed finite set. A subsequence preserves one fixed defect in a limit $y\in\Omega$ satisfying the $\varpi$ relation on a positive half-plane. Double periodicity of $y$ moves that defect into the good half-plane, a contradiction. Thus $\Omega$ is finite.

Choose their common period $N'u$ and $W\geq\max(k,N'+\delta)$. Compactness implies that each sufficiently late $T^{nd}G$ agrees with some $y^{(n)}\in\Omega$ on rows $[-W,W]$. Successive choices satisfy $y^{(n+1)}=T^dy^{(n)}$ on at least $N'$ consecutive rows, hence globally by their common period. Undoing translations gives agreement with the single field $T^{-n_0d}y^{(n_0)}$ on $[-n\delta-W,-n\delta+W]$ for all $n\geq n_0$. These intervals cover a negative half-plane.

The proof of Theorem 8.12 (p.27) now adds one opposite tail, shrunk if necessary to $V_b=\{\pi_b\leq\min(\beta,t_b-1)\}$ so that it misses $U_b$. Rechoose $N$ to include the new background and repeat. Each step removes one unfinished index, so the induction terminates.

## 6. Normalisation, closure, and review boundary

In Lemma 8.17, $h$ must be tangent to a fully periodic half-plane of a non-doubly-periodic component. Otherwise orient $h$ inward. The extension's $h$-difference is doubly periodic and zero on the half-plane, hence everywhere. Moving every site inward by $h$ then identifies the component with its doubly periodic extension, a contradiction. Its disjoint tails therefore have thresholds $\pi<\ell$, $\pi>r$, with $\ell\leq r+1$.

Absorb doubly periodic components using common tangential periods. Merge parallel terms using period common multiples and tails $\pi<\min\ell_i$, $\pi>\max r_i$. If merging creates a doubly periodic term, absorb it. Each operation preserves the sum and disjoint tails while shortening the decomposition. One remaining term would make the total periodic. Termination therefore gives at least two distinct-direction, non-doubly-periodic terms satisfying the star conditions.

Orbit closure cannot increase complexity; injective reduction of the alphabet modulo $p$ preserves patterns and nonperiodicity despite unbounded integer summands. Normalisation preserves the total, completing the reduction to Theorem A and the rectangular case (Corollary 8.19, p.28). Dependencies are acyclic: Morse–Hedlund and D.3/D.5/D.7 give D.1; D.1 feeds 8.14; 8.15–8.16 give second tails; normalisation feeds Theorem A. The forward reference to 8.17's alignment uses only 8.2.

No reproducible obstruction materially affecting this chain was found. Closure membership, nonprimitive residues, recurrence indices and tail phases are made explicit under existing hypotheses. Theorem A, the remaining paper, full external proofs and journal versions remain outside this certification. No stronger bound, priority, award eligibility, finite-sample proof or formal verification is claimed.

OpenAI Codex used an author context and four fresh read-only GPT contexts in the first-stage audit. This stage uses an author context, two fresh GPT contexts for the reduction and Appendix D/source contracts, and a further fresh context for adversarial manuscript review. These are separate contexts, not distinct model families or human endorsements. Claude (Opus 5.5) coordinated the work and set its scope, but did not independently re-derive this reduction; the mathematical checks reported here were made by separate GPT contexts.

7.title: Complementary complexity bounds for Case B star configurations: convex sections and all quadratic positions
7.excerpt_md: We give complementary bounds for Case B stars in Apex Intelligence's convex Nivat paper (CN, 12 September 2026). The main estimate extends K…
7.body_md:
We give complementary bounds for Case B stars in Apex Intelligence's convex Nivat paper (CN, 12 September 2026). The main estimate extends Kari–Szabados (KS) counting to lattice-convex windows in KS's existing configuration class, broader than Case B. The second strengthens CN's quadratic count on arbitrary finite windows. Their maximum weakly dominates Theorem T, strictly on explicit infinite families.

Manuscript v1.1; [repository](https://github.com/iamwangxi/apex-p03-nivat-complementary-bounds), tag `v1.0`. [CN](https://math.apexin.net/papers/convex-nivat.pdf): locally hashed version. KS numbers: *An Algebraic Geometric Approach to Nivat's Conjecture*, [arXiv:1605.05929v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.05929v1).

## 1. A section-count theorem

Use $(T^u c)(z)=c(z+u)$ and $R=\mathbb C[T_1^{\pm1},T_2^{\pm1}]$. Reverse exponents when transferring KS series identities. $P_c(S)$ counts distinct functions $s\mapsto c(u+s)$ over all $u\in\mathbb Z^2$.

Fix a finite-valued integer configuration $c$ with no nonzero period and with $\operatorname{Ann}(c)\ne(0)$. KS Corollary 24 gives
$$
\operatorname{Ann}(c)=\varphi\mathcal H,\qquad
\varphi=\prod_{j=1}^r\varphi_j,\qquad r\ge2,
$$
where the line polynomials have pairwise distinct directions, $\mathcal H$ is an intersection of finitely many maximal ideals (possibly $R$), and $(\varphi)+\mathcal H=R$. Each direction includes its entire grouped line factor. Fix a nonzero $f\in\operatorname{Ann}(c)$ minimal under divisibility: no proper nonunit divisor of $f$ annihilates $c$.

For direction $i$, choose a primitive $v=v_i$ and normalize its grouped factor, up to a Laurent unit, as
$$
\varphi_i=A_i(T^v),\qquad A_i(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{d_i}a_jt^j,
\quad d_i\ge1,\quad a_0a_{d_i}\ne0.
$$
Put $g_i=f/\varphi_i$, $\pi_v(z)=\det(v,z)$, and
$$
w_i=\max_{s\in\operatorname{supp}\varphi}\pi_v(s)
-\min_{s\in\operatorname{supp}\varphi}\pi_v(s)>0.
$$
For every nonempty finite lattice-convex $S=\operatorname{Conv}(S)\cap\mathbb Z^2$, define
$$
E_i=\{z\in\mathbb Z^2:z+\operatorname{supp}g_i\subseteq S\},\qquad
K_i=\#\{t\in\mathbb Z:|E_i\cap\pi_v^{-1}(t)|\ge d_i\},
$$
$$
\ell_i=\max_{a\in\mathbb Z}\min_{a\le t<a+w_i}|S\cap\pi_v^{-1}(t)|,
\qquad \varepsilon_i=\mathbf1[A_i(1)=0].
$$
Empty sections have length zero. Empty erosions, $K_i=0$, $\ell_i=0$, points and segments are allowed. The claim is
$$
\boxed{P_c(S)\ge (K_i+\varepsilon_i)(\ell_i+1).}\tag{SC}
$$
Maximize valid bounds; do not add them.

**Filtered ideal.** Write $f=\varphi h$, $h\in\mathcal H$. If an irreducible factor $p$ of $\varphi$ divided $h$, comaximality would make $p$ invertible modulo $\mathcal H$, hence $h/p\in\mathcal H$. Then $f/p$ would annihilate $c$, contradicting minimality. Thus $\gcd(h,\varphi)=1$. For $c_i=g_i(T)c$, if $qc_i=0$, then $qg_i\in\varphi\mathcal H$ and $\varphi\mid qg_i$. Canceling $\varphi/\varphi_i$ and using coprimality gives $\varphi_i\mid q$. Conversely $\varphi_i c_i=fc=0$, so
$$
\operatorname{Ann}(c_i)=(\varphi_i).
$$
Minimality is essential (KS Lemma 38).

**Disjoint pattern lines.** With $C=\operatorname{Conv}(S)$,
$E_i=(\bigcap_{s\in\operatorname{supp}g_i}(C-s))\cap\mathbb Z^2$ is lattice-convex. Each $v$-section consists of consecutive lattice points. In each of its $K_i$ sections of length at least $d_i$, select $d_i$ consecutive points, obtaining $D_i$ with $|D_i|=d_iK_i$.

No nonzero multiple of $\varphi_i$ can have support in $D_i$: grouping by transverse layer, every nonzero one-variable section of a multiple of $A_i$ has exponent span at least $d_i$, whereas a selected section has span $d_i-1$. Reflections needed in KS's convention preserve this fact. The orthogonality argument of KS Lemma 32 therefore gives full rank $d_iK_i$ for the $D_i$-patterns of $c_i$.

Each pattern line $\{c_i|_{u+kv+D_i}:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ obeys recurrence $A_i$ and spans dimension at most $d_i$. A selected pattern supplies $d_i$ consecutive values per section; nonzero end coefficients determine all previous and next values. Sharing one pattern therefore forces identical pattern lines. Distinct lines are disjoint; full rank requires at least $K_i$.

Because $D_i+\operatorname{supp}g_i\subseteq S$, original patterns determine filtered patterns equivariantly under $v$-translation. Choosing one original line above each disjoint filtered line gives disjoint original lines.

**The conditional extra line.** If $q(T)c_i$ is constant, both $(T^{e_1}-1)q$ and $(T^{e_2}-1)q$ belong to $(\varphi_i)$. The two coordinate binomials are coprime. Comparing irreducible multiplicities gives $\varphi_i\mid q$, so the constant is zero. Thus $c_i$ is normalized. The same orthogonality argument gives rank $d_iK_i+1$ for augmented vectors $(1,c_i|_{u+D_i})$. If $A_i(1)=0$, their constant coordinate satisfies the same recurrence, and a line still spans dimension at most $d_i$. At least $\lceil(d_iK_i+1)/d_i\rceil=K_i+1$ disjoint lines are required. If $A_i(1)\ne0$, retain only $K_i$. For $K_i=0$, one original line exists if $\varepsilon_i=1$; otherwise the bound is zero.

**Patterns per original line.** The primitive $v$ makes $\pi_v$ surjective onto $\mathbb Z$. A stripe consisting of $w_i$ consecutive transverse layers has extreme-layer span $w_i-1$ and cannot contain a translate of $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$; a stripe with one more layer can. It is a maximal-width stripe of KS Lemma 39, so every translate of it is nonperiodic along $v$.

Choose layers attaining $\ell_i$. For every anchor $u$, the translated stripe has a nonperiodic fiber: periodic words on finitely many fibers would have a common period. Its intersection with $u+S$ has at least $\ell_i$ consecutive points. Translation through $kv$ reads all length-$\ell_i$ words; Morse–Hedlund gives $\ell_i+1$ patterns per original line. For $\ell_i=0$, nonemptiness suffices. Multiply by the disjoint-line count to prove (SC).

This modifies KS Lemmas 38 and 40 using Corollary 24 and Lemmas 32 and 39. Actual convex sections replace the rectangular size estimates; their original statements retain their size conditions.

## 2. The Case B interface

A CN star is $\theta=\sum_{i=1}^mF_i:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb F_p$, $p$ prime, $m\ge2$, with pairwise nonparallel primitive $v_i$. Each $F_i$ has period $k_iv_i$, $k_i\ge1$, is not doubly periodic, and has possibly unequal doubly periodic tails outside a finite-width strip. Backgrounds can be absorbed into a component. Choose $H_i=\kappa_iv_i$, $\kappa_i\ge1$, preserving its component and all tails (CN Section 0.3); set $D=\prod_i(T^{H_i}-1)$. Case B is $D\mathbf1[\theta=a]=0$ for every color in characteristic zero; only the component sum is mod $p$.

Stars are aperiodic independently of T. The isolating limit along $nH_i$ is $\Xi_i^+=F_i+B_i^+$, with doubly periodic $B_i^+$ and period $H_i$ (CN Section 2.1). A nonzero period $u$ of $\theta$ passes to the limit. Choose $v_i\not\parallel u$: the limit, hence $F_i$, would be doubly periodic, a contradiction.

An integer injection gives $c=w(\theta)$ finite-valued and aperiodic, $Dc=\sum_aw(a)D\mathbf1[\theta=a]=0$, preserving patterns. All Case B stars enter (SC), including unequal tails, higher periods and backgrounds.

To identify KS's $\varphi$ with CN's exceptional-spectrum polynomial, fix instead the *same spectrum-preserving* injection of CN Lemma 2.2, put $\eta=w(\theta)$, and define
$$
A=\prod_i\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda_i}(T^{v_i}-\lambda),\qquad
Z=\operatorname{Newt}(A)=\sum_i[0,|\Lambda_i|v_i].
$$
We accept CN Lemma 2.4 (every polynomial sending $\eta$ to a constant is divisible by $A$) and Proposition 3.3 ($b_\eta=A\eta$ is doubly periodic) as upstream inputs. Here is the parameter bridge, not a replacement of CN's structure proof. Every annihilator is divisible by $A$. The common polynomial divisor of the KS ideal $\varphi\mathcal H$ is $\varphi$, since a finite-point ideal has no common nonunit polynomial factor; hence $A\mid\varphi$. For two independent periods $u,w$ of $b_\eta$, both $A(T^u-1)$ and $A(T^w-1)$ annihilate $\eta$. Their binomial factors are coprime, so $\varphi\mid A$. Consequently, up to a unit,
$$
\varphi=A,\qquad\operatorname{Ann}(\eta)=A\operatorname{Ann}(b_\eta).
$$
The second identity follows by dividing each annihilator by $A$. When $b_\eta\ne0$, generally $f=A$ is not an annihilator: choose a valid minimal $f=Ah$ and compute $E_i$ from its actual $g_i$. Unit shifts translate erosion. Arbitrary injection alone does not justify $\varphi=A$.

## 3. Fixed convex shapes and strict infinite families

Fix the configuration, minimal filter $f$, and positive-area lattice polygon $P$ before letting $n\to\infty$. Set $S_n=nP\cap\mathbb Z^2$. In a basis $(v,u)$ with $\det(v,u)=1$, define
$$
W_v(P)=\max_P\pi_v-\min_P\pi_v,\qquad
L_v(P)=\max_t\operatorname{length}\{s:sv+tu\in P\}.
$$
Length is measured in $v$-lattice steps. Fixed-filter erosion removes only a bounded-width boundary layer. Except for boundedly many layers at the projection ends, its sections have at least $d_i$ lattice points; hence $K_i(S_n)=nW_v(P)+O(1)$. Polygonal section lengths are piecewise linear. One can select $w_i$ consecutive layers near a longest chord, from the interior even if that chord is on a boundary; their lengths differ from the maximum by $O(1)$. Integer rounding also costs $O(1)$, so $\ell_i(S_n)=nL_v(P)+O(1)$. Therefore
$$
P_c(S_n)\ge n^2\max_i W_{v_i}(P)L_{v_i}(P)-O(n).
$$
The constants depend on the fixed configuration, filter and shape. The area identity in these determinant-one coordinates gives $\operatorname{area}(P)\le W_v(P)L_v(P)$. Equality requires constant section length in the interior: convexity of the left endpoint and concavity of the right endpoint then force both to be affine, giving a parallelogram with sides parallel to $v$.

For any fixed triangle, the section-length graph has integral $WL/2$, including directions parallel to a side. Thus
$$
P_c(nP\cap\mathbb Z^2)\ge2|nP\cap\mathbb Z^2|-O(n).
$$
The error cannot be dropped for finite triangles. Three or more directions guarantee a strict area-coefficient gain for every fixed polygon; with two, only parallelograms along both directions can lack it. This does not imply finite-window equality.

For an explicit fixed configuration, reuse
$$
c(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^2\mathbf1[y-2ix=i],\qquad v_i=(1,2i).
$$
Intersections have $x=-1/2$, so $c\in\{0,1\}$ encodes its mod-2 Case B star, with zero tails. A finite operator produces finitely many parallel lines per direction; evaluating far from other directions isolates each coefficient. Each component must separately be annihilated, so $\operatorname{Ann}(c)=(A)$, $A=D=\prod_i(T^{v_i}-1)$ and $f=\varphi=A$.

For $S_n=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2:x+y\le n\}$, $n=5r\ge20$, use $v_2=(1,4)$. Then $d_2=\varepsilon_2=1$, $w_2=6$, $E_2=S_{n-4}$, and $K_2=|S_{n-4}|-|S_{n-9}|=5n-25$. The section at $y-4x=t$ has length
$$
\max\left(0,\left\lfloor\frac{n-t}{5}\right\rfloor
-\max\left(0,\left\lceil-\frac t4\right\rceil\right)+1\right).
$$
Only $t=0$ can have length $r+1$; layers $0,\ldots,5$ have minimum $r$. Thus $\ell_2=r$ and (SC) gives $n^2+n/5-24$. The all-position bound below is $(n^2+17n-52)/2$, while T gives $(n+1)(n+2)/2+1$. The section bound exceeds both for every $n=5r\ge20$: its difference from the all-position bound is $(n^2-83n/5+4)/2>0$. The configuration and shape do not change with $n$.

## 4. All legal quadratic positions

Fix the Case B star, spectrum-preserving $w$, $\eta,D,A,Z$ above. Accept CN Lemmas 1.1 and 4.2 as supplying a genuine displacement $d$ with
$$
J_d(z)=D_z[\eta(z)\eta(z+d)]\not\equiv0
$$
of finite support. Fix the witness with the same configuration and operators. Convex comparison uses CN Proposition 5.3 and Corollary 6.2: $d=q_1-q_0$, $q_0,q_1\in Z\cap\mathbb Z^2$. Case B implies $J_0=D\eta^2=0$, so $d\ne0$.

For any nonempty finite $S$, with full pattern set $\mathcal L_S$, put
$$
U_S=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{1,\gamma\mapsto w(\gamma(s)):s\in S\},
$$
$$
R_Z(S)=\{r\in\mathbb Z^2:r+Z\subseteq\operatorname{Conv}(S)\},\qquad
T_d(S)=\{s\in S:s+d\in S\}.
$$
Since $0\in Z$, erosion is finite. For any such $S$,
$$
\boxed{P_\theta(S)\ge\dim_{\mathbb Q}U_S+|T_d(S)|
\ge |S|+1-|R_Z(S)|+|T_d(S)|=:B_{\rm quad}(S).}\tag{Q}
$$

**Affine budget.** Relations $\sum_{s\in S}c_s\eta(u+s)=c_0$ for every anchor are the kernel of a finite integer matrix, one row per distinct pattern. Extending scalars from $\mathbb Q$ to $\mathbb C$ preserves its rank. A nonzero relation gives nonzero $F=\sum c_sT^s$ (otherwise also $c_0=0$), and CN Lemma 2.4 gives unique $F=Ag$. Newton additivity yields
$$
Z+\operatorname{Newt}(g)=\operatorname{Newt}(F)\subseteq\operatorname{Conv}(S).
$$
Thus $\operatorname{supp}g\subseteq R_Z(S)$. Mapping a relation to $g$ is injective, since $F$ determines $c_0$. The relation space has dimension at most $|R_Z(S)|$, whence $\dim U_S\ge |S|+1-|R_Z(S)|$. Convexity was unused (CN Lemma 2.5).

**Quadratic independence.** Each $s\in T_d(S)$ defines a legitimate function $\Psi_s(\gamma)=w(\gamma(s))w(\gamma(s+d))$. If a nontrivial rational combination belonged to $U_S$, writing $h(z)=\eta(z)\eta(z+d)$ and evaluating on all anchors would give
$$
\sum_{s\in T_d(S)}a_sh(u+s)=b_0+\sum_{t\in S}b_t\eta(u+t).
$$
Applying $D$ in $u$ annihilates the right side and gives $F(T)J_d=0$ with nonzero $F=\sum a_sT^s$. For $\widehat J_d(X)=\sum_zJ_d(z)X^{-z}$ this becomes $F(X)\widehat J_d(X)=0$, impossible in the Laurent integral domain. Consequently the quadratic functions are independent modulo $U_S$, and their enlarged space has dimension $\dim U_S+|T_d(S)|\le|\mathcal L_S|$. This extends CN Lemma 7.2 from $R_Z(S)+q_0$ to all legal starts; empty $T_d$ is allowed.

For lattice-convex $S$ and the localized witness, $R_Z(S)+q_0\subseteq T_d(S)$, so $B_{\rm quad}\ge|S|+1$, strictly when $|T_d|>|R_Z|$. With $Z$ two-dimensional, points and segments have empty erosion; a singleton gives at least two patterns. For nonconvex $S$, $|T_d(S)|\ge|R_Z(S)|$ is a configuration-dependent sufficient condition for the same bound; its failure is inconclusive.

For rectangles $R_{a,b}=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$, write $W,H$ for the coordinate widths of $Z$ and $\alpha=|d_x|,\beta=|d_y|$. Then
$$
|R_Z(R_{a,b})|=(a-W)_+(b-H)_+,\quad
|T_d(R_{a,b})|=(a-\alpha)_+(b-\beta)_+.
$$
Here $x_+=\max(x,0)$. For the fixed three-line example $W=3,H=6,\alpha=\beta=1$, giving $P_c(R_{a,b})\ge ab+5a+2b-16$ for $a\ge4,b\ge7$. Under proportional dilation this improvement is of boundary order.

If $S=S_0\setminus H_0$ has the same convex hull, its erosion is unchanged and precisely the legal edges with at least one endpoint in $H_0$ are lost. At most $2|H_0|$ are lost. Hence $2|H_0|\le |T_d(S_0)|-|R_Z(S_0)|$ suffices for $P_\theta(S)\ge|S|+1$. This hole criterion is conditional, not a general nonconvex Nivat theorem.

## 5. Joint comparison, exact evidence and limitations

For Case B and a convex window, with each term satisfying its own premises,
$$
P_\theta(S)\ge\max\left\{|S|+1,B_{\rm quad}(S),
\max_{i,f}(K_i(S)+\varepsilon_i)(\ell_i(S)+1)\right\}.
$$
The baseline is redundant for a localized witness. Directions, filters, witnesses and methods cannot be summed. Case A retains CN Proposition 1.3's existing $|S|+1$ bound for all nonempty finite windows; Case B arguments do not automatically apply. This Case A result is not new here.

For the same three-line configuration, the portable evidence gives:

| Window | Theorem T | All-position bound | Section bound | Actual patterns |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $R_{6,9}$ | 55 | 86 | 60 | 347 |
| $S_{30}$ | 497 | 679 | 882 | 7037 |

On $S_{30}$, $(K_i,w_i,\ell_i)$ are $(23,6,26),(72,4,10),(125,6,6)$, giving 648, 803, 882. Also $|R_Z|=253$, $|T_d|=435$. The reconstructed 12-point witness includes $J_{(1,1)}(-5,-9)=1$. Since $Ac=0$, all affine relations are exactly $Aq$ with support of $q$ in $R_Z$; convexity gives the converse. Hence affine rank is $497-253=244$, and extended rank $244+435=679$ by (Q). This is analytic rank plus geometry, not a 679-order numerical minor; 882 is a theorem bound, not rank or actual complexity.

Global enumeration uses $Q_i=\{y-2ix:(x,y)\in S\}$ and $t_i=i-Y+2iX$. Zero hits give zero. Every single-hit section is realized by moving along $v_i$ while avoiding finitely many forbidden intersections. Multiple hits are exhausted by pairs $t_i\in Q_i,t_j\in Q_j$:
$$
X=\frac{t_j-t_i-(j-i)}{2(j-i)},\qquad Y=i+2iX-t_i.
$$
Retain integer anchors and evaluate all pixels. On $S_{30}$ this gives 6795 distinct multiple-hit anchors and 7062 representatives, deduplicating to 7037 patterns, without finite-box sampling. Their fingerprint is `c68c8a66cce70a8dd0cc9b3b4ed3ceee0ed057cc121c30a01e1c23b13f563646` (lexicographic window order, first point at low bit, sorted integers, 62-byte little-endian blocks).

Reused certificates certify reconstructed matrices by integer minors and rational right kernels. On $R_{6,9}\setminus\{(2,4)\}$ the general bound is **83**, actual affine rank 46 plus 38 quadratic columns gives **84**; T does not apply. Reconstruction/tampering tests cover higher degrees, $\varepsilon=0$, missing layers, periodic background, empty erosion, points and segments. Stress cases test only general SC nonzero-background handling; the Case B parameter bridge is proved above. Tests support implementation, not the general proof.

On this same configuration, KS Lemmas 38 and 40(b), direction $(1,2)$, already give $(3n-12)\lceil(n+1)/2\rceil$ on $R_{n,n}$ for $n\ge12$. At $n=30$: KS 1248, (Q) 1094, (SC) 1296. Existing KS gains are area-order. We claim no comprehensive superiority over previous methods or their optimizations.

Strictness has two obstacles. Fix $k\ge2$: the disjoint supports $L_1=\{(2kt,t)\}$ and $L_2=\{(k+2kt,-t)\}$ give a fixed mod-2 Case B star. Nonzero columns have spacing $k$ and one point each. Every $R_{k,N}$ contains at most one point; every singleton and zero pattern occurs. Hence $P(R_{k,N})=kN+1$ for all $N\ge1$, infinitely many two-dimensional windows. Changing $k$ to produce large square equalities changes the configuration.

Separately fix $c(x,y)=\mathbf1[y=0,x\equiv0\pmod2]+\mathbf1[x=1,y\equiv0\pmod2]$, a Case B star with disjoint supports and tangential periods 2. For $M,N\ge5$, both supports are identifiable: both visible give $MN$ patterns, only horizontal $2N$, only vertical $2M$, and neither one. Thus $P_c(R_{M,N})=MN+2M+2N+1$, with square area coefficient 1. This prevents a universal proportional improvement for fixed Case B stars, consistent with the two-direction parallelogram exception.

## 6. Attribution, scope and AI assistance

(SC) extends KS counting to convex shapes; (Q) strengthens CN Lemmas 2.5 and 7.2. Configuration and prior certificates are reused. The two estimates serve one complexity improvement; no organizer approval or prize eligibility is asserted.

Search records (30 September 2026) found no exact-form antecedent in checked queries/passages. No new search was done here. Priority is unverified; equivalent optimized estimates may exist. Rank/stripe methods and rectangular area-order gains are established.

No optimality, general nonconvex Nivat result or higher periodicity threshold is claimed. A single-point defect already has $P(S)=|S|+1$ without periodicity. CN's structure proof is not replaced, nor its Section 8 reduction revalidated or extended. Its divisibility and witness localization are explicit inputs.

Codex/GPT assisted derivations, searches, certificates, this proof and its evidence/checker. Claude coordinated scope, without independently rederiving the mathematics. A fresh gpt-6.1-sol context completed adversarial review with no mathematical blockers: `对抗复核-v1.0.md`, bound to v1.0 SHA-256 `3bd81a166c53f8a073ad893eeaef24fe05b83468023151b3b550db385d9fd52c`. v1.1 changes wording only; formulas and proof sections 1–4 are unchanged.

8.title: A scalar bridge replacing the spectral and background modules of the convex Nivat star proof
8.body_md:
## 1. Claim and scope

Category: 突破贡献（显著简化证明） — Breakthrough contribution (significant proof simplification).

Accepting Kari–Szabados (KS) Corollary 24(a), we replace the exceptional-spectrum construction, spectrum-preserving encoding choice and color-background gluing in Case B of Apex Intelligence's convex Nivat paper (CN, 12 September 2026). Three scalar interfaces suffice for the retained quadratic-witness mechanism and the same star-complexity conclusion. Any integer injection is allowed. This is a modular simplification using a known structure theorem, with a substantive external dependency; we claim no more elementary or fully self-contained proof, no new numerical bound, and no revalidation of Section 8.

Use $R=\mathbb C[T_1^{\pm1},T_2^{\pm1}]$ and $T^uc(z)=c(z+u)$. A CN star is $\theta=\sum_iF_i:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb F_p$, with $m\ge2$, pairwise nonparallel primitive $v_i$, and $\pi_i(z)=\det(v_i,z)$. Each $F_i$ has period $k_iv_i$ ($k_i\ge1$), is not doubly periodic, and equals doubly periodic $L_i,R_i$ on $\pi_i<\ell_i$, respectively $\pi_i>r_i$, with $\ell_i\le r_i+1$. Keep the original $H_i=\kappa_iv_i$, preserving $F_i$ and every tail, and
$$
D=\prod_i(T^{H_i}-1),\qquad Q_i=\prod_{j\ne i}(T^{H_j}-1).
$$
Only the component sum is mod $p$. Retain CN Lemmas 1.1–1.2: local functions have finite-support $D$-differences, and nonzero Laurent operators cannot annihilate nonzero finite-support fields. Case A is CN Proposition 1.3. Case B requires
$$
DI_a=0\ (a\in\mathbb F_p),\qquad I_a=\mathbf1[\theta=a].
$$
Any injection $w:\mathbb F_p\to\mathbb Z$ gives $\eta=w(\theta)$ and $D\eta=D\eta^2=0$ by color-indicator linearity, not by additivity of $w$.

## 2. The external input

KS Theorem 21 applies to finite-valued integer configurations with a nonzero annihilator. Corollary 24(a) gives
$$
\operatorname{Ann}_R(\eta)=\varphi\mathcal H,\qquad (\varphi)+\mathcal H=R,
$$
with grouped line factors in distinct directions and a finite intersection $\mathcal H$ of maximal ideals, allowing $\mathcal H=R$. Theorem 21 gives root-of-unity binomial factors. We do not use Corollary 24(b) or its configuration decomposition. Here $D\ne0$ and $D\eta=0$ supply applicability without a low-complexity hypothesis.

KS uses an ordinary polynomial ideal and configuration-series multiplication. Localize at coordinate monomials, then reverse exponents $X^u\mapsto T^{-u}$. This is exactly our Laurent ideal: a Laurent annihilator becomes ordinary after multiplication by a monomial, whose action is invertible. The finite-point part remains a finite intersection of Laurent maximal ideals. Normalize $\varphi$ up to a Laurent unit.

## 3. The scalar bridge

**Proposition.** In Case B, for every integer injection, normalize the KS line part as
$$
\varphi=\prod_{i=1}^m A_i'(T^{v_i}),\qquad
A_i'\mid t^{\kappa_i}-1,\qquad
1\le d_i':=\deg A_i'\le\kappa_i,
$$
with $A_i'$ monic. Its roots are distinct and nonzero. The three interfaces are:

1. Every star direction occurs, and $Z':=\operatorname{Newt}(\varphi)=\sum_i[0,d_i'v_i]$ is a two-dimensional lattice zonotope.
2. For every $f\in R$, $f(T)\eta$ constant implies $\varphi\mid f$.
3. $b:=\varphi(T)\eta$ is doubly periodic and satisfies $T^{H_i}b=b$ for every original $H_i$.

We do not identify $\varphi$ with CN's exceptional-spectrum polynomial $A$, or reconstruct its full color-vector background.

### 3.1. A nonzero strip in every direction

This is a direct reproof of CN Lemma 4.1, used earlier. For fixed $i$, as $n\to+\infty$, $T^{nH_i}\theta$ stabilizes on every finite set to
$$
\Xi_i=F_i+B_i,\qquad B_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\epsilon_j,
\qquad
\epsilon_j=\begin{cases}R_j,&\pi_j(H_i)>0,\\L_j,&\pi_j(H_i)<0.\end{cases}
$$
Indeed $\pi_j(H_i)\ne0$ for $j\ne i$, and $H_i$ preserves all tails. This eventual stabilization survives any pointwise encoding. Put $G_i^R=R_i+B_i$, $G_i^L=L_i+B_i$ and $\delta_i^{R/L}=w(\Xi_i)-w(G_i^{R/L})$.

Since $(T^{H_i}-1)Q_i\eta=0$, $f_i:=Q_i\eta$ is $H_i$-periodic. Taking the finite-window limit in $f_i=T^{nH_i}f_i$ gives
$$
f_i=Q_iw(\Xi_i)=Q_i\delta_i^R=Q_i\delta_i^L.
$$
Every factor of $Q_i$ kills each encoded $G_i^{R/L}$, and $Q_i$ has at least one factor. The right difference vanishes for $\pi_i>r_i$, the left difference for $\pi_i<\ell_i$. Finitely many shifts therefore confine $f_i$ to a strip of bounded width in direction $v_i$.

Injectivity and the non-double-periodicity of $F_i$ imply $\delta_i^R\ne0$: otherwise $F_i=R_i$. Its nonzero integer layers have a maximum $t_*$. Choose $z_*$ in that layer with $\delta_i^R(z_*)\ne0$. In the formal expansion
$$
Q_i=\sum_{C\subseteq[m]\setminus\{i\}}(-1)^{m-1-|C|}T^{H_C},\qquad H_C=\sum_{j\in C}H_j,
$$
the unique minimum of $\pi_i(H_C)$ is attained by $C_*:=\{j\ne i:\pi_i(H_j)<0\}$. Every other subset strictly increases this projection. Evaluating $Q_i\delta_i^R$ at $z_*-H_{C_*}$ leaves only $\pm\delta_i^R(z_*)$, so $f_i\ne0$. Coincidences of other subset sums cannot cancel this unique extreme term. No spectral projection or pure-tail orbit-closure argument was used.

### 3.2. Finite codimension gives double periodicity

First observe
$$
\operatorname{Ann}_R(b)=\mathcal H:
\quad hb=0\iff h\varphi\in\varphi\mathcal H\iff h\in\mathcal H.
$$
Cancellation is in the integral domain. Although $\varphi$ may have complex coefficients, $b$ is finite-valued: it is a fixed linear combination of finitely many values of $\eta$.

We prove the needed finite-codimension fact directly. If a finite-valued configuration $c$ is annihilated by an ideal of finite codimension, its translation span
$$
V=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{T^uc:u\in\mathbb Z^2\}
$$
is finite-dimensional, being an image of the corresponding ring quotient. Point evaluations separate functions in $V$, so finitely many evaluations give an injective map $V\to\mathbb C^r$. All translates of $c$ take at those points values in the same finite alphabet, so there are only finitely many translates. Repetition along each coordinate axis, and invertibility of translations, give two independent coordinate periods.

A finite intersection of distinct Laurent maximal ideals has finite codimension by CRT; each residue field is $\mathbb C$. Apply the preceding fact to $b$. If $\mathcal H=R$, then $b=0$ and the conclusion is immediate. Thus no configuration decomposition from KS Corollary 24(b) is required.

### 3.3. Recovering invariance under the original periods

Double periodicity alone is insufficient. Choose an actual sector $K$ of $\mathbb R^2\setminus\bigcup_i\mathbb Rv_i$, and let $\Theta_K$ be the sum of the tails selected by its signs of $\pi_i$. This field is doubly periodic and preserved by every $H_i$.

Take a narrower open cone $K'$ whose closed angular interval lies inside $K$. Put $\delta=\min_{i,u\in\overline{K'}\cap S^1}|\pi_i(u)|>0$, where $S^1$ is the unit circle, and choose $M>0$ with
$$
\delta M>\max_i\left(\max(|\ell_i|,|r_i|)+\max_{s\in\operatorname{supp}\varphi}|\pi_i(s)|\right).
$$
For every lattice point $z\in K'$ with $\|z\|>M$, all $z+s$, $s\in\operatorname{supp}\varphi$, lie in the selected tail half-plane for every component. Consequently
$$
b(z)=\varphi(T)w(\Theta_K)(z)=:b_K(z)
$$
